Discovery & Design · UX & Design Collaboration

Shravasti Labs: The Renderer and the Renewal

The engineering decision that won a thousand kiosks is the reason a blind pass-holder cannot renew her own pass.

1. Sunday night, Pune

At twenty past eleven on Sunday 11 October 2026, Debarati Kanjilal sat at her dining table in Baner, Pune, with her father's phone in front of her. He was seventy-one, a pass-holder since 1979, and in June he had asked her to renew it for him: the screen "went small and then went away". His font scale was at maximum; on that setting the renewal screen of the app her own team shipped lost two fields below the fold and its continue button behind the keyboard.

By Monday evening she owed the board sub-committee of Shravasti Labs Private Limited a one-page recommendation; the call was set for 7:30 pm India time — 4:00 pm in Berlin, 10:00 am in Toronto and New Jersey, 10:00 pm in Singapore. The Nagpur-region re-bid, worth ₹9.20 crore a year and ₹46 crore over five years, closes on Friday 30 October, and now demanded a third-party audit no older than twelve months and a signed self-declaration. Shravasti's audit, dated 7 August 2026, said the rider app failed 31 of the 44 applicable WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA success criteria.

Beside it lay three cost estimates for fixing that, differing by a factor of 2.3, which she had realised were not estimates of the same thing. And her chief executive had written, in the pre-read she had just annotated, that 57 per cent of the order book carried an accessibility obligation (Exhibit 3) — a figure she could reconcile with her own only by excluding a contract she thought belonged inside it.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Shravasti Labs was founded in Pune in 2018 by Dipankar Khaund and two classmates to do one unglamorous thing well: collect bus fares. Its platform spans a rider app, a conductor handheld that replaced paper ticket machines, a pass-issuance kiosk, and a backend reconciling cash, UPI and National Common Mobility Card taps to the operator's ledger. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it booked revenue of ₹49.60 crore and EBITDA of ₹4.10 crore, a margin of 8.3 per cent, on a headcount of 206 of whom 62 were engineers.

The decision that shaped everything came in 2023. A four-city consortium tendered for 900 kiosks on hardware it specified itself: a ₹14,000 Android box, one gigabyte of memory, mounted outdoors, refreshed no sooner than seven years. Dhiman Khataniar, then a senior engineer in Pune, proposed drawing the whole interface as one custom-rendered surface — a single canvas, every control painted by Shravasti's own layout engine — so that it behaved identically on the cheap box, the handheld and a ₹6,000 rider phone. It worked: Shravasti won the order in June 2023, the base grew to 1,240 kiosks by 2026, and the renderer became the platform's core — one code path, three surfaces, an economy competitors shipping native screens could not match.

A custom-drawn surface, however, publishes no structure to the operating system: no buttons for a screen reader to find, no labels, no focus order — only pixels. With TalkBack enabled the rider app announces its name and then, on most screens, nothing. Nobody called this a defect until 2026, because nobody inside the company had run the app with a screen reader.

3. The industry

Indian urban mobility software sits between two buyers: the public transport undertaking, procuring under rules that reward the lowest responsive bid, and the rider, who no longer cares which app issues the ticket — Chalo and Tummoc taught riders to expect live tracking and in-app passes, Paytm and PhonePe put metro QR tickets in wallets people already have, and ONDC's Beckn-based rails make it plausible to buy a bus ticket from an app that is not the operator's. NPCI's NCMC card is the instrument every tender asks for.

Regulation arrives from three directions. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 obliges service providers to make services accessible and underpins India's ICT accessibility standards; the Bureau of Indian Standards' IS 17802 is increasingly cited in tenders alongside the WCAG guidelines, and complaints go to the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the disability certificates riders upload for concessional passes. In the European Union, Directive (EU) 2019/882 has applied since 28 June 2025 to new consumer services including e-commerce and elements of passenger transport, with EN 301 549 as the reference standard; terminals in lawful use before that date may run for up to twenty years, so an incumbent's installed base is grandfathered and a new entrant's is not.

Shravasti's exposure is not only Indian. Its Dubai customer, Siyaha Mobility DMCC, a tourist travel-pass operator, has contracted for an Arabic right-to-left interface and WCAG 2.1 AA with liquidated damages; the three European prospects Devarsh Khanikar works through partners all ask for a conformance report Shravasti has never produced.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The clause that started this was not an accessibility initiative. In April 2026 the Nagpur-region undertaking, rebuilding its tender on a model envelope circulated for urban transport procurement, inherited a conformance paragraph. Durjoy Kirtania gave the question to a graduate trainee, who ran an open-source rule engine across the web pass portal on Tuesday 12 May 2026 and reported that 2,861 of 3,144 rule instances passed (91.0 per cent). For the nine weeks until the manual audit began on 14 July, the company believed it was substantially compliant.

The scan's own output said more than its headline number. It covered the web portal, not the app, the kiosk or the handheld — which is to say, not the renderer. Its rules mapped to 23 of the 50 Level A and AA success criteria in WCAG 2.1, so a clean run was silent about the other 27. And its unit was the rule instance, not the criterion: one unlabelled control on forty screens is a single criterion failure and forty small blemishes.

In July, pressed by Deblina Kundu, Debarati commissioned a manual audit from Suhrid Access Labs in Hyderabad across all three surfaces, delivered on Friday 7 August 2026 (Exhibit 1). A panel study with 24 assistive-technology users followed in Nagpur and Pune (Exhibit 2). On Thursday 3 September the undertaking forwarded a rider's complaint about a concessional pass she could not renew, copied to the Chief Commissioner's office, and asked for a remediation plan. Nothing has been adjudicated. But the complaint now sits in the file with the re-bid, and the undertaking's general manager has twice asked whether the declaration Shravasti signs on 30 October will be consistent with the audit attached to it.

5. The people

  • Debarati Kanjilal, VP Product. Owns the recommendation; thinks the audit directionally right and the cost debate unanswerable on what she has. Not saying: her father's pass, and that she twice deferred the renderer question after Deblina raised it in 2024.
  • Dipankar Khaund, co-founder and CEO. Wants the Nagpur bid filed and the metro renewal protected; drawn to the fixed price. Not saying: he signed the Siyaha damages clause without engineering review, and the board does not know the Arabic interface is late for the reason the screen reader is silent.
  • Durjoy Kirtania, VP Engineering. Argues for rebuilding the app's screens in native views: 46 person-months, his own plan. Not saying: he knew the May scan covered only the portal, and a system rebuild reads as a verdict on his last three years.
  • Dhiman Khataniar, staff engineer, author of the renderer. Insists a virtual view hierarchy can be bolted on in nine person-months, and has a branch covering two screens. Not saying: the branch breaks on the firmware 680 of the 1,240 kiosks run, and he has an offer from a Bengaluru fintech.
  • Deblina Kundu, principal designer, Berlin. Wants one component library across all three surfaces, right-to-left and accessibility designed in: 59 person-months. Not saying: her estimate assumes a designer nobody has budgeted, and her evidence is the auditor's; she has never run a task with a screen reader.
  • Dhrubo Kakoti, data scientist, Toronto. Holds that the company cannot choose with the data it has. Not saying: he found the telemetry gap in June and left it in a backlog ticket.
  • Damanjeet Kotoky, customer success, Singapore. Wants the narrow fix; the eastern-India extension and eleven small-operator renewals are hers. Not saying: she has told Siyaha's programme office that January is safe.
  • Devarsh Khanikar, sales head, New Jersey. Wants a conformance report before his European prospects' February gate. Not saying: he answered two of three procurement packs with "available on request".

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

Durjoy Kirtania, email, Tuesday 12 May 2026, 18:40 IST

"Portal scan is back — 91 per cent clean. Whatever is left is cosmetic. I'd put this to bed before the envelope closes."

Audit debrief, Suhrid Access Labs, Hyderabad, 7 August 2026

"Be careful with your 31 failures. The app does not fail in 31 places. It is invisible to the screen reader in one place, and sixteen of those failures are that one place, counted against each criterion it defeats. Whether that is cheap or expensive news is your question."

Participant P07, 54, concessional pass-holder, Nagpur, 18 August 2026

"Nine years I have had the same conductor on the 3B. He knows my stop. I don't need the app to be clever. I need the renewal to not need my son."

Deblina Kundu to Debarati, chat, Thursday 3 September, 09:12 Berlin / 12:42 IST

"We are about to pay twice. The Arabic layout is blocked on the same renderer, and Durjoy rebuilds screens without rebuilding what draws them. Patch the app now and we do the kiosk again in 2028, and the terminals we sell into Europe will not be grandfathered as the incumbents' are."

Dhrubo Kakoti to the working group, Saturday 10 October, 09:10 IST (23:40 Friday, Toronto)

"Two corrections. The deck's 33 per cent divides 32 completions by 96 attempts, but four were never made; over the 92 that happened it is 34.8 per cent, which changes nothing. The second does: our 0.40 per cent cannot count anyone who could not get past sign-in, and nine of the panel's eleven screen-reader users could not. That number is not small, it is uninformative."

Damanjeet Kotoky to Debarati, Sunday 11 October, 22:00 Singapore / 19:30 IST

"I have told Siyaha's programme office January. Please do not make me un-tell them in Diwali week."

8. The options as Debarati currently sees them

A. Declare and defer. Attach the August audit with a self-declaration of partial conformance and a dated roadmap; spend nothing before April. Dipankar's instinct, and the cheapest. It puts a signed representation into a public procurement file, where a materially false declaration can mean debarment, and the complaint in that file names the flow the audit calls worst.

B. Fix the blockers. The Hyderabad vendor's 14 person-months at a fixed ₹88 lakh for the twenty worst findings on the rider app. Those months sit outside the 70 free to 31 March; after B's own 6 internal months, NCMC-v2's 24 and Arabic's 11, 29 are spare. It touches neither kiosk nor handheld, and if 16 of the 31 app failures share one cause, nobody knows whether twenty findings is twenty fixes or three.

C. Rebuild the surface. Durjoy's 46 person-months and ₹147.50 lakh (Exhibit 4). With NCMC-v2 at 24 and Arabic at 11, that is 81 against 70 — eleven short before anything slips.

D. Rebuild the system. Deblina's 59 person-months and ₹200.00 lakh, Arabic included, which with NCMC-v2 is 83 against 70 — thirteen short, and NCMC-v2 is what the ₹14.60 crore metro renewal was sold on. Against FY2026 EBITDA of ₹4.10 crore, her plan is 48.78 per cent and Durjoy's, which excludes Arabic, 35.98 per cent.

Devarsh has sized the European opportunity on Exhibit 5's 0.40 per cent. Nobody has costed the 12.0 per cent of sessions running above 130% font scale, a setting at which the renewal screen may fail, though the threshold was never tested.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

On the eastern-India contract, 1,74,460 of 2,86,000 pass renewals last quarter (61.0 per cent) were made at a counter; the app flow is optional there.

The Nagpur envelope closes on Friday 30 October and requires an audit no older than twelve months; the only one Shravasti has documents 31 failures. Siyaha goes live on 15 January 2027 with damages of ₹3.55 lakh a week to a cap of ₹53.25 lakh. The metro renewal falls on 31 March 2027 and was sold on NCMC-v2. Free capacity to 31 March is 70 person-months; 680 of the 1,240 kiosks run firmware on which Dhiman's branch fails, and the hardware refresh is contractually no earlier than 2030. Nothing in FY2027 is budgeted, and the sub-committee has asked for a recommendation, not options.

At a quarter past midnight she picked up her father's phone again and started the renewal with TalkBack on, holding it to her ear as the panel participants had. The app said its name. Then nothing, for eleven seconds, while her thumb moved across a screen that was, as far as the phone was concerned, a photograph. She put it down, opened the board template, and typed a heading she did not believe: Recommendation.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each column of Exhibit 1 measure, and what must be established about its denominator before either number is quoted to the undertaking?
  2. Read Exhibits 2 and 5 together. Who is Shravasti's accessibility problem about, and which exhibit would you trust less?
  3. The report traces 16 of the 31 app failures to a single absence. What does that do to the three estimates, and to the vendor's "top 20 findings"?
  4. Options A to D all answer one question. What is it, and what question has nobody in the case asked?
  5. Whose stated position would change if the renderer had been written by an engineer who had since left? What does that imply for how Debarati runs Monday's call, and for what she asks Dhiman to show her first?
  6. It is Monday morning, 12 October. What goes in the board paper, what does she tell the undertaking before 30 October, and what does she say about the declaration she must sign either way?
case20v1-ux.accessibility:
Rupantar Pay: Can Everyone Use This?

A decision case on accessible and inclusive design

1. Opening

At 6.30 pm on Monday 12 October 2026, Chandrima Joardar sat in Rupantar Pay's Bengaluru office with a September audit report open on her screen, reading it for the third time. As vice-president of product she had until Friday 23 October to tell the leadership team what her engineers would build over the next six weeks. Two pieces of work competed for the same people. One was Gold Saver, a festive savings feature due to ship on Monday 26 October, two weeks before Diwali on Sunday 8 November. The other was a repair of the app, which the audit had just shown to be largely unusable for people who rely on a screen reader. Both sat on her planning board, and the board made plain that they could not both fit. Gold Saver let a customer commit ₹100 a week toward digital gold bought through a partner,.

2. Company background

Rupantar Pay, founded in Bengaluru in 2019, is a bill-payment and small-savings app for first-time digital users in cities such as Guwahati, Siliguri, Nashik and Coimbatore. Customers pay electricity, water and gas bills, recharge mobile and DTH connections, and set aside as little as ₹50 a week in digital gold and fixed deposits offered through partner institutions. The app has 62 lakh monthly active users, runs in nine Indian languages, and booked ₹148 crore of revenue in FY26 (April 2025 to March 2026), mostly from convenience fees and partner commissions.

It competes with PhonePe, Paytm and Google Pay for bill payments, and with Groww for savings. It wins by being plainer and lighter than they are: a large minority, 31 per cent, hold a ₹9,000-class Android phone with two gigabytes of memory or less. Of 210 employees, 54 are engineers in Bengaluru and Pune.

3. The situation

The audit began with a complaint. In July a customer in Siliguri wrote that her father, who is blind, could not finish the KYC upgrade needed to raise his savings limit, and that a neighbour had completed it for him, reading out his Aadhaar OTP. Charu Jash, the customer-success lead in Singapore, forwarded the email. It was the eleventh such message she had tagged since January; nobody had counted them before.

Chinmoy Jana, the design lead in Berlin, then commissioned an audit against WCAG 2.1 level AA, the international standard behind most accessibility law. Between 21 and 25 September twelve screen-reader users recruited through a Bengaluru NGO each tried six core journeys on the TalkBack reader, using a ₹9,000 phone with two gigabytes of memory, typical of that segment. Exhibit 1 gives the result. Of 72 attempts, 32 succeeded, or 44 per cent. The failures were not evenly spread. Sign-up, KYC upgrade and raising a dispute, the three journeys through which a person enters, stays eligible and obtains redress, succeeded in 10 of 36 attempts.

Exhibit 2 asks how many customers this touches. The Census of 2011 counted 2.68 crore Indians with a disability, 2.21 per cent of the population. Applied to 62 lakh users that gives about 1.37 lakh people, a crude figure, since Rupantar has never asked.

The business side then sharpened the question. A public-sector bank had issued a request for proposals for a white-label bill-payment front end, worth ₹1.8 crore a year to the winner. Its clause on accessibility requires a conformance statement for onboarding, KYC and grievance journeys on a live build by the bid date, Friday 4 December. The Supreme Court's 30 April 2025 ruling in Amar Jain v. Union of India on the accessibility of digital KYC had already made that clause unsurprising.

4. The people

Chandrima Joardar, Bengaluru, owns the roadmap and must recommend. Chinmoy Jana, Berlin, wants all six journeys fixed, and fears that a partial repair becomes a permanent one. On a call at 6.30 pm IST on Thursday 8 October, 3.00 pm for him, he said that "an app that works for 44 per cent of attempts does not work." From 25 October Berlin is 4.5 hours behind India, so the same call will fall at 2.00 pm for him.

Charu Jash, Singapore, has the tickets and the stories, and wants the dispute journey first, because a customer who cannot complain has no other recourse. Chandan Jha, head of engineering in Pune, wants Gold Saver shipped on time. He would give the work to a squad of six engineers, which has already lost two weeks this year to UPI rule changes, and the savings and bill-payment fixes touch a payment component that Gold Saver also uses.

5. The options

Exhibit 3 shows how the dates fall, and Exhibit 4 sets the three courses open to her side by side.

Option A: ship Gold Saver now, repair later. No remediation money is spent before Diwali and the festive forecast of ₹3.6 crore holds. The cost is the bank bid: the clause asks for a conformance statement on a live build, so a roadmap would probably be a non-conforming bid, and a continuing exclusion of customers like the Siliguri father.

Option B: remediate all six journeys first. Chinmoy's preference. It costs ₹40.5 lakh and 27 person-weeks and, because of the shared component, moves Gold Saver to Monday 30 November. The forecast's phasing puts 70 per cent of the ₹3.6 crore, ₹2.52 crore, before 30 November, and that revenue would be lost. Rebuilding the shared payment component accounts for the delay beyond the 27 person-weeks.

Option C: fix the gate journeys, and build Gold Saver to standard. Sign-up, KYC and disputes take 18 person-weeks, ₹27 lakh, about three weeks for a squad of six. Gold Saver's design is final but three of its five screens are not yet coded; those are built to the standard within the same estimate, and the two already coded are audited with the savings journey in January. The other three journeys, 9 person-weeks and ₹13.5 lakh, follow by 31 January.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 tell you that a single overall completion rate hides?
  2. Which of the groups in Exhibit 2 would benefit from the repairs even if the Census-based estimate were wrong by half?
  3. What distinguishes the three journeys in Option C from the other three, and is that distinction one a customer would recognise?
  4. What would you need to learn by 23 October to change your recommendation?

7. A note for the learner

Accessible design asks whether people whose abilities or circumstances differ from the team's can complete the task. It is a test of the product, not a feature, and it is cheapest at the moment screens are first drawn. The decision therefore turns on sequencing, not on whether to do it. A strong answer first separates harms: a blocked entry, a blocked KYC and a blocked complaint exclude a person entirely, while the other three journeys, which fail 25 to 50 per cent of attempts, hurt but do not shut a person out.

One defensible path is Option C. Option A leaves the worst failures standing and gives up the chance to bid for a ₹1.8 crore annual contract, one Rupantar might not win, to save ₹27 lakh. Option B buys only 9 more person-weeks, ₹13.5 lakh, of repair on journeys that are not gates, and costs ₹2.52 crore of festive revenue to do so. C meets the bank's clause, fixes the exclusions that carry legal and moral weight under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, and stops new debt on the screens still to be built. Its risk is Chinmoy's: the last ₹13.5 lakh may slip. The answer is to write the 31 January date into the quarter's commitments, and to have Charu report completion rates monthly.
exp40v2-ux.accessibility:
Accessible and inclusive design

Can everyone use this — including people whose abilities or context differ from mine?

1. Two October decisions

On Thursday 8 October 2026, Gaurika Marathe, head of product for the member app at Vitaan Health Insurance in Mumbai, read a cohort analysis she had commissioned a week earlier. Vitaan had told its board it would move 60 per cent of retail claim intimations to self-service by 31 March 2027. September's volume was 41,250 intimations, of which 5,750, or 13.9 per cent, were filed by the member in the app. An assisted intimation cost ₹184 to handle; an app intimation cost ₹11. The commitment therefore meant shifting 19,000 intimations a month at ₹173 each, a saving of ₹32.87 lakh a month, or ₹3.94 crore a year.

The analysis changed the shape of the problem. Of 9,200 intimations started in the app in September, 5,750 were completed: 62.5 per cent. Split by age the pooled figure dissolved. Members aged 60 and over completed 920 of 2,300 starts, 40.0 per cent; members under 60 completed 4,830 of 6,900, 70.0 per cent. Marathe's instinct was to call this a 30-point gap. Her analyst, Gulnar Mandrekar, objected that the denominator was wrong for the board's question, which was about a share of intimations: on that base older members self-served 920 of 19,250, or 4.8 per cent, against 4,830 of 22,000, 22.0 per cent.

On Friday 9 October, Gajanan Mhatre, VP product at Vikalp Workforce Cloud in Bengaluru, faced a harder deadline. Vikalp sells shift-scheduling software to hospital groups, and a Netherlands-based hospital staffing group with 34,000 employees had issued a tender worth ₹2.1 crore a year for three years, ₹6.3 crore in all, requiring a written accessibility conformance report against WCAG 2.2 at level AA. An audit of 42 sampled screens, run from 28 September to Monday 5 October, found defects on 40. Responses were due Friday 30 October, and Mhatre had three engineers for the fifteen weekdays from Monday 12 to Friday 30 October: 45 engineer-days against 68 of identified work.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

Accessibility is the degree to which a product can be operated by people across the range of human ability, including through assistive technology: a screen reader, magnification, a keyboard, switch or voice instead of a pointer, and the operating system's own text and contrast settings. Inclusive design is the method that treats exclusion as a design output: find the mismatch between a person and the context the product assumes, and remove the assumption.

The intellectual history runs through three traditions that arrived separately. The first is architectural: universal design, associated with Ronald Mace and the Center for Universal Design at North Carolina State University, whose emblem is the curb cut, cut for wheelchair users and used far more by people with prams and trolleys. The second is political: the social model of disability, developed by disability activists from the 1970s onward, which locates disability in the environment rather than the body, so that a form which cannot be read aloud is what disables the person who cannot see it. The third is engineering: the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines from the World Wide Web Consortium, published in 1999 and now at version 2.2, organised under four principles (perceivable, operable, understandable, robust) and graded A, AA and AAA. The inclusive design movement added the persona spectrum: a permanent limitation, a temporary injury and a situational constraint produce the same mismatch.

The schools differ on a proposition each would and would not sign. The standards school signs that conformance at a stated level is the only claim a buyer, regulator or court can act on, and refuses to sign that conformance means usable. The inclusive design school signs that designing for the extreme of a dimension improves the product for everyone on it, and refuses the checklist. The disability rights school signs that access is an entitlement regardless of segment size, and refuses the business case, because an argument that wins on large numbers loses on small ones. The universal design school signs that one design needing no adaptation beats an adapted one, and refuses the separate accessible version. Most practitioners hold two at once, which is why these arguments are really about premises.

3. Mechanics in depth

The mechanism a product manager must understand is the accessibility tree. When an application draws a screen, the platform also builds a parallel, text-only structure in which each element carries a role (button, checkbox, heading), a name (the words identifying it), a state (expanded, disabled, selected) and sometimes a value. A screen reader never inspects pixels; it walks this tree, in order. An element drawn from generic containers has no role and is announced as nothing; an icon with no text has no name and is announced as "button"; and the order of the tree, not the visual arrangement, is the order a keyboard or switch user meets.

Two steps are left implicit. Anything appearing asynchronously, such as a saved draft or a validation error, must be announced, because a screen reader does not notice what it is not reading: in Figure 1 the message exists on screen and not in the tree. And decorative imagery must be hidden, or the user hears noise before anything useful.

Where the practice becomes quantitative it becomes genuinely so. Contrast is a luminance ratio, (L₁ + 0.05) / (L₂ + 0.05), where L₁ is the relative luminance of the lighter colour, L₂ of the darker, and relative luminance weights the linearised red, green and blue channels 0.2126, 0.7152 and 0.0722. At level AA ordinary text needs at least 4.5:1; large text and the visible boundaries of interface components need 3:1. Two properties of the formula are rarely noticed: it is symmetric, so a pair and its inversion give the identical ratio, and green dominates, so a palette tuned by eye on blues will mislead.

The amber row is the interesting one. White on Vitaan's amber gives 2.08:1 and cannot be rescued by nudging the amber; the brand's dark ink on the identical amber gives 7.09:1. The slot label at 3.83:1 fails for ordinary text yet would pass the 3:1 rule as large text, and darkening only the text to #55606E reaches 5.68:1.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions can be stated as testable claims. First: the excluded cohort is on the critical path to an outcome you already own. The board's 60 per cent of 41,250 is 24,750 intimations a month, and members under 60 produced only 22,000 intimations in September, so even if every one of them self-served Vitaan would be 2,750 short. The target is unreachable without the cohort that completes 40.0 per cent of its starts. For Mhatre the gate is contractual instead: ₹6.3 crore does not open without the document.

Second: the defect sits in a shared layer, so one fix propagates, which separates a tractable programme from an endless one. Vikalp passes it — 8 causes carry 100 findings — while Vitaan's unnamed upload control fails it, being one control on one screen. Third: someone can observe the failure. Neither company had anyone in-house who used a screen reader daily, so in both the condition fails and the defects stay invisible to ordinary review.

The idea misleads in three situations. Where the real barrier is cost, bandwidth, memory, language or literacy, the inclusive-design method transfers but the accessibility checklist does not, and a team that conflates them spends a quarter on contrast tokens while users abandon on a 14 MB bundle. Where a product is a back-office utility with a small, known, employed user population, individual accommodation is the right instrument. And where conformance has become the objective the standard misleads: every checkable criterion can pass on a screen that takes forty tab stops to reach the submit button.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies the audited surface is rarely the worst one: Vitaan's member app drew scrutiny, while its field agent app, used outdoors in glare, one-handed, on cheaper devices, had never been examined. Two-sided situations break the feedback loop structurally, because Vikalp's buyer is a procurement committee and its user is a charge nurse at 6 a.m. In regulated products the failure often sits in the document layer rather than the interface: a policy schedule delivered as a scanned image is unreadable to a screen reader however good the app around it.

Hardware plus software adds constraints software cannot answer: the mounting height of a wall terminal, whether a control can be found by touch, whether audio output exists at all. AI-native products add two classes. Speech interfaces trained on typical speech degrade for atypical speech, including the dysarthria that often accompanies motor conditions. And streaming generative output is hostile to screen readers: text that updates continuously is announced continuously, so a live transcript becomes an interruption the user cannot escape.

At the organisational seam the honest account differs from the stated one. The stated version is a programme with an owner; the operating version is that requirements are enforced at exactly two chokepoints, the component library and the release checklist, and everything outside them depends on whether a particular designer cares. The defect that never gets fixed is the one in a shared component owned by a platform team with no customer.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Conformance is a floor

A floor is not a verdict. The tell is a clean report beside a poor completion rate: Vitaan's flow passed an automated scan in July and its 60-and-over cohort still completed 40.0 per cent of its starts. The audit measured what it measures.

Analytics cannot see the people already defeated

The 2,300 app starts from older members came from people who got far enough to be counted; those who never installed appear nowhere in app analytics. The tell is a metric that improves when the excluded cohort churns. An expert anchors one measure outside the product, which is why 4.8 per cent of intimations beats 40.0 per cent of starts.

Native components are a subsidy; custom controls a loan

A platform button arrives with role, name slot, focus behaviour and state reporting already correct; a control drawn from generic containers must have all four rebuilt, and will drift. The tell is an audit's root-cause list: if most causes sit in bespoke controls, the company is paying interest on an old decision.

Colour-only encoding fails sighted users too

Status shown only by hue was the commonest class in Vikalp's audit, and the usual framing, colour blindness, understates it. In Figure 3, its "on shift" and "unfilled" chips differ by 1.27:1 once reduced to their own luminances. The tell is a ticket saying "it won't let me".

Text scaling regresses first

Many people with low vision simply enlarge the system font, and a layout that clips or overlaps at twice the default size has failed them silently. Nobody sees it, because design review happens at default size on a large screen.

Automated coverage is partial, and not a constant

Scanners reliably find missing names and measurable contrast; they cannot judge whether a name is meaningful or an order sensible. Experts distrust the borrowed statistic about what share of defects tooling catches, because that share is a property of a codebase: Vikalp's keyboard trap was not machine-findable.

Assistive technology is a stack

Behaviour differs across screen reader, browser and operating system version, and a bug report naming only one of the three is usually unreproducible. The tell is a ticket that says "works with VoiceOver". A definition of done names which combinations are supported, because claiming all of them is unkeepable.

Procurement documents are engineering artefacts

A conformance report is a technical statement about a specific version, tested by a stated method, with exceptions listed. The tell that a company misunderstands this is a report with no exceptions column, or one signed by sales.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the binding constraint is reach and reputation, and the excluded users are invisible in the funnel. In B2B and enterprise the constraint is procurement: a conformance statement can gate a deal outright, so the work is budgeted, and for that reason prone to being satisfied on paper. Platforms and marketplaces have the genuinely distinctive problem, because the defect may be in third-party content or code, so a platform can only set defaults, validate submissions and make the accessible path the cheap path. For hardware, decisions become irreversible at tooling freeze. In AI products the output itself can be the barrier.

By stage the difference is real but smaller than usually claimed. An early company can adopt native components, a contrast-checked palette and a naming habit at close to zero marginal cost: the one genuine free lunch in the field. A late company has money and no leverage, so only the two chokepoints work. What does not differ is the audit itself; the defect classes above are the same at eight engineers and eight hundred.

8. Three worked examples

Vikalp: where the leverage actually is

The audit's finding list is the wrong unit of work; grouped by root cause it becomes tractable.

Defect classFindings (screens affected)Distinct root causesEngineer-daysFix locus
Unnamed icon-only controls31414component library
Keyboard trap in shift grid915component library
Focus lost after modal close2226component library
Colour-only roster status3813tokens + component
No text alternative on exported charts7318reporting module

Total1211368—

Audit of 42 sampled screens, 28 September to 5 October 2026; 40 of the 42 carried at least one finding. A screen appears in every class it fails, so the findings column counts screen-class pairs, not screens.

The first four classes resolve in the component library and tokens: 8 of the 13 root causes, 100 of the 121 findings, 28 of the 68 engineer-days. The remaining 5 causes carry 21 findings and 40 engineer-days. That is 3.57 findings per engineer-day of scoped work in the shared layer against 0.525 outside it, a factor of 6.8 — a crude comparison, since findings differ in severity.

Vitaan: a target that cannot be met from the easy cohort

Cohort, September 2026IntimationsApp startsApp completionsCompletion of startsSelf-service share of intimations
Members aged 60 and over19,2502,30092040.0%4.8%
