Total / pooled rate41,2509,2005,75062.5%13.9%

The last two columns are pooled rates computed on the totals, not means of the rows above: the mean of 40.0 and 70.0 is 55.0, while 5,750 of 9,200 is 62.5 per cent.

Older members were 19,250 of 41,250 intimations, 46.7 per cent; 2,300 of 9,200 app starts, 25.0 per cent; 920 of 5,750 completions, 16.0 per cent. Their presence falls at each stage.

The failure: Vitaan's parallel "Saral mode"

In April 2026 Vitaan had already tried this. A simplified parallel interface of nine screens, built for 210 engineer-days, was offered as an opt-in "Saral mode". By July 1,480 of 4,60,000 app-active members had switched to it, 0.32 per cent, and by its retirement at the end of September 800 of those 1,480, 54 per cent, had stopped using it within sixty days of switching. The reason was structural: maintained by a separate squad, it fell two releases behind and never received the cashless-claim flow that by September carried a growing share of intimations, so a member in Saral mode could not file that claim type at all. Of the 210 engineer-days Vitaan carried forward about 25 and wrote off roughly 185.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

The one-time audit. Sign: a clean report one quarter and new failures the next. Diagnostic: rerun the scan on the newest build and count findings added since. Caught late, the report you hand a buyer describes a version you no longer ship.

Testing with the team instead of with users. Sign: sighted engineers declare a screen-reader flow fine after ten minutes. Diagnostic: ask a daily screen-reader user to complete one task while everyone stays silent, and time it. Caught late, the cost is rebuilding a flow that passed every criterion.

Remediating findings rather than causes. Sign: the backlog has 121 tickets and the component library none. Diagnostic: group findings by root cause and compare counts. Caught late, you pay for the same defect once per screen.

Overclaiming in a conformance document. Sign: a report with no exceptions and no test matrix. Diagnostic: ask who tested which version with which assistive technology. Caught late, the cost is a contractual remedy, a different order of problem from a defect.

A business case that wins the first argument and loses the second. Sign: the justification rests on one revenue estimate. Diagnostic: ask what happens if the cohort is a tenth of the assumed size. Caught late, the programme is cancelled by the logic that funded it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Standards versus outcomes. The standards position: accessibility is the only part of user experience with an externally auditable definition, and removing it produces no better outcomes, only no accountability; its evidence is that discretionary programmes decay without a scoreboard. The outcomes position, steelmanned: conformance correlates weakly with task completion by real assistive-technology users, so it measures effort rather than access, its evidence being pairs like Vitaan's, a passing scan beside a 40.0 per cent completion rate on starts. The first would be wrong if conformant products failed users at rates close to non-conformant ones; the second would be wrong if programmes without a checkable floor produced less access in practice.

Rights versus the business case. The rights position holds that access is an entitlement and that arguing it commercially concedes the principle, because the argument reverses whenever the segment is small. The commercial position holds that where capacity is finite an unquantified claim loses to a quantified one every planning cycle. This is not resolvable by evidence; it is a disagreement about what kind of reason a company responds to.

Specialists versus the design system. One camp holds that accessibility expertise is deep enough to need dedicated practitioners; the other that expertise held outside delivery teams becomes a gate teams route around. The second has the better evidence from Figure 4's leverage ratio; the first from the keyboard trap, which no platform default prevents.

One apparent disagreement is not a real one. Third-party overlay scripts that claim to remediate a site from outside are marketed as an alternative to engineering work; the technical case against them, that they cannot supply semantics the underlying code does not express, is unanswered.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs an audit and schedules remediation. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They ask what the denominator is before accepting a rate. They fix in the shared layer by default and treat a screen-level fix as a confession. They keep one measurement anchored outside the product. And they refuse to write a conformance claim they cannot test.

12. The decisions

Marathe decided on Tuesday 13 October. She moved the three defects of Figure 1 into the 23 October release train, commissioned five moderated sessions with daily screen-reader users and five more with magnification users, on the strength of Figure 6, and asked finance to restate the board target as a share of intimations with the 22,000 ceiling written into the paper. Her reasoning was that 40.0 per cent of starts is a true answer to a different question from the board's, and that a target shown to be unreachable without the excluded cohort is a stronger instrument than any revenue estimate.

Mhatre decided on 9 October, the day the capacity arithmetic was in front of him. He allocated 28 engineer-days to the component library and tokens, 12 more to the two reporting causes that between them account for 6 of that module's 7 affected screens, and held 5 of his 45 days for retesting and documentation. On that plan 106 of 121 findings close, 87.6 per cent, leaving between 14 and 15 screens still carrying the unresolved zoom and chart defects. The report he will file on 30 October claims support with those exceptions named, with the test matrix attached, rather than the unqualified AA claim his sales lead had drafted.

1. Marathe's 40.0 per cent of starts and her 4.8 per cent of intimations describe the same members in the same month. Which belongs in the board paper?

2. Mhatre's shared-layer work is scoped at 6.8 times more findings per engineer-day. On what grounds should he ever not maximise that ratio?

3. Saral mode failed for reasons of ownership and release cadence, not design. When, if ever, is a parallel accessible interface right?

13. Going deeper

UX fundamentals for PMs — the principles this topic widens to every user.

Accessibility standards and law — what conformance levels mean contractually, and where India's Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 creates obligation.

Usability heuristics — the vocabulary for arguing that a conformant screen is still bad.

Information architecture and navigation — headings and landmarks are what a screen-reader user navigates by.

User flows and task analysis — the unit in which access must be measured, because task completion is the outcome.

Usability testing — how to recruit and run the sessions Figure 6 sizes.

Design systems and components — the chokepoint where 100 of Vikalp's 121 findings resolve.

Content design and microcopy — names, error messages and announcements are text, so most defects are writing defects.
exp20v2-ux.accessibility:
Accessible and inclusive design

Can everyone use this, including people whose abilities or circumstances differ from mine?

1. The audit that arrived on a Monday

On Monday 5 October 2026, Esha Lokhande, head of product at Tamrapan Fresh, a Pune-based grocery delivery app, opened a nine-page report from an outside accessibility auditor. The firm had worked through the six screens of the checkout flow with an Android screen reader, a keyboard and a magnifier, and it had found 31 failures. The festive sale began on Thursday 12 November. Engineering would freeze code on Friday 30 October, which left ten weekdays, 19 to 30 October (Dussehra falls on the 20th, which Eeshan’s team agreed to work), and Eeshan Ladkat, the Android lead, could spare two engineers: 20 engineer-days in all.

It arrived beside a number from her own analytics. Of 480,000 checkouts started in September, 9,600 came from phones with a screen reader running. Those users completed 41 per cent of the time. Everyone else completed 78 per cent. Esha’s decision was what to fix in 20 engineer-days, what to leave, and how to argue for it to a finance head who had asked, reasonably, what the company got for the money.

2. The idea

Accessibility is the degree to which a product can be used by people with the widest range of abilities, using whatever assistive means they rely on: a screen reader (software that speaks, or turns into braille, what is on screen), a keyboard instead of touch, a switch, voice control or enlarged text. Inclusive design is the broader method: recognise that people are excluded when a product assumes one body, one context and one set of conditions, and design so that the exclusion does not happen. Universal design is the older architectural cousin, associated with the architect Ron Mace in the 1980s.

The problem it solves is that products are built by people who can see, hear and grip, on good phones, in good light. For everyone else the product is a locked door. The scale is not marginal: India’s 2011 census counted 2.68 crore people with disabilities, 2.21 per cent of the population, and advocates argue that was an undercount, partly because it used a narrower pre-2016 definition. Add temporary and situational cases and the share meeting a barrier in any month is far larger.

The technical standard most products work to is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, WCAG, from the World Wide Web Consortium. It first appeared in 1999; the current version, 2.2, was issued in 2023. It organises requirements under four principles (content must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust) and grades them into levels A, AA and AAA. The sentence Esha could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: a feature is not finished until someone who cannot see, hear, grip or hurry can finish the task it exists for.

3. How it works

The mechanism most PMs never see is the accessibility tree. When an app draws a screen, the operating system also builds a parallel, text-only description of it: each element has a role (button, checkbox, heading), a name (the words that identify it), a state (selected, disabled, expanded) and sometimes a value. A screen reader never looks at pixels. It walks this tree and speaks it. If an element exists visually but has no name, the user hears "button" and nothing else.

Six steps follow from this. First, every interactive element needs a name that says what it does, not what it looks like: "Place order", not "arrow". Second, the reading and focus order must match the logical order, because a keyboard or switch user moves through elements one at a time. Third, nothing may be conveyed by colour, size or position alone. Fourth, targets must be large enough to hit and text legible enough to read. Fifth, errors must be identified in words and be recoverable. Sixth, someone must test with the assistive technology itself.

Practitioners leave three things implicit. Decorative images should be hidden from the tree, or the user hears noise. A change that appears on screen, such as "coupon applied", must be announced, because a screen reader does not notice what it is not looking at. And text must scale: many people with low vision raise the system font size, and a layout that clips at 200 per cent has failed them quietly.

4. A worked example

Esha asked Elina Lanjekar, the QA lead, to sort the 31 failures by whether they stopped a shopper finishing checkout (blockers) or merely made it harder. Eeshan then estimated effort.

Failure typeIssuesEngineer-days per issueEngineer-daysBlocks the task?
Missing labels70.53.5Yes
Wrong focus order41.255.0Yes
Unclear error messages51.05.0Yes
Low contrast90.54.5No
Small touch targets60.53.0No
Total31—21.016 issues block

Blockers: 7 + 4 + 5 = 16 issues, 3.5 + 5.0 + 5.0 = 13.5 engineer-days. Non-blockers: 9 + 6 = 15 issues, 4.5 + 3.0 = 7.5 engineer-days. 13.5 + 7.5 = 21.0.

The full 21.0 engineer-days exceed the 20 available. The blockers cost 13.5. Contrast, though classed as non-blocking, is cheap and fixed in one place, because the colours come from a shared set of design values (tokens), so Esha added it: 13.5 + 4.5 = 18.0, leaving two days for retesting. Touch targets, 3.0 days, move to the sprint after the freeze.

Now the case for the money. Of 9,600 screen-reader checkouts, 41 per cent completed: 3,936. Had they completed at the 78 per cent the other 470,400 achieved, 7,488 would have, a shortfall of 3,552 orders. At an average basket of ₹640, that is ₹22,73,280, about ₹22.7 lakh a month. Now change one input. Suppose screen-reader users plausibly complete at only 70 per cent even with a perfect flow, because they browse differently. At 70 per cent they would complete 6,720 against today’s 3,936; the gap is 2,784 orders and ₹17,81,760, about ₹17.8 lakh. The answer moved by roughly a fifth, but its sign did not. The base matters: both figures are measured over the 9,600 flagged checkouts only, not over all 480,000.

A second calculation concerns legibility. WCAG measures contrast as a ratio, (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the relative luminance (a 0-to-1 brightness measure, weighting green most heavily) of the lighter colour and L2 of the darker. For ordinary text, level AA requires at least 4.5:1; large text and interface component outlines need 3:1. Tamrapan’s grey #767676 has luminance 0.1812; on white (1.0) the ratio is 1.05 / 0.2312 = 4.54, a pass. Its delivery-slot text sits on the card colour #F2F2F2 (luminance 0.8879): 0.9379 / 0.2312 = 4.06, a fail. Changing the one input, the text to #595959 (luminance 0.0999), gives 0.9379 / 0.1499 = 6.26.

Figure 4 also shows white text on the orange button: 3.58, enough for icons and large type but not for the small “Add” label. A darker rust at 5.18 passes.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Three words, three scopes

Accessibility asks whether a disabled person can use the product at all. Inclusive design asks who is being excluded by assumptions and removes the assumption. Universal design aims for one design that needs no adaptation. A team that says “we are inclusive” because it passed an audit has confused the first with the second.

Permanent, temporary, situational

Figure 2 matters commercially. The one-handed shopper on a crowded bus is not a rare case; designing for a permanent limit routinely helps the other two columns. Curb cuts, which disability activists pushed into American cities from the 1970s, are the classic example: parents with prams and couriers with trolleys use them daily.

Conformance is not usability

A screen can satisfy every checkable criterion and still be exhausting: forty elements to traverse before the order button, headings that say nothing. WCAG is a floor. Only people who use assistive technology can tell you whether a flow is humane.

Automated tools see a subset

Scanners reliably detect missing labels and measurable contrast. They cannot judge whether a label is meaningful, whether focus order is sensible or whether an error message helps. A clean scan is evidence of absence of some defects, not of usability.

Native components beat custom ones

A standard button or checkbox arrives with role, state and keyboard behaviour free. A hand-drawn custom control must rebuild each of these. Much accessibility debt comes from custom controls.

What your data cannot tell you

The 9,600 figure is a lower bound: it counts screen readers, not people with low vision using magnification, people with motor impairments, or those who abandoned the app long ago and no longer appear. Analytics describe those who got in. They cannot describe those who could not.

Inclusion is wider than disability

In India, a product that fails on a low-memory phone, a patchy 4G connection, a vernacular script or low literacy excludes people as surely as a missing label. The method transfers; the checklist does not.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and late

In consumer products the argument is reach and trust, and failure is public. In B2B, accessibility is a procurement gate: enterprise and government buyers may ask for a conformance statement, often a completed US template called a VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template) report, before signing, so a gap can block a sale outright. In marketplaces there are at least two products. Tamrapan’s shopper app drew the audit, but its delivery-partner app, used for hours outdoors in glare, one-handed, on cheaper phones, fails the situational column daily and nobody had audited it.

An early-stage company can build on native components, a contrast-checked palette and a labelling habit at near-zero marginal cost; retrofitting later is dearer, and Tamrapan’s 21 engineer-days are that bill. A large company has the opposite problem: capacity, but many teams, legacy screens and no single owner, so the discipline lives in shared components and release checklists rather than heroics.

7. Common mistakes

The one-time audit

Symptom: a clean report in March and a new failing screen by June. Misunderstanding: accessibility as a project with an end date. Cheapest diagnostic: run the same automated scan on the newest release and count the new failures.

Testing with the team, not the users

Symptom: sighted engineers declare the screen reader flow “fine” after ten minutes. Misunderstanding: that hearing the output equals using it by ear at speed. Cheapest diagnostic: ask a regular screen-reader user to complete one purchase while you stay silent, and time it.

Colour as the only signal

Symptom: errors shown only by a red border; support tickets saying “it won’t let me continue”. Misunderstanding: that what you see is what everyone sees. Cheapest diagnostic: view the screen in greyscale.

8. What good looks like

Had Tamrapan handled this well from the start, the audit would have confirmed rather than surprised. Components would come from a shared library with names, roles and 48-dp-class targets built in; Google’s Material guidance recommends about that size. Contrast would be checked when a colour is chosen. The definition of done for every ticket would include a screen-reader pass. And Elina Lanjekar would be running quarterly sessions with users of assistive technology, whose findings arrive as ordinary backlog items, not as an external report in October.

9. Closing

Esha decided on Tuesday 6 October. The 16 blockers and the contrast tokens went into the freeze, 18.0 of 20 engineer-days; touch targets were scheduled for the first sprint after it. She presented the revenue case as a range, ₹17.8 to ₹22.7 lakh a month of gross order value (screen-reader checkouts only), with the caveat that it understated the harm, and added an accessibility pass to the definition of done. Her reasoning was that blockers turn a feature into a closed door, while the rest merely adds friction, and that a range which survives a sceptical finance head is worth more than a point estimate that does not.

The natural next topic is accessibility standards and law: what WCAG conformance levels mean contractually, and what India’s Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 obliges organisations to do. Read that to learn where the obligation, rather than the opportunity, begins.

Two questions to sit with. Which of your product’s users never appear in your analytics because the product defeated them first? And if your next release had to be usable with one hand, in sunlight, on a noisy platform, which screen would fail first?
exp20v2-ux.flows:
User Flows and Task Analysis

Discovery & Design, UX and Design Collaboration. The question: how many steps does the task take, and which could go?

1. Six thousand nine hundred sessions that did not pay

On Monday 5 October 2026, Madhumita Varman, head of product at Ektara, a Kolkata app through which households pay electricity, water, gas and broadband bills, opened a dashboard that she had asked her analyst to rebuild. It covered 28 September to 4 October. In that week 18,400 sessions (a session being one continuous visit to the app) had reached the first screen of the bill-payment task. Only 11,500 had reached the confirmation screen. The remaining 6,900, or 37.5 per cent, had ended without a confirmed payment.

The next morning she was due to meet Mrigank Vasistha, head of growth, who proposed a cashback, budgeted at ₹60 lakh for the quarter, to bring back people whose sessions ended unpaid. People who abandon a payment lack a reason to finish it, he argued, and money is a reason. Varman doubted the premise. A person who has opened the app, chosen a category and begun typing a consumer number has already decided to pay. She suspected the app rather than the incentive.

If she was wrong, Ektara would spend ₹60 lakh to bribe people through a flow that still lost nearly four in ten of them. If Vasistha was wrong, a growth lever would wait one fortnightly sprint. Her tool for settling the question was a drawing of the task, with the steps counted.

2. The idea

A task is something a person is trying to get done, stated without reference to any screen: pay this month's electricity bill. A user flow is a diagram of the route one kind of person takes through a product to complete one task, drawn as boxes (the screens or states they see) joined by arrows (the actions that move them on). Task analysis is the older and broader discipline underneath it: breaking a task into sub-goals and operations, and asking what each demands of the person doing it.

In the 1960s the British psychologists John Annett and Keith Duncan developed hierarchical task analysis to train industrial plant operators, who kept erring in procedures that looked simple on paper. In 1980 and 1983 Stuart Card, Thomas Moran and Allen Newell published models that attached times to individual operations, so that a computer task's duration could be predicted before anyone built it. Information architects around 2000, among them Jesse James Garrett, standardised the box-and-arrow drawing now called a flow. All three met one problem: people judge a task by its total effort, designers build it one screen at a time, and nobody sees the total unless somebody draws it.

Every step is a place a person can leave, so count the steps before you price the incentive.

Varman could repeat that in a meeting without sounding glib, because it concerns order of work, not whether incentives fail.

3. How it works

The mechanics run in five moves. State the task and the person: here, a returning household paying an electricity bill by UPI (the Unified Payments Interface, the real-time payment rail run by the National Payments Corporation of India). List the sub-goals, as Figure 1 does. Convert them into the screens that serve them and the actions between screens. Count screens, decisions and inputs. Attach a cost to each: time, error rate or share of people who leave.

Figure 1 holds two steps the product team had never drawn. Step 1.3: before typing a twelve-digit consumer number, the person must find it on a paper bill, SMS or email. Ektara's usability sessions of 2 October timed this at a median of 24 seconds across eight participants. Step 3.4 is the interval while the UPI application and the customer's bank complete authorisation. A drawing that shows only screens omits both, and flatters the product.

Figure 2 puts the counts on the boxes. The cliff is at screen 3, where 25.0 per cent of the 15,732 sessions that arrived (3,933) never reached the bill. The dashed box beside it suggests why: the screen asks for something the person may not have to hand.

4. A worked example

Varman priced the path with the keystroke-level model, which sums standard operators: a tap costs 1.10 seconds, a keystroke 0.28, and mental preparation before any new screen 1.35. These are desktop figures; phones are slower, so every total below is a floor.

Her redesign had two parts. Returning payers would see their saved bill on the home screen, so one tap replaces the category, provider and number screens. And the payment method would default to the last UPI app used. The returning payer's path becomes: tap the bill (2.45), tap Pay now (2.45), enter the PIN (3.57), wait (7.00). That is 15.47 seconds against 55.08, a reduction of 39.61 seconds or 71.9 per cent, and eight decisions become three.

Now change one input. The saving applies only to people who already have a saved bill. A first-time payer sees the full flow, plus one new tap to offer saving the bill: 55.08 + 2.45 = 57.53 seconds, which is worse than before. The blended gain therefore depends on the share of payments that come from returning payers. In Ektara's week, 6,900 of the 11,500 confirmed payments came from accounts that had paid the same consumer number before, which is 60.0 per cent. The blended time is 0.6 × 15.47 + 0.4 × 57.53 = 9.282 + 23.012 = 32.29 seconds, a 41.4 per cent reduction from 55.08. If the returning share were only 30 per cent, it becomes 0.3 × 15.47 + 0.7 × 57.53 = 4.641 + 40.271 = 44.91 seconds, an 18.5 per cent reduction. The break-even share is 2.45 ÷ 42.06, or 5.8 per cent: below that, the change makes the average payment slower.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Screens, decisions and actions are three different counts.

The current flow has nine screens (the seven in Figure 2, plus Home and the PIN entry), eight decisions or inputs, and 24 taps and keystrokes. Say which unit is counted.

The implicit step is usually the expensive one.

Looking for the consumer number cost about as much as everything on screen put together. Whatever the person must fetch, remember or wait for belongs in the drawing.

A flow is a journey drawn at screen level, not the journey.

Customer journey mapping covers the whole experience across weeks and channels. A flow covers one task, one persona, one session.

The happy path is not the path.

Figure 2 shows only the route where nothing goes wrong. A mistyped digit or a declined payment creates a branch, and branches are where trust is made or lost.

A step is not a unit of cost.

One tap on an unfamiliar permission screen can cost more than twelve keystrokes of a familiar number. Time models measure effort, not anxiety.

Some steps are there on purpose.

The review screen lets people see the amount before money moves, and the PIN is a second factor of authentication that Reserve Bank of India rules require.

The count cannot say why people left.

3,933 sessions ended at screen 3. That tells you where, not whether the cause was the missing number, a slow search or a phone call.

Questions to ask before relying on it.

Which person, device and week? Is each screen instrumented identically? Are the counts sessions or people?

6. How it differs by product and by stage

In consumer products the task is short and repeated, and tolerance is thin: each removed step compounds across millions of repetitions, as at Ektara. In B2B products the flow spans roles, so an approval may wait days for someone other than the user; the diagram needs swim lanes, one row per actor, and the long pole is often a hand-off rather than a screen. In marketplaces there are at least two flows, buyer and seller: a short checkout is worthless if the seller's listing flow is so long that supply never arrives.

An early-stage company draws flows on a whiteboard and tests them with five people, since its traffic is too thin for a funnel to mean anything. A large company has abundant data but many teams each owning one screen, so no one owns the whole path; there the diagram names a total nobody is accountable for.

7. Common mistakes

Counting screens and calling it done. Symptom: a flow cut from seven screens to five, with median completion time unchanged. Misunderstanding: that a screen is the unit of effort. Diagnostic: time five people through old and new versions with a stopwatch.

Deleting a step that carried trust or compliance. Symptom: completion rises for a week, then complaints or failed audits follow. Misunderstanding: that every step is friction. Diagnostic: write beside each step one sentence on what it protects; a step with no sentence is a candidate.

Averaging different people. Symptom: a redesign that moves the dashboard and helps few people. Misunderstanding: that one flow serves one user. Diagnostic: split the count by first-time and returning, as the break-even above does, before building.

Drawing only what the product shows. Symptom: a tidy diagram and a funnel cliff nobody can explain. Diagnostic: sit beside three people with a real bill and note every moment they look away from the screen.

8. What good looks like

The flow is drawn on one page within a day, with off-screen and system steps in a different line style. Each step has a count, a time and a sentence on its purpose. The drawing is split by first-time and returning users. The change names the steps removed and added, and the metric that will show whether it worked, with the comparison group fixed in advance.

9. Closing

At the meeting on Tuesday 6 October, Varman set the diagram beside Vasistha's budget. She did not ask him to withdraw the cashback, only that it follow a change to the flow, so that any money spent would meet a path that skips the number screen for returning payers. He agreed to hold the ₹60 lakh until the 19 October comparison had run for a fortnight. The saved-bill change with the default payment method was scheduled for 10 per cent of users on 19 October, the other 90 per cent forming a comparison group. Her reasoning: the modelled time gain was large and testable, while the cashback could wait.

What to learn next: friction audits and step counting, which turns this one-task drawing into a repeatable inspection of a whole product, and onboarding and first-run design, which attends to the first-time payer whom the redesign made slightly worse off. Two questions to sit with. Which step in a product you use daily would you refuse to remove, and what does it protect? And if the 24-second search for a number had been invisible in your data, what would you have concluded the app's problem was?
case40v1-ux.flows:
Indian School of Business · Software Product Management

Darwaza Retail Cloud: Ten Steps to a Bill

A team has counted the steps in a checkout, and cannot agree what a step is, which bills the count is over, or whether removing two changed anything.

The company is fictional; the market around it is not.

1. Sunday night, Bengaluru

At a quarter past nine on Sunday, 18 October 2026, the seventh floor of Darwaza Retail Cloud's office in Bellandur, Bengaluru, held three people: a security guard, an engineer waiting on a deployment window, and Lalitya Thind, Vice-President of Product, who had a decision to carry into a leadership meeting at nine.

Four printouts lay on the table. A field study of how long a cashier at an Indian supermarket counter takes to finish a bill on Darwaza's point-of-sale software: ninety-five seconds for the commonest bill, seven screens of ten, twenty-one taps. A telemetry memo from Toronto reporting that 93.6 per cent of bills started on Darwaza's counters finish on them, which its author called "healthy" in the subject line. The read-out of a pilot in fourteen stores, seven of them running a flow with two of the ten steps removed, which measured those counters 5.8 seconds faster — a number for which two colleagues had computed different standard errors and drawn opposite conclusions. And the January clause under which Darwaza's largest Gulf customer would withhold eight per cent of its fee unless the median bill at its tills fell below ninety-five seconds by 31 March 2027.

Thind had drawn the flow on a whiteboard eleven times that year. Each time, somebody told her the drawing was wrong.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Darwaza Retail Cloud was founded in Pune in 2016 by two engineers who had spent a decade on billing software for pharmacy chains. The product is unglamorous: a cloud point-of-sale, inventory and loyalty suite for chains too large for a desktop package and too small to run SAP. By FY2026 it ran in 9,630 stores across 264 chains on ₹134.00 crore of revenue (Exhibit 1), backed by ₹310 crore from a Mumbai fund expecting a listing in 2029.

The decision that shapes October 2026 was made in April 2023. Four large chains each wanted the billing screen sequenced differently — loyalty before the first scan or after, the tender screen opening on cash or on UPI. Rather than fork the product, the founders shipped a server-driven flow definition: an ordered list of screens, fetched at login, that a customer-success engineer could reorder for any chain without a release. Sold as "configurable checkout", it won the accounts behind the Series B.

By September 2026 there were 1,940 distinct flow definitions in production. Exhibit 2's ten-step sequence is the standard definition shipped with version 7.4, in force in 3,210 of the 5,940 India stores on that version, or 54.0 per cent. Every other store runs one of the remaining 1,939.

3. The industry

Indian retail software in 2026 is squeezed from three directions. Below it sit cheap billing packages — Zoho's Zakya, GoFrugal, Petpooja in food service — good enough for one store. Above it sit Lightspeed and Shopify POS, which large chains evaluate for omnichannel. Beside it sits quick commerce: Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart have taught urban shoppers that a basket can be assembled in ninety seconds, and chain managements now benchmark their queues against that feeling, unfairly.

Three regulatory facts bear on the flow. The NPCI's UPI rails carry most of Darwaza's in-store volume, and a collect request involves a wait the software does not control. GST requires a business customer's GSTIN at the counter for a tax invoice. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 led legal, in May 2026, to add a consent line to the loyalty step, which Exhibit 2 shows costing 11.5 seconds, up from 6.8.

Exposure beyond India is concentrated. ₹27.60 crore of the ₹134.00 crore top line comes from the Gulf, and ₹9.80 crore of that ₹27.60 crore, or 35.5 per cent, from one customer: Rawabi Fresh Markets LLC, a Dubai grocery group running 420 of the 1,180 Gulf stores, or 35.6 per cent. Rawabi's bills carry a UAE VAT invoice with the buyer's TRN where supplied — the eleventh step.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

On Wednesday, 14 January 2026, Rawabi renewed for three years. Its group IT director, Lehan Takhar, had come to Dubai from Jalandhar twenty years earlier and negotiated in detail; his clause named a median bill time below ninety-five seconds at Rawabi's tills by 31 March 2027. Nobody asked how that median would be computed, or over which bills.

On Monday, 2 March, the board approved an FY2027 objective worded "reduce the counter task to six steps or fewer", from a slide Lubhika Taneja presented from Berlin. Engineering read it as a commitment to ship a flow; sales, as a commitment to a demo. On Monday, 11 May, Taneja circulated Flow C: a six-screen redesign in which the first scan opens the bill, loyalty is inferred from the payer's UPI handle, offers apply themselves and the invoice shares itself. It has never been built or measured.

On Friday, 3 July, the field study landed (Exhibit 2) — the first time anyone had timed a counter with a stopwatch rather than read logs. Of its 126.5 seconds of step medians, 44.0 belonged to scanning items, which no redesign removes.

From Tuesday, 18 August, fourteen stores ran an eleven-day randomised pilot, seven of them on Flow B: the standard, with step 1 folded into the first scan and step 10 into the share screen. On 5 October Thapar's telemetry memo arrived with the 93.6 per cent figure (Exhibit 3), reaching the product committee before anyone read its third footnote. On 6 October the pilot read-out (Exhibit 4) was presented; within four days the two engineers who most trusted each other were arguing about denominators.

5. The people

Lalitya Thind — VP Product, Bengaluru
Owns the objective, the clause and the budget. Wants Flow B now, Flow C after Diwali; her bonus rides on the six steps Flow B misses. Unsaid: she wrote that objective herself and no longer believes the step count is the right measure.
Lakhbir Tiwana — Head of Engineering, Bengaluru
Flow B is cheap and written; Flow C a nine-month programme disguised as a redesign. Four regulatory items cannot slip. Unsaid: he has promised two engineers Flow C will never happen.
Lovepreet Toor — Principal Engineer, Pune
Built and maintains the 2023 flow definition. The pilot result is not significant and the company is about to spend on noise. Unsaid: he finds the 1,940 definitions unmaintainable and would welcome a forced consolidation.
Lubhika Taneja — Design Director, Berlin
Flow C whole, or nothing; it is the work she was hired for. Unsaid: her six-step count assumes exception paths are not steps, and never costed them.
Lohraj Thapar — Senior Data Scientist, Toronto
The telemetry says the flow is fine; the field study is 1,206 bills against his 2.4 crore. Unsaid: he knows what footnote 3 implies and kept it out of the subject line.
Leesha Tatla — Customer Success Lead, Singapore
The problem is not the count but the three steps that fail in front of a customer. Unsaid: two of her chains have configured their flows into thirteen steps and are happy.
Luvdeep Thukral — Head of Sales, New Jersey
Needs a six-step demo for a January pipeline; his plan rewards new logos, none in India. Unsaid: three prospects quoted that flow do not know it is unbuilt.
Lehan Takhar — Group IT Director, Rawabi Fresh Markets, Dubai
The clause is the clause. Unsaid: Rawabi's queue is partly a staffing problem, and his median excludes bills voided at the till.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"Ten steps. Five on every bill, five conditional. Delete the two that are housekeeping and it is eight. That is hygiene, not a redesign, and it costs twenty-six lakh."

— Lakhbir Tiwana, product review, 7 October

"4.9 seconds, ten standard errors, eleven thousand bills in the treatment arm. I have never sent you a cleaner result."

— Lohraj Thapar, email to Thind, 6 October, 21:14 IST

"You randomised stores, not bills. Seven and seven. The standard deviations of the seven store means — 4.81 and 6.37 — put the standard error of the difference at 3.02 seconds. The unweighted store-mean difference, 5.8, is 1.9 of those; your 4.9 is 1.6. Either way p is above 0.05. We may have found nothing."

— Lovepreet Toor, reply, 7 October, 00:41 IST

"Both of you answer a question nobody at a till asked. My chains do not complain about the count. They complain that the UPI confirmation takes twenty-six seconds, and that when it fails the cashier has nowhere to go."

— Leesha Tatla, on the 20:30 IST call of Sunday 18 October: 17:00 Berlin, 11:00 Toronto and New Jersey, 23:00 Singapore, 19:00 Dubai

"I was asked for six steps in March and gave six screens in May. If we ship eight, I will be asked in April why not six, and the answer will be that we spent the money on two screens we already had."

— Lubhika Taneja, same call

"Ninety-five seconds, median, at our tills, by the thirty-first of March. I did not say whose median or which bills. Neither did you."

— Lehan Takhar, Dubai, in a call minuted 9 October

8. The options as Thind sees them tonight

Ship Flow B in November. Written, piloted, ₹25.53 lakh. Steps fall ten to eight, modal taps twenty-one to nineteen. Against it: the gain may be nothing, it misses the board's six, and it was never piloted on the Gulf variant, where the contract bites.

Build Flow C for Q1 FY2028. Six screens, ₹83.22 lakh, the only option that answers the objective as written. Against it: never measured, it takes 65.0 per cent of the uncommitted ₹128 lakh, and its count excludes Exhibit 5's exception paths.

Attack the twenty-six seconds instead. Step 6 is the largest removable block in Exhibit 2 — scanning, at 44.0 s, is larger but is the work itself. Moving small-value tenders on-device would cut the wait, but needs NPCI certification, a queue Tiwana puts at fourteen weeks. It changes no step count.

Consolidate the 1,940 definitions first. Toor's position, never formally proposed. It makes later changes cheaper and lets Darwaza say what "the flow" is, but ships nothing customer-visible in FY2027.

Thind has written the four on the whiteboard in that order, with the budget against each. Beside the first she has pencilled "3,210?" and circled it twice. Beside the other three there is nothing.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Friday, 30 October 2026, and expects a recommendation against the March objective. Rawabi's annual break date falls on 31 January 2027; the ninety-five-second test falls on 31 March, and failing it costs eight per cent of ₹9.80 crore, or ₹78.40 lakh. The FY2027 product budget is ₹6.40 crore, of which ₹5.12 crore is committed, leaving ₹1.28 crore — ₹128 lakh. Flow B takes 19.9 per cent of that, Flow C 65.0 per cent. Four regulatory items cannot slip: two NPCI, one GST e-invoice schema change, one DPDP consent record. The consent line in step 3 can be moved, not removed. Taneja's Berlin contract runs to September 2027 at some three times a Bengaluru engineer-week. The festival freeze bars any counter release between 1 and 16 November.

At twenty past eleven Thind wrote one line on the last printout, under the clause: 95 s — of what? She turned off the lights on the seventh floor without answering it, and the deployment window opened for the engineer two desks away.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Draw the counter sale from Exhibit B. How many steps does the task take? Exhibit 2 says ten, Exhibit 5 eleven in the Gulf, section 2 says 1,940 definitions are live. What is the denominator for "our flow has"?
  2. Exhibit 2 yields 95.0, 90.5 and 86.0 seconds for one flow. Say what each measures, and which a contract, a cashier and a board should see.
  3. Exhibit 2 predicts 3.8 seconds from deleting steps 1 and 10; Exhibit 4 measures 5.8 between store means and 4.9 between bill-weighted means. Reconcile the three.
  4. Exhibit 3 was circulated as 93.6 per cent; footnote 3 gives 87.65 on a wider denominator. Which belonged before the product committee, and what changes if the second is the headline?
  5. Thapar and Toor compute different standard errors from the same fourteen stores. Decide the unit of analysis, say what it costs in power, and design the next pilot within ₹128 lakh.
  6. It is Monday, 19 October. What does Thind do first, what does she stop, and what does she tell the board about an objective written in steps when the only number outsiders can enforce is in seconds?
case20v1-ux.flows:
Nine Steps to a Reminder

Chabi Ledger and the first credit entry

1. Opening

At 8:40 on Monday 19 October 2026, Kiran Sandhu opened a spreadsheet of thirty-one candidate items for Chabi Ledger's festive-season release. The head of product, based in the company's Bengaluru office in HSR Layout, had room for one. The release list had to be locked by Friday 23 October, because engineering began the festive build on Monday 26 October and would take on nothing new after it. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, and every year the weeks before it brought Chabi's largest wave of first-time shopkeepers.

Item nineteen was the one she kept returning to. It read, in full, "Shorten the first credit entry." Nobody had said by how much, or by removing what.

2. Company background

Chabi Ledger was founded in 2019 in Pune by two former bank engineers. Its app lets a small shopkeeper record udhaar, the goods sold on credit, against a customer's name, and send that customer a payment reminder over WhatsApp with a UPI link attached. It served kirana stores, stationers, tailors and hardware shops, mostly in towns such as Ludhiana, Indore and Nagpur. By 2026 it had about fourteen lakh registered merchants and a team of ninety-one, spread across Bengaluru, Pune, Berlin, Toronto and Singapore.

The market was not empty. Khatabook and OkCredit had taught a generation of shopkeepers what a digital ledger looked like, and Vyapar sold billing software to the same counters. PhonePe and Paytm already put a QR code on most of them. The merchants Chabi lost seldom went to a rival. They simply stopped opening the app, and went back to a paper bahi-khata beside the till. Chabi earned money when a merchant stayed active enough to buy the Plus plan, and its finance team valued each merchant who completed a first reminder at ₹210 of twelve-month contribution.

3. The situation

Each month about 1,00,000 merchants tried to record their first credit entry with a reminder. Kiran's analysts had mapped the task as it then existed: nine screens, from tapping "Add entry" to sharing the reminder. Exhibit 1 shows where a representative sample of 10,000 attempts, taken between 28 September and 4 October, fell away. Only 4,000 finished. Exhibit 2 draws the same funnel to scale: steps five to seven, the compulsory note, the due date and the reminder channel, shed 1,100, 800 and 600 attempts in turn, and the final share step takes the largest single bite. The mapping exercise had also shown something the dashboards never had: a finisher spent 56 seconds across the nine steps, and a shopkeeper with a customer waiting at the counter does not have 56 seconds. Festival weeks made it worse. In the days before Dhanteras and Diwali a Ludhiana cloth merchant might serve a customer every two minutes, and an app that demanded a minute of attention for each credit sale was an app left in the pocket.

The team saw the problem from four time zones. Karishma Sodhi, the product designer in Berlin, wanted the whole task redrawn as a single screen. Kavneet Sekhon, the data scientist in Toronto, who had built the funnel, pointed out that the reminder-timing model depended on the due date, one of the steps under suspicion. Kunwar Sachdeva, who led customer success from Singapore, had spent two weeks of calls with merchants in Ludhiana and Indore and said that the note field, step five, was where he heard the most complaints. Of fourteen merchants he observed, nine typed a single dot there to get past it.

4. The people

Kiran Sandhu, head of product, Bengaluru. She owned the release list and answered to the founders for its completion-rate target. She wanted a change small enough to ship before Diwali and large enough to be seen in November's numbers. She also knew that the founders, who had sold the board on a 50% completion target, would ask what the change had cost the data.

Karishma Sodhi, designer, Berlin. Three and a half hours behind India until the clocks changed on 25 October, she wanted to retire the step-by-step design and had already prototyped a one-screen entry. She tested it with twelve merchants in Ludhiana, and nine completed it unaided.

Kavneet Sekhon, data scientist, Toronto. Nine and a half hours behind until 1 November, she wanted the data the flow collected kept intact, and was wary of any change that could not be measured cleanly.

Kunwar Sachdeva, customer success, Singapore. Two and a half hours ahead of India, he wanted the complaints to stop quickly, and distrusted anything that arrived after Diwali. A call for all four was set for 19:30 IST on Thursday 22 October, which was 16:00 in Berlin and 10:00 in Toronto.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Kiran read Exhibit 1 first for its losses. The compulsory note cost 1,100 attempts, the due date 800 and the channel choice 600, together 2,500 of the 6,000 who failed to finish. The share step lost 1,400 more. Kavneet's data showed that of the 6,300 who completed the due-date step, 4,800 (76.2%) left it at the pre-filled seven days.

Option A removed steps five to seven: the note became optional, the date defaulted to seven days, and the channel defaulted to WhatsApp, which step nine already used. The flow cut a finisher's path from nine steps and 56 seconds to six steps and 29. If the other steps converted as before, the 8,200 who completed step four would yield 5,754 finishers, a ceiling of 57.5%. Kiran planned on half the gain, 4,877 or 48.8%. It cost three engineers about a week and a half, ₹3.0 lakh in all, and it shipped on Wednesday 4 November, four days before Diwali. What it surrendered was the note and a precisely chosen due date.

Option B was Karishma's one-screen rebuild. Its upside in Exhibit 3 was the largest, but it rested on a 65% assumption, shaded down from the 9 of 12 merchants (75%) who completed the prototype, and it arrived after Diwali, in the week of 8 February, and cost ₹22.5 lakh against A's ₹3.0 lakh.

Option C left the flow alone, adding a tutorial and a cashback to nudge merchants through. It was safe for the data and, with three engineers for two weeks, could ship by 6 November. Assuming 44% finished, it returned ₹8.4 lakh per monthly cohort against ₹12.5 lakh up front, about 0.7 times in the first month, the lowest of the three.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the nine steps does the shopkeeper need to reach her goal, and which does Chabi need for itself? Defend each classification.
  2. Why can step nine not be removed, though it loses more attempts than any other step? What would you ask about it next?
  3. What must be true for Option A to deliver Kiran's planning case rather than the ceiling, and what does Kavneet lose?
  4. Which option should Kiran lock by 23 October, and what would you check once the November cohort has passed?

8. A note for the learner

Task analysis asks one question before any design opinion: how many steps does the task take, and which could go? The discipline is to draw the path, count it, and sort every step into the user's goal, the company's need, or habit. Here the goal steps are the customer, amount, confirmation and sharing. The note, date and channel were company needs or habit, and Kavneet's 76.2% shows that the date was habit.

One defensible path is Option A now and Option B later. A is the only option that is cheap, ships before Diwali and attacks the three costliest removable steps. Its numbers are a planning case, not a promise, so Kiran should log the optional note and the defaulted date, and have Kavneet rebuild the timing model on the default. B is not rejected; it is sequenced. If the November cohort lands near 48.8%, the share step becomes the next target, and a smaller test of Karishma's design can tell her whether twelve merchants generalise.

A weaker answer picks B for its headline value, ignoring that its 52.5 lakh rests on one untested assumption and arrives after the season. The worst answer treats fewer steps as an end in itself and strips step nine.
exp40v2-ux.flows:
User flows and task analysis

Discovery & Design › UX & Design Collaboration · near-expert reading · session of 28 October 2026

Draw the path through a task and count the steps. How many steps does the task take, and which could go?

1. Two decisions, both about step counts

On Monday 12 October 2026 Nasreen Yeasmin read the only number Girvi Finserve's board asks about. Girvi lends against household gold through a mobile application and a valuation visit; September's average ticket was ₹66,000. Of the people who tapped Apply for a gold loan in September, 9,400 of the 20,000 had money in an account by 10 October (47.0 per cent): ₹62.04 crore disbursed. A point of completion is 200 applications, ₹1.32 crore a month of disbursals — hence the growth team's 9 October memo, Seven steps to four.

Her hesitation had a date attached. In March 2026 Girvi had run that experiment in its purest form: an eleven-screen application collapsed onto one scrolling screen, and completion fell from 42.0 to 33.5 per cent. The step count, under one definition, went from eleven to one. Under another it did not move.

On Tuesday 29 September 2026 Nripen Yadab, VP product at Ghuri Instruments, was reading a different document. Ghuri makes the HX-200 benchtop haematology analyser and the app that drives it; 380 were installed in Indian pathology laboratories as of 31 August 2026. In August his team timed 96 batch runs in 14 laboratories. A ten-sample batch took 38 interaction steps, executed as 119 input atoms, median 22.0 minutes. Yadab had to put a proposal to the quality committee on Friday 23 October.

Both decisions turn on the same two questions.

Exhibit 1. Girvi Finserve, gold-loan application funnel, September 2026 cohort.
StepEnteringCompletingStep rateLost here
1 Mobile number + OTP20,00017,40087.0%2,600
2 PAN + name match17,40015,80090.8%1,600
3 Identity verification15,80013,45085.1%2,350
4 Amount + gold declaration13,45012,80095.2%650
5 Bank account + penny drop12,80011,50089.8%1,300
6 Valuation appointment slot11,50010,00087.0%1,500
7 e-Sign agreement10,0009,40094.0%600
Whole path20,0009,40047.0%10,600

Cohort-based, not period-based: the 20,000 are applications started in September 2026, each followed ten days — to 10 October for a 30 September start. Each step rate is that step's own completions over its own entrants. Disbursal follows e-Sign with no further user step. The seven losses sum to 10,600, which is 20,000 minus 9,400. Step 1 loses the most people, 2,600; step 3 converts worst, losing 2,350 of the 15,800 who reach it — 14.9 per cent against step 1's 13.0 points.

2. The idea, and four schools that will not agree about it

Three terms need separating. A task is a goal-directed unit of work defined by the state the user wants to reach: release today's blood counts. Task analysis decomposes that goal into subgoals and operations, with their conditions, independently of any interface. A user flow is the path through one product by which a user accomplishes the task, drawn at the level of screens, actions and system responses: the customer journey zoomed in far enough that implementation choices stop looking like choices.

The lineage starts in industrial engineering. Frank and Lillian Gilbreth decomposed manual work into elementary motions, the therbligs, and formalised the flow process chart standardised in 1921; their problem was that work was invisible and so unmanageable. In 1967 John Annett and Keith Duncan, on naval training at Hull, published hierarchical task analysis: decomposition stops when the probability of inadequate performance times its cost — p × c — is small enough to ignore. Computing added prediction, in Stuart Card, Thomas Moran and Allen Newell's keystroke-level model of 1980 and GOMS in 1983: an expert's time on a routine task is the sum of a few operator times, computable in advance. Constantine and Lockwood's essential use cases of 1999 demanded technology-free intention-and-responsibility pairs.

Four positions descend from that history.

The minimisation school holds steps are cost and the work subtraction. It would sign: two designs for one task can be ranked on predicted expert time before either is built. It would not sign fewer screens is better.

The essential-model school holds a screen-level flow freezes the implementation into the specification. It would sign: six intention-and-responsibility pairs beat a fourteen-box screen flow. It would not sign that screen count is a design target.

The foraging school, out of Pirolli and Card's information-foraging work and Jared Spool's studies, holds clicks cheap and uncertainty dear. It would sign: a step that raises confidence can raise completion. It would not sign the three-click rule.

The instrumentation school holds the only real flow is the one in the event log. It would sign: the flow is the twenty most frequent observed paths, weighted. It would not sign that a workshop drawing is evidence.

What gets counted follows from which school a team belongs to, and Exhibit 2 counts four tasks three ways.

Exhibit 2. Four tasks counted three ways: intentions (essential-use-case sense), interaction steps (discrete user actions), input atoms (taps, keystrokes, field entries).
Task and versionIntentionsScreensInteraction stepsInput atoms
Girvi application, February 20266111131
Girvi application, March 2026611131
Girvi identity step, old11420
Girvi identity step, new (DigiLocker)1233
Ghuri ten-sample batch, August 202641338119

Rows are not comparable down a column. Ghuri's thirteen screens are nine app screens plus four device panels; the old identity step's twenty atoms are eighteen keystrokes — a twelve-digit Aadhaar number, a six-digit password — plus two taps.

3. Mechanics: what expert practice actually consists of

Competent practitioners draw the flow; experts perform nine operations, of which drawing is third. First, fix the unit: nothing can be counted until the team says which column of Exhibit 2 it means. Second, observe rather than convene: Ghuri's Bengaluru-drawn flow had 22 steps against the 38 observed. Third, draw it, with the branches and error paths teams omit. Fourth, mark each step required, conditional or repeated.

Fifth, compute the expected step count across branches. At the identity step, 9,796 of the 15,800 entrants had a CKYC record on file and completed the whole application in nine interaction steps spread across Exhibit 1's seven stages; 4,898 went through DigiLocker and took twelve; 1,106 — 7.0 per cent — fell to manual upload and took nineteen. The expected length is 0.62 × 9 + 0.31 × 12 + 0.07 × 19 = 10.63 interaction steps. Nobody experiences 10.63 of them; the figure budgets engineering effort, and it hides what matters — one user in fourteen is in a nineteen-step flow.

Sixth, price the loops. Of the 9,000 control-arm applications in Girvi's summer test, 1,980 — 22.0 per cent — asked for at least one OTP resend. That is a request, not the rejection the diamond in Figure 2 tests. Treat it as a per-attempt rate anyway — an approximation — and expected attempts are 1 / (1 − 0.22) = 1.282. Price the cycle off the drawing: the loop returns to Tap “Send OTP”, so one extra pass costs 1.55 + 6.40 + 3.03 + 0.20 = 11.18 seconds, and 0.282 of a pass is 3.15 seconds. Seventh, price the time where the task is routine and the operator skilled, as Exhibit 3 does: M = 1.35 s mental preparation, K = 0.28 s a keystroke, a tap operator T = 0.20 s, and R from Girvi's logs rather than assumed.

Exhibit 3. Keystroke-level model of the identity step. Constants from Card, Moran and Newell; R from Girvi's logs for July 2026.
OperatorSeconds eachOld countOld secondsNew countNew seconds
M, mental preparation1.3534.0534.05
K, keystroke0.28185.0400.00
T, tap0.2020.4030.60
R, system responsemeasured29.5026.10
Whole sequence—2518.99810.75

The predicted saving is 18.99 − 10.75 = 8.24 seconds, 43.4 per cent of the old sequence. System response is 9.50 of the old 18.99 seconds, 50.0 per cent: half the cost of proving identity was Girvi's systems responding, and two-thirds of that half — 6.40 seconds, 33.7 per cent of the sequence — was waiting for an SMS. The model is also error-free: adding the 3.15 seconds of expected resend cost lifts the old mean to 22.14 seconds, and still says nothing about users who never completed.

Eighth, reconcile the drawing against the log: every drawn branch needs an observed frequency, every frequent path a branch. Ninth, ask of every step proposed for deletion: who does this work if it goes? Steps rarely die; they relocate — to support, to backstage operations, to a later step, or into the user's head. Girvi found this in March, when support contacts rose from 41 to 58 per thousand completions, 41 per cent higher, in a month when the funnel was simpler.

4. The conditions, stated as claims you can test

Step reduction is a bet with four testable preconditions. One: the step is the binding constraint. Ask what share of its losses have a cause the step controls. At Girvi's appointment step, 918 of the 1,500 who dropped — 61.2 per cent — were shown no valuation slot within 48 hours, and removing a step cannot create capacity, so the claim fails. Two: attention is scarce relative to the work. True of a borrower on a phone at a bus stop, false of a technician paid to be there. Three: the step carries no record-keeping or consent function. Girvi's e-Sign and Ghuri's per-sample confirmation fail outright. Four: the work does not simply move. A step-reduction project without a support-volume and rework metric cannot know whether it worked.

The idea turns actively misleading twice over. Once where as much of a flow's cost is waiting as acting — 9.50 seconds of system response against 9.49 of user work — so counting user steps aims effort at half the problem. Again where the user's problem is doubt: there each reassurance is a step added and a conversion gained.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature firms actually do

Ghuri's batch run crosses three surfaces: eight steps at the bench, eleven on the instrument panel, nineteen in the app. Of the 22.0 median minutes, 9.0 are at the bench, 5.0 at the analyser and 8.0 in the app — 8.0 of the 22.0 minutes, 36.4 per cent. A team counting only its own steps optimises just over a third of the task.

The seams are where mature firms differ from their own descriptions. Ghuri's field-service head, Nishant Yashobanik, owns the installation flow, the app team the worklist, firmware the panel; nobody owned all 38 steps until the August study. The seam can be a legal boundary: NABL accreditation under ISO 15189 requires every released result to be traceable to the person who released it, so the per-sample confirmation is not a UX choice. Girvi's equivalent is the Reserve Bank's know-your-customer requirement: it fixes the identity step's existence and leaves only its routing negotiable. On two-sided products the seam is the other side of the market: a step deleted from the borrower's flow reappears in the valuer's day. In AI-native flows the count is not a property of the design — a conversational application may take one turn or nine — so the metric becomes expected turns to resolution.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

They refuse to count before fixing the unit. The tell-tale sign is two people quoting different counts for one flow and neither noticing; Exhibit 2's middle rows make 11, 1 and 31 all true at once, and neither is wrong.

They separate the modal path from the expected path. The tell is a one-number answer to “how long is the flow?” Girvi's expected 10.63 averages branches taken by 62, 31 and 7 per cent of users, and the nineteen-step branch is where to look first.

They treat waiting as a step. The tell is a diagram with boxes only for user actions. Half of Girvi's old sequence, 9.50 of 18.99 seconds, was system response; draw only user action and you redesign the typing, leaving the waiting.

They know what the time model cannot see. The tell is a business case resting on predicted seconds. The keystroke model predicted 8.24 seconds on the error-free path; the test moved completion by 8.0 points. Those are different quantities; abandonment has no operator in the model at all.

They price loops before straight lines. The tell is a diagram with no cycles in it. A 22.0 per cent resend rate adds 3.15 seconds to an 18.99-second sequence, because the loop re-runs four operations, not one.

They ask who inherits the work. The tell is a step-removal proposal with no downstream metric. Girvi's March simplification moved work to support, 41 to 58 contacts per thousand completions; a removal is net positive only once that work is priced.

They recognise steps whose function is evidence. The tell is a step called redundant because it tells the user nothing new. Its function is to create a record for somebody else: deleting it saves no effort and destroys the trail that keeps a laboratory accredited.

They choose the flow's boundaries, and go where the task is performed. The tell is a funnel beginning where instrumentation happens to begin. Girvi's 47.0 per cent is measured from the tap on Apply; from the advertisement it is far smaller, and where the flow starts decides which step looks worst. The same reflex sent Ghuri's interaction designer to the bench, where eight steps appear in no log.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the currency is abandonment: attention is scarce and unpaid, and a point of completion is worth ₹1.32 crore a month of disbursals to Girvi. In B2B and enterprise, users cannot abandon, so the analysis converts into labour minutes, errors and training: Ghuri's gain is 13.4 minutes per laboratory per day, a renewal argument rather than a conversion one, and the buyer who signs is not the user who waits. On platforms the two sides' flows interlock, and a step removed on one side reappears on the other. In hardware, steps are constrained by physics and release cadence: Ghuri cannot ship a panel change monthly, so the app absorbs the flexibility. In AI products the count becomes a distribution.

Where it does not differ is worth saying plainly: the discipline is identical in all five settings — fix the unit, observe, mark required against conditional, price the loops, ask who inherits the work. By stage, seed teams have no log and must observe; growth teams optimise within the existing flow, where the essential-model warning bites hardest; at scale the flow spans teams, and seams become the dominant source of steps.

8. Three worked examples

The one that worked. Girvi's identity test ran from Tuesday 7 July to Monday 10 August 2026, randomising at entry to the identity step, 9,000 applications an arm. Identity-step completion was 7,065 of 9,000 in control, 78.5 per cent, against 7,785 of 9,000 in treatment, 86.5 per cent: 8.0 points on a standard error of 0.56 points. The new flow went to all users on 1 September 2026. September's blended 85.1 per cent then sat below the test arm's 86.5, a gap nothing in this cohort explains.

The second-order arithmetic that nearly fooled them. The four steps downstream of identity converted at 9,400 of 13,450, 69.9 per cent, in September, so multiplying the 8.0-point gain by 0.699 predicts 5.6 points overall. The test delivered 4,941 of 9,000 against 5,399 of 9,000: 5.1 points. The temptation is to make the half-point shortfall a finding: the 720 rescued applications produced 458 extra disbursals, not the 503 that 69.9 per cent implies, a rate of 63.6 per cent. The arithmetic will not carry it. The standard deviation of the difference between the arms' disbursal counts, √(9,000 × 0.549 × 0.451 + 9,000 × 0.600 × 0.400), is about 66, so a 45-disbursal shortfall is 0.7 of one, and the 63.6 per cent carries some nine points of uncertainty. These data are consistent with 69.9 per cent; the second-order question needs a bigger test.

The one that failed. In February 2026 the application ran across eleven screens and 6,384 of 15,200 starts completed, 42.0 per cent. In March the eleven became one scroll — step count unchanged on every convention except screens — and 5,360 of 16,000 completed, 33.5 per cent. The diagnosis, from Nayonika Yashogupta's six sessions with lapsed applicants, was that one screen destroyed the sense of progress: the design optimised a number nobody experienced. The recovery was not eleven screens again but four, with a progress indicator and the heaviest fields last, reaching 6,913 of 15,500, 44.6 per cent, in May.

The one still open. Ghuri's proposal removes 7 of the 19 app steps, 36.8 per cent of them, by building the worklist from the laboratory information system, saving a median 3.0 minutes a batch. It adds a reconciliation step whenever the system's order and the physical rack disagree — 6 of 96 observed batches, 6.25 per cent — at a median 9.0 minutes of rework. Expected time is 22.0 − 3.0 + (0.0625 × 9.0) = 19.56 minutes: 2.44 minutes saved a batch, 13.4 minutes per laboratory per day at 5.5 batches. The rework tax takes 18.8 per cent of the gross saving, and since the baseline already holds those six batches, 19.56 minutes is conservative.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

The drawn flow and the logged flow diverge. Early sign: no branch for a path the log shows is common — Ghuri's 22 drawn steps against 38 observed. Diagnostic: what share took each branch last month? Caught late, engineering serves a path a minority uses.

Deleting the record. Early sign: a step called “just a confirmation”. Diagnostic: if this result is challenged in nine months, what shows who released it? Caught late, an accreditation finding and months of releases to rebuild.

Optimising the happy path. Early sign: the diagram has no error branches. Diagnostic: draw what happens when each step fails, with frequencies. Caught late, the fallback path's 7.0 per cent can become most of the support load.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The minimisation school, steelmanned, rests on a consistent body of funnel experiments where removing a field or a screen raised completion. For it to be wrong, completion would have to be bounded by something other than effort. At Girvi's appointment step, where 61.2 per cent of losses were slot scarcity, it is wrong.

The essential-model school rests on the stronger historical record: the gains that matter came from reframing tasks, not optimising flows. For it to be wrong, the task's structure would have to be genuinely fixed, as regulation sometimes makes it — the identity step must exist, and only its routing was in play.

The instrumentation school rests on the finding that drawn flows miss the modal path. For it to be wrong, the decisive steps would have to be invisible to instrumentation — as Ghuri's eight bench steps, 9.0 of 22.0 minutes, are to every log the company has.

The foraging school rests on studies where users tolerated more clicks when each one confirmed they were on the right path, and on the three-click rule's long record of failure. For it to be wrong, confidence would have to be free: users would have to know, unprompted, that the next step is the right one. Girvi's recovery, which added a progress indicator and removed no step, is a point in its favour — though it changed three things at once, so it settles little.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this draws flows; someone who has internalised it asks what decision the drawing is for. They want the denominator before the rate and the distribution before the average, and they go and watch, having been wrong about work-as-done too often. They refuse a step-count target while insisting on a step-count convention. And they can say which part of a redesign's gain the model predicted and which part came from where it cannot see.

12. The decisions

Yeasmin rejected Seven steps to four on 14 October 2026. The appointment step stays: 918 of the 1,500 losses there are slot scarcity, and no interface change makes a valuer appear. She attacked the first step instead, which loses the most people, 2,600, and where 1,742 of those 2,600 — 67.0 per cent — have no SMS delivery receipt. The flow's step count will not change.

Yadab will take the worklist automation to the quality committee on 23 October, with the reconciliation step in the design and its 0.56 expected minutes priced in. He will not take the auto-release proposal, which would have removed a mean 7.6 of the 119 input atoms — 6.4 per cent, one for each of the 7.6 results a ten-sample batch returns normal on average — by releasing those results unconfirmed. His reasoning: the step's function is traceability, not information, and the way to buy those atoms back is a batch-level release with per-sample exception review.

Discussion questions. First: the March redesign cut screens from eleven to one and nothing else. Which column of Exhibit 2 should have been its target? Second: the test could not resolve whether rescued users convert like everyone else. What would a test powered to settle that cost, and what decision would turn on it? Third: who should decide the fate of a step whose purpose is evidence — the technician, the pathologist who signs, or the product manager who costed it?

13. Going deeper

  • Customer journey mapping — the same path, coarser; which flow to draw.
  • Onboarding and first-run design — step count against confidence.
  • Friction audits and step counting — this arithmetic, product-wide.
  • UX fundamentals for PMs — vocabulary for refereeing a critique.
  • Usability heuristics — the checklist that catches omitted error paths.
  • Information architecture and navigation — what sets how many steps a task can take.
  • Usability testing — work-as-imagined against work-as-done.
  • Design systems and components — why step cost varies.
  • Content design and microcopy — the cheapest fix for doubt.
