The Second Tap

Kriyal Health Systems and release 8.4

A diagnostics software firm in Pune rebuilt the screen its customers' front desks live on. Nine weeks later its largest client served notice.

1 · Sunday night, Baner

At 11.40 p.m. on Sunday, 18 October 2026, rain had driven Tanisha Dulat from her balcony in Baner to the dining table, under Navaratri lamps. At 9.30 next morning the Senior Vice-President, Product of Kriyal Health Systems had to say what went into release 9.0.

Four documents were open. A letter of Tuesday, 29 September: Kundara Diagnostics — 410 collection centres, a quarter of Kriyal's revenue — invoking clause 7.3, forty-five days to cure, expiring Friday, 13 November. A memo from Thea Dhupia in Berlin: 8.4 was the first usable thing Kriyal had shipped, and the data saying otherwise measured the wrong people. A term sheet for Kawthar Medical Group in Dubai, ₹14.60 crore over three years, due by 30 November, specifying the dense single order screen 8.4 had abolished. And a spreadsheet from Tarika Dasmana in Toronto, tabbed same data, two bases.

On Thursday, 22 October, she was to present to a board that wanted "a clear view on 8.4". She had a design she believed in, a safety number that had moved the right way, a throughput number that had moved the wrong way, and two measurement systems seventeen percentage points apart.

2 · Kriyal Health Systems

Kriyal was founded in Pune in 2017 by Tejinder Dhanoa, eleven years an operations head at a pathology chain, and Dulat, then a product manager on hospital billing. Its first module printed a barcode label for a blood tube at the moment the order was taken, so tube and requisition could not drift apart.

By 2023 Kriyal was a suite — Kriyal Desk at the counter, Kriyal Field on the phlebotomist's phone. Then it won Kundara, whose condition was that its own screen layout survive: field order, density, branding. Kriyal built Layout Studio, a per-client override for field ordering and screen density, in six weeks and shipped it in October 2023. It worked. It also meant that by mid-2026, 41 layout variants covered 468 of its live centres — 40.8 per cent of the installed base — each needing re-authoring by hand before it could take a new information architecture.

A Series B of ₹168 crore closed in November 2024. Revenue for the year to 31 March 2026 was ₹72.10 crore (Exhibit 1), ₹18.45 crore of it Kundara's.

3 · The industry

Indian diagnostics in 2026 was consolidating and price-compressed. Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis Healthcare and Thyrocare held the national brands; Redcliffe Labs and Healthians had made home collection a volume game; Tata 1mg and Apollo 24|7 took margin at the funnel's top. Regional chains like Kundara competed on turnaround and panel price, so rework and queue time landed in one quarter.

NABL accreditation governed what a lab could report; the National Health Authority's ABDM programme pushed labs to link results to a patient's ABHA number; and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 required a consent notice before health data was collected — in Kriyal Desk, two taps that could not be removed. Counter payment had moved to UPI on the NPCI rails, and Kriyal's subscription attracted GST at 18 per cent where its customers' services did not.

Against CrelioHealth and Attune, Kriyal's international exposure was small and strategically loud: 23 centres in the UAE and Singapore produced ₹7.82 crore, ₹34.00 lakh a centre against ₹6.50 lakh for an Indian chain centre. Kawthar would add some 62 per cent to that, ₹4.87 crore a year, and brought a Dubai Health Authority regime and a bidirectional Arabic–English interface.

4 · What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The thesis behind 8.4 was an onboarding cost. In January 2026 Tarannum Dhall's team costed an old complaint: nine working days of supervision before a new front-desk operator could take an order unaided, against Kundara front-desk attrition of 44 per cent a year. Dhupia's team rebuilt Desk on four commitments — one primary action per screen; the 180-test catalogue behind search and a four-panel hierarchy instead of a flat grid of 24 tiles; a mandatory patient-confirmation step before the label printed; and touch targets enlarged from roughly 7 mm to 11 mm (Exhibit 2).

The 60-centre pilot in June went well: supervised onboarding fell from nine days to four. Nobody flagged until August that none of the 60 was Kundara's: two other chain clients had opened them all in the previous eleven months, staffed almost entirely by operators with under a year's service.

Release 8.4 reached Kundara's 410 centres on Monday, 27 July, in the second of four waves; by the week of 21 September all but the 58 on the other Layout Studio variants were on it. Kundara's weekly median handle time (Exhibit 4) went from 129 seconds in its last week on 8.3 to 168 in its first on 8.4, settled near 150, and did not return. On 29 September Kundara served notice.

Then the measurements disagreed. The August time-and-motion study on nine centres (Exhibit 3) found 8.4 slightly faster overall; telemetry found it 16.0 per cent slower on Kundara. Dasmana's note observed that the study's centres came from those not on layout overrides, excluding every Kundara centre, and that its operator mix bore no resemblance to Kundara's, where 890 of 1,435 front-desk operators had over three years' service.

Dhupia's memo made a narrower claim: scoring both catalogues with the same equiprobable Hick–Hyman form, RT = a + b log2(n+1) at a = 0.20 s and b = 0.15 s/bit, the old flat grid of 24 tiles gives log2(25) = 4.64 bits and 0.90 s for one decision; the new four-panel-then-six-test hierarchy gives log2(5) + log2(7) = 5.13 bits over two decisions and 1.17 s. The difference is 0.27 s per test selected, or 0.93 s at Kundara's mean of 3.4 tests an order — 4.4 per cent of the 21.0-second gap. She declined to re-score either side with the frequency-weighted entropy form: there was no clean frequency table for the Kawthar catalogue, and two forms on two sides of one comparison would give a number she could not defend. Her memo conceded one defect — the new teal primary-action fill measured 3.1:1 against its label on the WCAG 2.1 contrast ratio, where 8.3's blue measured 5.8:1 and the standard asks 4.5:1.

5 · The people

Tanisha Dulat — SVP Product (Pune)
Owns release 9.0 and the board slide; says the question is which users 8.4 is for. Incentive: a clean Series C narrative. Not saying: she approved the pilot's centre selection herself, without asking how the centres were picked.
Tejinder Dhanoa — co-founder and CEO (Bengaluru)
Wants the mis-labelling result on the deck's front page and the notice treated as a negotiation. Incentive: the Series C. Not saying: he has told a director 8.4 "cut mis-labelling by two-thirds", which Exhibit 5 does not support.
Thea Dhupia — Principal Designer (Berlin)
Argues 8.4 is right and the measurement wrong; reversing it would be the third time Kriyal traded usability for a renewal. Incentive: the first work she can show. Not saying: she holds a Berlin offer, decidable by mid-November.
Tanmeet Dhindsa — VP Engineering (Bengaluru)
Estimates 14 person-weeks per Layout Studio variant, 560 for the forty remaining. Incentive: stop nine engineers being torn between Dubai and a rollback. Not saying: Kundara's variant took 16 person-weeks in May, and his estimate is that figure rounded down and multiplied.
Tarika Dasmana — Staff Data Scientist (Toronto)
Has shown Exhibits 3 and 4 measure different populations on different bases, and will not say which is right. Incentive: to be the one who was careful. Not saying: she thinks the 58-centre cohort too small for the weight it will carry.
Tarannum Dhall — Director, Customer Success, APAC (Singapore)
Originated the onboarding thesis and still believes it. Incentive: renewals across 318 standalone labs, where 8.4 has gone down well. Not saying: three large accounts want the old grid back and she has kept the requests out of the queue.
Tegbir Dewan — Head of Enterprise Sales, North America (Edison, New Jersey)
Needs Kawthar signed by 30 November and has called its dense single-screen order form "configurable". Incentive: commission clearing in December. Not saying: what he showed Kawthar in September was an 8.3 screenshot.
Tirath Dogra — COO, Kundara Diagnostics (Gurugram)
Served the notice; wants the old layout back and the clause 7.3 baseline fixed at the seven pre-release weeks. Incentive: a renewal he must take to his board in April. Not saying: his abandonment figure comes from counters at 18 of his 410 centres.

6 · Exhibits

7 · Voices

Dhupia, product chat, Tue 29 Sep, 18.12 IST (14.42 Berlin)

"Read the notice again. It says handle time. It does not say anyone sent the wrong tube to Gurugram. We moved 21 seconds and halved the thing that gets a patient the wrong result."

Dasmana, email, Wed 30 Sep, 07.05 IST (21.35 Toronto, Tuesday)

"Exhibits 3 and 4 cannot be reconciled as stated, and I am not going to pick one for the board. Both bases are in the footnotes. Read them before Thursday."

Release review, Fri 2 Oct, 09.30 IST, transcript

Dhanoa: "We cut mis-labelling by two-thirds. That goes on slide two."
Dasmana: "It is 13.0 against 26.1 per ten thousand. On the printed rates that is 13.1 off 26.1 — 50.2 per cent, just over half, not two-thirds."
Dhindsa: "On four weeks and a cohort of 58 centres nobody picked for the purpose."

Dhall, chat, Thu 8 Oct, 20.40 IST (23.10 Singapore)

"Standalone labs love it. But three accounts want the grid back as a toggle and I have not raised the tickets."

Dogra, call note, Fri 16 Oct, 16.00 IST (14.30 Dubai)

"My operators are not slow. Your screen asks them twice what it used to ask once, and the second tap is the one they do not expect. Give me back my layout. And do not send me the August study — none of those nine centres is mine."

8 · The options as Dulat sees them

One: restore the 8.3 layout for Kundara through Layout Studio. Sixteen person-weeks went into Kundara's variant for 8.4 in May; Dhindsa thinks reversing it is twelve. It cures clause 7.3 if the gap is the layout, keeps ₹18.45 crore, and leaves 1,435 operators on the screen that produced 26.1 mis-labels per ten thousand.

Two: hold 8.4 everywhere and negotiate the baseline. Kriyal's position would be that clause 7.3's baseline is the figure recorded at the April 2025 renewal, 147 seconds, not the seven pre-release weeks; on that reading the ceiling is 161.7 seconds and nothing has been breached (Exhibit 4). Dogra reads it the other way. The clause does not say.

Three: ship a density preference in 9.0. One account-level setting, dense grid or guided flow, defaulting to guided. Dhall's three accounts get their toggle and Dewan, whose Dubai lab directors run 60 to 90 orders a shift on one screen, can sell Kawthar honestly. Dhupia calls this "two products with one test suite"; Dhindsa prices it at nine person-weeks plus every future screen designed twice.

Four: keep 8.4 and attack the 21 seconds. Keyboard entry for the test field, a recently-used strip, the confirmation collapsed into the print action, the teal fill fixed to 4.5:1. Dhupia estimates twelve of the twenty-one seconds back without touching the information architecture. Nobody has measured whether the twelve come back from the operators who lost them.

Dulat's margin note was not a fifth option but a question: which of these four would I still believe in a month? She had written it before Dogra's call note and had not revised it after.

9 · The deadline and the hard constraints

Release 9.0 cuts on Monday, 19 October and ships a fortnight later; the board meets Thursday, 22 October. The cure period ends Friday, 13 November, after which ₹2.21 crore of credits accrue and April's renewal opens worse. Kawthar's window closes Monday, 30 November.

The front-end team is nine engineers and will not grow before Q1 FY2028; design is three, one in Berlin. Cash on 30 September was ₹96.4 crore against a September net burn of ₹3.1 crore a month — roughly 31 months of runway before anything here is funded. Layout Studio is the constraint nobody voted for: forty variants over 58 centres still sit on 8.3, and Dhindsa has said in writing he will not re-author them and build Kawthar's interface in the same two quarters.

The rain had stopped. Dulat opened same data, two bases and looked again at the two numbers that would not sit together: a study saying her release saved a second and a half, telemetry saying it cost twenty-one. It was 1.20 a.m., and the deck was still on slide two.

10 · Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, does each of Exhibits 3 and 4 measure — unit, population, filter, period? Name the denominator of every rate you quote.
  2. Exhibit 5 shows mis-labelling halved and rejection unchanged. What must be true of the rejection reason codes for that to be evidence about 8.4 rather than about how technicians fill in a form?
  3. Reweight Exhibit 3's four tenure medians with the operator mix in Exhibit 6's footnote. What do you get, and what does it do to Dasmana's claim that the exhibits cannot be reconciled?
  4. Dhupia shows the menu change accounts for 0.93 seconds of the 21.0-second gap. If the law explains 4.4 per cent of the movement, what is the other 95.6 per cent, and which of 8.4's four commitments would you test first?
  5. Exhibit 6 declines to total its rows. Make the case for option one and for option two using only rows from it, and say which measurement each leans on.
  6. It is 9.30 on Monday. What goes into release 9.0, what does Dulat tell Dogra, and what does she say on Thursday about how Kriyal will decide this class of question next time?

UX fundamentals for PMs: the few principles that decide whether people can use the thing

Five load-bearing claims, the quantitative laws misquoted about them, and what a product manager adjudicates when two competent designers disagree.

Discovery & Design › UX & Design Collaboration · Exp40 reading page · 15 October 2026

1Two decisions, one day apart

On Thursday 8 October 2026, in Bengaluru, Yashaswi Gangopadhyay had a design review she did not want. Gangopadhyay is Director of Product at Moulik Health, a teleconsultation app with 4.1 million monthly active users reached mostly through employer benefits tie-ups. The screen in dispute was booking step two, a flat list of fourteen specialities. In September 2026, 1,46,000 sessions reached it and 38,000 ended there without a speciality chosen: 26 per cent abandonment on one step.

Yadunath Guhathakurta, who leads design research at Moulik, proposed four groups of at most four. A moderated prototype test on 1 and 2 October returned a mean System Usability Scale score of 78.8 against 61.5 for the live screen. Gangopadhyay suspected the hierarchy would be slower for almost everybody, and SUS the wrong instrument.

The next morning in Pune, Yaman Gogoi faced the same question with a bill attached. Gogoi is VP Product at Madhuban Instruments, whose milk-collection terminal — weighing pan, fat analyser, touchscreen — stands at 2,840 village collection centres run by district co-operative unions. Yachika Ghatak, a field engineer, had spent nineteen mornings at centres in Kolhapur and Sangli during the September pilot: the Confirm and Void keys are 12 mm wide and 4 mm apart, pressed with a milk-wet thumb while forty farmers watch. Re-moulding the bezel would cost ₹1.9 crore, or ₹6,690 a terminal; the alternative was a training video.

Both decisions ask where the knowledge required to act correctly is stored, and what it costs to move it. These principles are claims about the location of knowledge, each locally unarguable and collectively in conflict, so the manager's job is pricing the trade between them.

2The idea, and who disagrees about it

A usability principle is a testable claim: if the knowledge needed to act correctly sits in the artefact rather than the user's head, performance improves and errors fall. The formulation is Donald Norman's, whose The Design of Everyday Things (1988; revised 2013) set knowledge in the world against knowledge in the head. He took affordance from James J. Gibson's The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979), where it meant what an environment truly offers; designers used it for what a thing looks like it offers, and Norman spent two decades repairing that, adding perceived affordance in 1999 and signifier in 2013.

The second tradition is evaluative. Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich proposed heuristic evaluation at CHI in 1990, which Nielsen refined to ten heuristics in 1994 — attributed work, best read in the original. Grouped by underlying move they collapse to five. One, show the state: the system's condition and the last action's consequence must be perceptible unasked. Two, make the right move obvious and the wrong move physically harder. Three, match the user's model, not the system's. Four, make recovery cheaper than care: if undoing costs less than caution, people act and learn. Five, spend attention as if audited.

Table 1. Four schools, each with a proposition its adherents would sign and one they would not.
TraditionWould signWould not sign
Cognitive-heuristic
Norman 1988; Nielsen 1990		A trained reviewer predicts most failures from the artefact.That conversion settles usability.
Experimental-behavioural
Kohavi, Tang & Xu 2020		Every principle is a hypothesis; experiment adjudicates.That review may veto a pre-registered win.
Contextual-activity
Suchman 1987; Beyer & Holtzblatt 1998		The unit of analysis is the task in its setting.That principles transfer without field work.
Aesthetic-affective
Kurosu & Kashimura 1995; Tractinsky 2000		Perceived usability is partly aesthetic, with behavioural effects.That beauty substitutes for completion.

The propositions are my compressions, not quotations.

3Mechanics: the quantitative treatments, worked

Two of these principles have quantitative treatments; so does the question of how much testing is enough. Paul Fitts, in the Journal of Experimental Psychology in 1954, showed that time to reach a target rises with the logarithm of distance over target width; the standard form is Scott MacKenzie's 1992 Shannon variant, MT = a + b · log2(D/W + 1), with W measured along the axis of movement and the logarithm the index of difficulty in bits. The constants are device- and population-specific, so the law is useless without them. Madhuban fitted its own between 3 and 7 August 2026 — eight operators, 720 presses on each layout with a wetted thumb — at a = 0.20 s, b = 0.16 s per bit.

The obvious conclusion is wrong. Layout B saves 0.32 s per press and each pourer needs three, so 0.96 s per pourer and 92.16 s per 96-pourer session. But the analyser takes 19 s a sample, occupying that session for 1,824 s, or 30.4 minutes, with hands free for most of it. The motor saving is 5.1 per cent of a machine-bound cycle: nothing.

What justified ₹1.9 crore was the second-order effect: 18 of 720 presses on layout A landed on Void, 2.5 per cent, against 3 of 720 on layout B, or 0.42 per cent. At 288 presses a session that is 7.2 mis-presses against 1.2, a difference of 6.0, each costing a 19 s analyser cycle plus 25 s of re-pouring: 44 s, so 264 s a session. That is 2.86 times the motor saving, and the queue cannot absorb it. Fitts's law is a diagnostic for error, not a calculator for speed.

Hick (1952) and Hyman (1953) supply the second treatment: choice reaction time rises with the information content of the set, RT = a + b · H, where H is the entropy of the choice in bits and reduces to log2n when the n alternatives are equiprobable. Moulik fitted a = 0.30 s, b = 0.18 s per bit on its own tap latencies. Its fourteen specialities are nowhere near equiprobable, and the real mix in Table 2 carries H = 3.0635 bits, giving RT = 0.851 s against the 0.985 s an equiprobable fourteen would cost. Guhathakurta's hierarchy removes none of that information: by the chain rule, the entropy of the group choice plus the entropy of the speciality given the group is the same 3.0635 bits. What it adds is a second intercept, RT = 2a + b · H = 1.151 s, so the hierarchy costs 0.300 s more per booking — about 35 per cent — and reduces nothing the user must resolve.

Table 2. Moulik's September 2026 speciality mix and its entropy, H = Σ p · log2(1/p).
SpecialityShare of bookings, pp · log₂(1/p), bits
General physician0.310.5238
Dermatology0.180.4453
Paediatrics0.130.3826
Gynaecology0.090.3127
Psychiatry0.070.2686

Total / all fourteen1.003.0635

Row six aggregates nine specialities at 0.05, 0.04, 0.03, 0.03, 0.02, 0.02, 0.01, 0.01 and 0.01; contributions are rounded to four places and the total is their sum. At 3.0635 bits the real mix carries 80 per cent of the 3.8074 bits (log214) that fourteen equiprobable specialities would, so RT = 0.30 + 0.18 × 3.0635 = 0.851 s.

The third treatment concerns how much testing is enough. Nielsen and Thomas Landauer modelled defect discovery in 1993 as 1 − (1 − L)n, L being the share of defects one participant reveals; at Nielsen's reported L of about 0.31, five find roughly 84 per cent, the origin of his claim that five users suffice. Laura Faulkner, in Behavior Research Methods in 2003, resampled 60 participants: five-person samples averaged near 85 per cent but ranged from 55 to 99.

So the rule is sequencing, not sample size: the marginal participant is worth 21.4 percentage points from one to two and 4.9 from five to six, which makes five right for a first round and wrong before an irreversible launch.

4When the principles apply, and when they mislead

Four testable conditions decide most cases. Is the task under time pressure or physical constraint? Then the motor principles dominate. Is exposure repeated? Someone performing a task five thousand times amortises learning and multiplies every later step, inverting the usual advice. Is an error's cost borne by whoever made it? If it lands on a third party, prevention replaces recovery. Does the user hold a prior model? Then violating the convention costs more than local gains.

Table 3. The four conditions, applied to both protagonists.
ConditionMoulik Health (booking)Madhuban (collection terminal)
Time pressure or constraint?No: seated, indoors, unhurried.Severe: wet thumb, glare, queue of forty.
Repeated exposure?Rare — median 1.4 bookings a year.Extreme — 192 transactions daily.
Error cost borne by the user?Yes: a wrong speciality wastes their slot.No: the farmer re-pours.
Prior model elsewhere?Yes: the delivery apps they already use.Almost none.

Median bookings covers the year to 30 September 2026; 192 is 96 pourers × two sessions.

The conditions also mark where the principles mislead. “Reduce steps” is sound for Moulik and harmful for Madhuban's operator, who benefits from a confirmation a novice finds redundant. “Spend attention as if audited” is dangerous in a regulated disclosure, where the law requires giving the user what they do not want. And “make recovery cheap” collapses where recovery is impossible: milk in the vat has no undo, so the answer must be prevention.

5Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product organisations break principle three first. A user's model of “my account” spans products owned by different teams, and the seam surfaces as two places to change one phone number. Mature companies give one team ownership of the shared object and charge others to deviate. Moulik has three surfaces that edit a dependant's date of birth; Guhathakurta's audit on 30 September 2026 found two validating age differently, sending 1,100 of September's paediatric bookings to an adult physician.

On two-sided products the principle that helps one side hurts the other: a doctor's cancellation one tap away satisfies “recovery cheap” for the doctor and destroys it for the patient. The resolution is not symmetry but choosing which side bears the friction — Moulik caps doctor-initiated cancellations at two a week.

Hardware plus software is where release trains differ by an order of magnitude. Madhuban ships firmware in a fortnight and a bezel in nine months, so software inherits a mould signed off three quarters earlier. Spend the hardware decision on constraint: a 36 mm key and 134 mm of separation are hardware-grade, the label is not.

AI-native features invert principle one in a way the 1988 vocabulary does not cover. Moulik's triage assistant, Mohor, infers a speciality from a free-text complaint, and the state needing display is confidence and reversibility, not progress. In the 1–2 October test, 9 of 12 participants accepted Mohor's suggestion unread when it was a pre-selected default, and 4 of 12 when it was a chip to tap. The first is better on steps and worse on all else: a default asserts a certainty the model lacks.

6Eight distinctions between an expert and a competent practitioner

One: the expert asks what the user is doing, not what they are looking at. The tell is vocabulary — “the speciality screen” against “a person with a rash deciding whether this app is for them”. Read as empathy, it is a change of unit, moving the measure from taps to whether the right doctor was seen.

Two: a usability score is a tripwire, not a target. SUS, John Brooke's ten-item scale from 1996, benchmarks near a mean of 68 in Sauro and Lewis's dataset. A 61.5 says something is wrong; a 78.8 does not say what was fixed. The tell is a delta with no defect named.

Three: distrust a prototype result when the prototype removed the hard part. Moulik's hierarchy tested well partly because its groups held only the specialities the tasks needed. The tell is a prototype with the edge cases absent: prototypes are meant to be simplified, and the error is forgetting the simplification is where the cost sits.

Four: Miller's seven is about memory span, not menus. Miller's 1956 paper concerns chunks held in immediate memory, and a visible list is read, not held. The tell is anyone capping a visible list at seven: fourteen visible items cost scanning, fourteen remembered ones recall.

Five: separate the aesthetic effect from the usability effect rather than denying it. A prettier design often scores better on perceived ease while performing identically on task time. The tell is a team that either dismisses visual quality as decoration or uses it to excuse a flat completion rate.

Six: consistency is a cost of change, not a virtue. It is valuable because knowledge transfers, expensive because it freezes every surface to the worst decision any has made. The tell is a design-system objection with no estimate of the inconsistency's cost: Moulik's date-of-birth control earns standardising at 1,100 misrouted bookings; the button radius does not.

Seven: recovery is budgeted against the physics of the domain. Where an action is irreversible in the world, software forgiveness does not help and the design must move to constraint. The tell is an undo for something already gone — a cancel on a dispatched shipment.

Eight: the exchange rate is stated before the argument starts. The question is not which principle matters more but what the trade is worth in the business's own currency — six mis-presses a session at 44 s each against ₹6,690 a terminal. The tell is a review ending in the senior person's taste: politics, read where it is arithmetic.

7Product type and company stage

Across product types the differences are real but narrower than the folklore. In consumer products the binding constraint is the first thirty seconds. In B2B the buyer is not the user, so a defect survives years behind a renewal. In enterprise software the inversion is sharpest: expertise is an asset, and the dense screen that fails a five-minute test is often right for someone who lives in it all day. Larry Tesler's law of conservation of complexity is the honest statement: the complexity sits in the domain and someone carries it; the question is who. Platforms add governance, since principles reach third-party developers through documentation, not code.

By stage, the question is which failure you can afford. Before product-market fit, skip the heuristic review: a usable version of the wrong thing is the costlier mistake. From roughly Series B the funnel has volume and principles become hypotheses with denominators. At scale the cost flips to consistency and accessibility, the installed base turning every change into a migration. Principle three is what does not change by stage: a product that misses the user's model is not fixed by growth.

8Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Madhuban. Gogoi approved layout B on the error arithmetic: 264 s of recovery avoided per session, or 34,080 mis-presses a day across 2,840 terminals at two sessions each — if the bench rate transfers, and that if keeps the claim honest.

Moulik, the measurement that did not mean what it said. Twelve participants scored the live version, on 17 and 18 September 2026, at 45.0, 50.0, 52.5, 55.0, 57.5, 60.0, 62.5, 65.0, 67.5, 70.0, 72.5 and 80.0 — a sum of 737.5, mean 61.5. On the prototype a fortnight later the same twelve scored 62.5, 67.5, 70.0, 72.5, 77.5, 80.0, 82.5, 82.5, 85.0, 87.5, 87.5 and 90.0, summing to 945.0 for a mean of 78.8: a shift of 17.3 points. Two things spoil it as a verdict: the same people saw the task twice, so part of the gain is practice; and Hick–Hyman makes the hierarchy 0.300 s slower per booking, 1.151 s against 0.851 s, which SUS cannot see because it asks about felt ease, not elapsed time. The 17.3 points show something is unpleasant, not that grouping is the fix.

SUS scoring for the live-version respondent who scored 72.5: odd items answered 4, 4, 5, 4, 3 contribute (response − 1) = 3, 3, 4, 3, 2, summing to 15; even items answered 2, 1, 2, 3, 3 contribute (5 − response) = 3, 4, 3, 2, 2, totalling 14. The raw 29 × 2.5 = 72.5.

Mrittika Compliance, the failure. Mrittika sells GST reconciliation software to chartered-accountancy firms. On 2 March 2026 it replaced a dense nine-field reconciliation table with a four-step wizard, citing “cognitive load”. Across the 31 firms running above 5,000 invoices a month, median invoices reconciled per hour fell from 148 to 96, a drop of 35.1 per cent, and weekly support tickets rose from 11 to 47. Principle five had been misapplied: the wizard lowered load for a novice and destroyed the expert's ability to see nine fields at once. On 27 April 2026 the dense table was restored as those accounts' default, the wizard surviving for a new user's first fourteen days. By 15 June 2026 median throughput was 161 an hour, 8.8 per cent above the original 148. The detour cost fifteen weeks and a renewal.

9Failure modes and their early warning signs

Principle-citation as argument: “cognitive load” with no number after it. Ask what would we measure to know we were wrong? Late, it produces Mrittika's wizard. Optimising the step, not the task: a funnel stage improves and end-to-end completion does not. Ask did the people who got past this screen finish? It costs a year of funnel work against flat revenue. Testing the easy case: every task succeeds, so the session tested the facilitator's task-writing. Ask which task could a user fail? Accessibility as a late audit: contrast and target size are geometry, expensive once a design hardens. Ask what are they, in numbers, today?

10Where experts genuinely disagree

The live dispute is not whether principles matter but what adjudicates them. The inspection position, at its strongest: usability defects are properties of artefacts, a trained reviewer finds most in an afternoon, and an experiment costs weeks while saying only which variant won, not why. It would be wrong if reviewers disagreed with each other as much as users vary — and the evaluator-effect literature, where independent reviewers of one interface overlap surprisingly little, is that case.

The experimental position, steelmanned: judgement about what users will do is unreliable at a documented rate, most proposed improvements do not win, and only a controlled comparison separates those that do. It fails where the metric is a poor proxy for the goal, where the population is too small for power — the unit of randomisation at Madhuban is the terminal, and a re-moulded bezel is a fleet-wide capital item, not a per-terminal variant — or where the harm falls outside the window.

The contextual position, steelmanned: both of the above evaluate a screen, and the screen is not where the trouble is. Ghatak's nineteen mornings produced the observation that mattered, and no remote testing would have surfaced a wet thumb. It fails if field observation generalises poorly from the few sites one can visit — a real risk, and the reason the bench study exists. These do not reconcile into a synthesis anyone holds. The strongest practitioners are sequential: observe to find the problem, inspect to generate candidates, experiment to choose — while saying plainly that the last step is unavailable in most products.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this quotes the principle and reaches for the list. Someone who has internalised it names the denominator before the rate — not “abandonment is high” but “38,000 of the 1,46,000 sessions that reached this screen” — prices the competing principles in the business's own currency before the meeting, and says which principle is being deliberately violated and what that buys. That last cannot be faked.

12The decisions, and three questions

Gogoi approved layout B on 9 October 2026 on the error arithmetic, with one condition: the firmware must add a void-reason code, so the next decision rests on field measurement. Gangopadhyay rejected the hierarchy on 8 October and approved a different change — the flat list retained, a search field added, the three specialities taking 62 per cent of bookings pinned above it — because grouping leaves the mix's 3.0635 bits untouched and merely charges the 0.30 s intercept twice. A second five-person round follows.

  1. Gangopadhyay overruled a seventeen-point SUS gain with a two-parameter model fitted on her own logs. What would the second round have to show for her to be wrong — and what if the hierarchy's benefit falls to the minority the dominant path ignores?
  2. Madhuban's case rests on a bench rate the field cannot confirm. At what field rate does ₹1.9 crore stop being justified, and who inside Madhuban has an incentive to measure honestly?
  3. Mrittika's wizard was defensible on every principle it cited. What single question in the February 2026 design review would have caught it?

13Going deeper

  1. Wireframes, mockups, prototypes — fidelity decides what you can test.
  2. Usability heuristics — the canonical lists in the original.
  3. Information architecture and navigation — principle three made structural.
  4. Design systems and components — consistency as asset and veto.
  5. Content design and microcopy — most signifiers are words.
  6. Accessible and inclusive design — contrast and target geometry.
  7. Design critique and collaboration — where rates get stated.
  8. Mobile, web and desktop constraints — Fitts constants differ by device.
  9. Emotional design and delight — the aesthetic tradition on its terms.
  10. Visual design literacy — Gestalt grouping, and how lists read.
  11. Industrial design and physical ergonomics — reach and glare.
  12. Trust and AI UX patterns — confidence as state.
  13. Enterprise UX: power users, bulk actions, configurability — Mrittika's inversion.
  14. Progressive disclosure and complexity management — when it works.
  15. User flows and task analysis — so step gains cannot pose as progress.
  16. Usability testing — the five, then the next five.
  17. Onboarding and first-run design — novice load over throughput.
  18. Design–research–PM handoffs — how a finding keeps its denominator.
  19. Friction audits and step counting — why step counts mislead.
  20. Designing for errors and recovery — principle four in full.
case20v1-ux.principles:
Jantri Pay: Fixing the Pay Button

A decision case on UX fundamentals

1. Opening

On Tuesday 13 October 2026, Sukhmani Cheema, head of product at Jantri Pay, sat in the Gurugram office with a printed funnel and a deadline. On Monday 19 October the company would lock its Diwali release plan, with Diwali falling on Sunday 8 November. She had about ₹40 lakh of uncommitted budget and room for one major piece of work before the festival. Three colleagues, in three countries, each wanted something different, and a fourth would have to build whatever she picked. The funnel in her hand showed that Jantri was losing people at the one moment that paid its bills. She had six days to choose, and every option had a persuasive advocate.

2. Company background

Jantri Pay was founded in Gurugram in 2019. It lets households pay society maintenance, school fees and rent through UPI, the payments rail run by NPCI, and charges an average convenience fee of ₹14 per payment. By September 2026 it served 26 lakh households in 9,400 housing societies across eleven cities, with a 140-person team and ₹180 crore raised from investors.

Its rivals were large. PhonePe, Paytm and Amazon Pay all offered bill payment inside apps people already opened daily, so Jantri's edge was narrow: it knew each society's dues and showed them without anyone typing an amount. Households liked that, and secretaries of resident welfare associations recommended the app to neighbours because collections arrived on time. If paying felt harder than a generic UPI transfer, the edge disappeared, and the recommendation with it.

3. The situation

In July the company redesigned the Dues screen. The new version added a cashback carousel, a "refer a neighbour" card and a banner for the Diwali offer. Pay Now became one of four tappable elements. The growth team had argued that dues are a dull screen and that cashback would turn it into a place people visit. Within weeks Sukhmani's dashboard moved. Exhibit 1 compares June with September. The share of people who tapped Pay Now fell from 78 to 65 per cent, and the share of payments that succeeded fell from 95 to 90 per cent. End to end, conversion dropped from 59.3 to 46.8 per cent.

Sarabjit Chopra, the customer-success lead in Singapore, saw the other side. Tickets reading "money debited, no confirmation" rose from 3,900 in June to 11,200 in September. When a user returned from the UPI app, the screen showed a spinner and nothing else, whereas UPI itself may take minutes to settle a pending transaction. Users could not tell a failed payment from a slow one, and many did the natural thing and tried again. Under RBI's rules on reversals, a failed debit returns automatically, but few customers knew that, and the app never told them.

In early October a Pune research pair ran sessions with ten users (Exhibit 2). Only six found Pay Now unaided, and only three could say whether their payment had gone through. Two of the six who failed the recovery task paid a second time. A data scientist in Toronto, working nights to overlap with Gurugram, confirmed that the drop was not seasonal: the funnel had been flat through the spring and broke in the fortnight after the July release.

4. The people

Sahil Chugh, vice-president of growth in Gurugram, owns the cashback calendar. He wants the carousel pushed harder for Diwali, because festive weeks bring the year's heaviest society billing and he has promised the board a record month. He reads the funnel as a traffic problem, not a design one.

Sanjog Chahal, design lead in Berlin, three and a half hours behind India until 25 October, has argued for months that Jantri needs a proper design system. He wants a full redesign, and he is wary of quick patches that might become permanent.

Sarabjit Chopra, in Singapore, two and a half hours ahead, sees every angry customer first. He wants the status problem fixed before anything else, and he points out that his team cannot absorb another quarter of angry calls.

Satnam Chatrath, engineering manager in Pune, can free eight engineers for two weeks, not fourteen weeks. He will build whatever Sukhmani chooses but wants it small, because the same team must also ship a compliance change in November.

Timeline scale: 5 pixels per day from 13 October.

5. The options

Option A: ship the festive carousel campaign. Sahil's plan costs ₹24 lakh, mostly a ₹20 lakh cashback pool, and goes live in two weeks. He projects a four-point rise in Pay Now taps, from 65 to 69 per cent. The upside is energy and visibility in the biggest billing weeks. The cost is that a banner adds one more competing element to a screen where only six of ten users already find the button, and it leaves the status screen untouched.

Option B: fix the pay flow against basic principles. Make Pay Now the single dominant action, show a plain-language status screen that explains pending payments in Hindi and English, disable a second attempt while the first is unresolved, and surface last month's receipt on the Dues screen. It costs ₹18 lakh and fits Satnam's two weeks, going live on Monday 2 November. Taps are projected to return to 74 per cent and success to 93 per cent. The cost is that it looks unambitious, it does nothing for screens beyond the Dues flow, and it leaves Sahil's cashback calendar in doubt.

Option C: commission the full redesign and design system. Sanjog's plan costs ₹95 lakh and takes fourteen weeks, so it lands on 25 January 2027. It would fix consistency across every screen, give engineers reusable components and speed later work. The cost is that it cannot help this Diwali, and it exceeds her uncommitted budget by ₹55 lakh.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, at which two stages did Jantri lose users, and which of them did the July redesign most plausibly cause?
  2. Match each row of Exhibit 2 to a ticket complaint and a funnel stage. What does the match tell you about where the problem sits?
  3. Which option does Exhibit 3 favour, and what would have to be true for the ranking to reverse?
  4. What would you decide on Monday 19 October, and what result in November would tell you the decision was right?

7. A note for the learner

This case asks how a handful of principles can decide whether people can use a screen at all: a clear visual hierarchy, visibility of system status, error prevention and recognition over recall. They are not craft skills; MBA programmes teach them at the level of judgement. A product manager does not draw the screen, but must judge whether it obeys them, and must say so when a growth plan breaks them.

A well-reasoned answer starts from evidence, not taste. Exhibit 1 locates the loss at two stages, and Exhibit 2 explains each of them with a named principle. It also keeps the options distinct: A adds to the screen, B repairs the flow, C rebuilds the system. Notice too that the tempting option is the one that spends the most visible effort, not the one that fixes the cause.

One defensible path is Option B, now. It is the only option live before Diwali that also fixes both broken stages. Its ₹4.62 lakh monthly gain recovers 18 lakh in under four months, and it leaves about ₹22 lakh of the ₹40 lakh uncommitted. Sukhmani should tell Sahil that the carousel waits until the status screen is live, then test it in the first week of December against a holdout group. She should tell Sanjog that B's patterns become the first components of his design system, so his plan starts with evidence rather than being abandoned. The review point is the first full week after 2 November: taps near 74 per cent and fewer "debited, no confirmation" tickets mean the diagnosis was right. If neither moves, the principles were not the problem, and she should say so.
exp20v2-ux.principles:
UX Fundamentals for PMs

The few rules that decide whether people can use the thing at all

1. A Tuesday review in Guwahati

On Tuesday, 8 September 2026, Vishrut Engti, the product manager for bill payments at Lilabati Pay, opened the weekly review with a number he disliked. Lilabati Pay is a Guwahati-based payments app that lets households pay electricity, water and broadband bills through UPI, the interbank payment rail run by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). In the week of 31 August, 1,80,000 people had tapped "Pay bill". Only 77,760 had completed a payment, a conversion of 43.2 per cent.

The design lead, Vandita Engleng, wanted the next three-week sprint spent on a home-screen refresh. Engineering preferred a rewards feature. Engti had a third suspicion, drawn from the funnel in Figure 1: a bigger loss than the payment step itself, where money is at stake, sat earlier, at a plain text field labelled "Consumer No." Of 1,44,000 people who chose a biller, only 1,15,200 got past that field. That is 28,800 people a week, against 25,920 lost at payment, abandoning a form that asks for one number.

Each completed payment earns Lilabati Pay about ₹4.50 in net fee. The week's 77,760 payments therefore earned ₹3,49,920, roughly ₹3.5 lakh. Three weeks of a six-person team is an expensive bet. Engti's problem was one of method: how to tell, in an hour, which of three proposals attacked a genuine usability failure, and which only felt like progress.

2. The idea

Usability principles are a short set of regularities about human perception and attention that predict where people will fail to use a screen, before anyone is put in front of it. They were invented to solve a specific problem: engineers in the 1970s and 1980s designed controls to match the machine's internals, and users paid for the mismatch. Psychologist Donald Norman gave the problem its vocabulary in The Psychology of Everyday Things (1988, later retitled The Design of Everyday Things). Jakob Nielsen, working first with Rolf Molich in 1990 and then alone in 1994, distilled a widely taught set of ten heuristics from factor analysis of observed usability problems.

Norman's central contribution is two gaps. The gulf of execution is the distance between what a person wants and what the product shows they can do. The gulf of evaluation is the distance between what the product did and the person's ability to tell whether it matches the intent. Most principles on a published list are, in the end, ways of narrowing one of these two gulfs. Figure 2 draws the loop.

If people cannot see what to do, or cannot tell what happened, no amount of value behind the screen reaches them.

That sentence is the one Engti could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib, because it is falsifiable: it tells a team to look for the specific step where one of the two gulfs is widest.

3. How it actually works

The method has four steps, and practitioners often leave the first and last implicit. First, fix the task: state the person's goal in their words, not the feature's. Engti's was "pay the September electricity bill before the due date", not "enter a consumer number". Second, walk the task one action at a time, asking at each screen the execution question (is it visible what to do next, and what to put here?) and then the evaluation question (after acting, can the person tell it worked?). Third, locate the widest gulf and name the principle at stake. Fourth, check the diagnosis against behaviour, using the funnel, session recordings or five people in a room.

Engti walked the consumer-number screen with Engleng. The field offered no signifier: a signifier, in Norman's later terminology, is any perceivable cue that shows where an action is possible and what it expects. (Norman adopted the word because psychologist James Gibson's older term affordance, a relation between an actor and its environment, had been misused to mean a visible hint.) A power-distribution bill prints the consumer number in a small box, mid-page, among other numbers. The screen did not show where to find it.

Evaluation failed too. A mistyped number returned "Invalid input E-417" only after the person tapped Continue. Nothing prevented the error, and the message named neither the error nor the fix. A constraint: a limit that makes the wrong action impossible or unlikely, such as accepting only digits and showing, as the person types, "9 of 12 digits". So the screen had gaps in both gulfs: a missing signifier and a missing constraint on the execution side, and unhelpful feedback on the evaluation side.

4. A worked example

Engleng proposed a sample-bill image with the consumer number highlighted, a live digit counter, and a plain-language error. The team estimated the effect on the pass rate of the consumer-number step, currently 80 per cent. Suppose it rose to 86 per cent. The funnel recomputes from the 1,44,000 who chose a biller. Passing the field: 1,44,000 × 0.86 = 1,23,840. Confirming the amount, at 90 per cent: 1,11,456. Completing payment, at 75 per cent: 83,592. That is 5,832 more payments a week than 77,760, worth 5,832 × ₹4.50 = ₹26,244 a week, or about ₹13.6 lakh over 52 weeks.

The second pass changes one input. Suppose the fix lifts the step only to 83 per cent. Then 1,44,000 × 0.83 = 1,19,520; × 0.90 = 1,07,568; × 0.75 = 80,676. The gain falls to 2,916 payments, ₹13,122 a week, or ₹6.8 lakh over 52 weeks. Halving the improvement from six points to three halves the value exactly, because every downstream step is a multiplier. Table 1 sets the two cases side by side.

Table 1. Weekly effect of the consumer-number fix (₹4.50 per payment)

Annual figures multiply the weekly gain by 52 and assume the week of 31 August is typical. Rates of 86 and 83 per cent are the team's assumptions, not measurements.

Arithmetic does not choose the sprint, but it makes the assumption explicit, which is where the argument should happen.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Principles are not laws

Nielsen's heuristics are rules of thumb distilled from observed problems. They predict where trouble is likely; they do not guarantee it.

Usable is not useful

A flawless flow for a bill nobody wants to pay through an app is still unused. Usability removes obstacles between a person and a goal they already hold. Whether the goal exists is a discovery question.

Signifier, affordance and convention

A button that looks pressable has a signifier. Whether it can be pressed is the affordance. People also rely on convention: Nielsen's observation, sometimes called Jakob's Law, is that users spend most of their time on other products and expect yours to behave likewise. Breaking convention is a cost.

Recognition beats recall

Showing a sample bill asks people to recognise a number; asking them to remember its label demands recall. Recognition is cheaper, which is why menus beat command lines for rare tasks.

The quantitative laws are narrow

Fitts's law (Paul Fitts, 1954) predicts pointing time; Hick's law (William Hick, 1952; Ray Hyman, 1953) predicts choice time as options grow. Both measure speed of a motor or choice action, not whether anyone understood the screen.

Prevention beats good error messages

A clear error is an apology. A constraint that stops the error is a better design, though not always possible: a customer may truly have a thirteen-digit number.

What principles cannot tell you

They find candidate problems, not their size, and they cannot say which problem is worth fixing. Nielsen's 2000 estimate, that five test users reveal about 85 per cent of problems, comes from the model 1 − (1 − L)n, where n is the number of users and L is the share of problems one user finds, taken as about 0.31: 1 − 0.695 ≈ 0.84. The model assumes every problem is about equally easy to find. Later studies (Spool and Schroeder; Faulkner, 2003) found five users covering as little as about 55 per cent, so treat 85 as a best case, not a guarantee of coverage.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products, first use is the test: the person has no training and leaves silently, as at Lilabati Pay. Convention matters most, and funnels are the diagnostic. In B2B products, people use the tool eight hours a day, so learning cost amortises. In a marketplace, there are two users with different gulfs. A seller who cannot tell whether a listing went live and a buyer who cannot find it are separate problems, and fixing one can worsen the other.

Size changes who applies the principles. A start-up with a six-person team can rely on the product manager and designer's judgement, with a hallway test on Fridays. A large company needs the principles written into a shared design system and critique routine, because no single person sees every screen. The risk at scale is that consistency hardens and nobody remembers why a pattern exists.

7. Common mistakes

Treating a visual refresh as a usability fix. Symptom: the redesign ships, and the funnel step rates stay flat. The misunderstanding is that a prettier screen narrows a gulf. Cheapest diagnostic: before approving the sprint, name the gulf the change narrows, in one sentence.

Reading the aggregate and missing the step. Symptom: a team debates the 43.2 per cent headline for weeks. The misunderstanding is that one conversion figure points to a cause. Diagnostic: compute each step's pass rate and rank the losses, as Figure 1 lets you do from its bar lengths.

Designing for the team's own screen. Symptom: everyone internal finds the flow obvious. The misunderstanding is that familiarity equals clarity. Diagnostic: ask someone who has never seen the product to perform the task, silently, while you watch.

Citing a principle to end an argument. Symptom: "Fitts's law says it must be bigger." The misunderstanding is mistaking a prediction about speed for a verdict on the design. Diagnostic: ask what measurement would change your mind.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Engti's Tuesday review does not begin with three proposals. It begins with the funnel, ranked by loss, and with the task written in a household's words. For the leading candidate, Engleng demonstrates the failure on a real bill, and the team states the gulf, the principle and a predicted pass rate range with its source. All three proposals are scored with the same arithmetic as Table 1, and the winner is the one whose assumptions the team can test soonest. A five-person test is booked before any code is written, and may overturn the diagnosis.

9. What Engti decided

Engti gave the consumer-number fix one week rather than three, with a release to ten per cent of users and a check on the step's pass rate after seven days. The reasoning was that the fix was cheap, the loss was the second-largest in the funnel, and the assumption of 83 to 86 per cent could be measured. He also asked Engleng to walk the final step, "Payment completed" in Figure 1, where UPI authorisation happens and which lost 25,920 people, the third-largest loss, and was unexplained. He set the 36,000 lost at biller selection aside for now: that screen is a pick-list of billers, not a form, so its loss may reflect people finding their utility missing, a coverage question rather than a usability one, and he asked for exit data to confirm it.

What to learn next: usability heuristics, to move from Norman's gulfs to a reviewable checklist; and information architecture, because a screen can be flawless while the structure that leads to it is not. Two questions to sit with. First, in a product you manage, where do you know that people succeed, and where do you only believe it? Second, if the fix raised the step only to 81 per cent, would you call the principle wrong, the diagnosis incomplete, or the estimate optimistic, and what evidence would tell you which?

Sources

D. Norman, The Design of Everyday Things (1988; revised 2013). J. Nielsen and R. Molich, "Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces", CHI 1990; J. Nielsen, "Enhancing the explanatory power of usability heuristics", CHI 1994. J. Gibson, The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979). P. Fitts (1954); W. Hick (1952); R. Hyman (1953); J. Spool and W. Schroeder (2001) and L. Faulkner (2003) on sample sizes; Lilabati Pay, its people and its figures are fictional.

Lohri Bills: Shipping Before Diwali

A decision case on usability testing

1. Opening

On Monday 19 October 2026, Vishnu Elahi, head of product at Lohri Bills, reached his Mohali office to find a short message from the build manager in Pune. The release branch for the Diwali version of the app would freeze on Friday 23 October at 6 pm. Whatever it held would reach merchants on Monday 26 October. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, and in the fortnight before it Lohri's merchants would settle more supplier invoices than in any other part of the year.

The week before, eight of those merchants had tried a redesigned "Pay supplier" flow on a prototype. Two of its three tasks had gone reasonably well. The third had not. Vishnu had promised the leadership team an answer by Thursday evening: ship the flow as built, fix it and test again, or hold the whole redesign until the new year. He had three days and one small set of observations to decide with.

2. Company background

Lohri Bills was founded in 2021 in Mohali. Its app lets kirana owners and small wholesalers pay distributor invoices by UPI, keep a digital khata of what they owe, and match payments to GST invoices. Merchants use it free; distributors pay a subscription. By September 2026 it had 1,40,000 monthly active merchants across Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Rajasthan and Delhi NCR, and revenue of ₹41 crore in FY2025-26.

The field is crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit own the habit of the digital ledger; PhonePe for Business and Paytm own the shopkeeper's QR code; Udaan and Jumbotail pull wholesale ordering onto their own apps. Most of its merchants run shops of one or two counters, buy from five to ten distributors, and pay in several instalments because cash arrives slowly after the festival season starts. Lohri's bet was narrower: the moment a shopkeeper pays a distributor, often in instalments, and wants the books to agree afterwards. Payments run on NPCI's UPI rails through a licensed partner. Fourteen engineers sit in Pune and nine in Bengaluru, with a designer in Berlin, a data scientist in Toronto, a customer-success team in Singapore and a sales head in New Jersey.

3. The situation

Between 12 and 14 October, Vanita Enayat, the Berlin designer, moderated eight think-aloud sessions on the Figma prototype: three merchants in Ludhiana, three in Jalandhar and two in Mohali. Each ran 45 minutes, in Hindi or Punjabi, with a local facilitator beside the merchant and written consent for recording, as the DPDP Act, 2023 expects. The first session each day began at 11 am in Mohali, which was 7:30 am for Vanita. Each merchant attempted three tasks: add a distributor, pay an invoice by UPI, and record a part-payment.

Exhibit 1 shows the outcome. Paying an invoice went smoothly. Adding a distributor stalled twice, once needing a hint and once ending in failure, when a GSTIN lookup returned nothing and the merchant could not tell whether to retype the number or give up. The part-payment task failed for four of eight merchants even with a hint. Five of the eight said aloud that the green button, labelled "Settle", would pay the whole invoice; all four who failed were among them. One typed ₹40,000 against an invoice of ₹1,12,000, saw "Settled" appear, and moved on satisfied.

The data scientist in Toronto supplied the stakes: 38 per cent of active merchants had made at least one part-payment in the previous 90 days (Exhibit 2). Vaneet Enoch in Singapore added that her team already received "Settle" tickets from the current app. Vikash Ebenezer in New Jersey added the calendar: a Dubai dry-fruit importer, Lohri's largest distributor, would pilot the new flow only if it went live by Thursday 5 November. Vanita, for her part, had watched the recordings twice from Berlin and sent the team three clips, each under a minute, of merchants hesitating over the same button. Vishnu, working from the same clips in Mohali, noticed that two merchants had asked the facilitator what the word meant before touching it, which no summary table would have shown him. A call was set for 7 pm on Thursday 22 October, which was 3:30 pm in Berlin, 9:30 am in New Jersey and 9:30 pm in Singapore.

4. The people

Vishnu Elahi, Mohali, head of product, owns the decision and will answer for it to the founders. He has never cancelled a release for design reasons.

Vanita Enayat, Berlin, lead designer, wants the part-payment screen reworked properly. She fears that "eight is too few" will be used to dismiss what she saw.

Vikash Ebenezer, New Jersey, head of sales, wants the flow live by 5 November. He gave the Dubai client that date in September and believes the test went well: seven of the eight paid an invoice unaided, and he asks why one confusing button should hold back a feature his clients have waited a year for.

Vaneet Enoch, Singapore, customer-success lead, wants fewer tickets in Diwali week, when her team is thinnest. She does not mind a later release if it is a clean one.

5. The options

Exhibit 3 places the dates on a line. Exhibit 2 puts a cost and a consequence against each. Diwali falls twenty days after 19 October; the January date falls sixty-four days after Diwali.

Option 1: ship as built on 26 October. The upside is nearly a fortnight of exposure, the Dubai pilot secure and no extra spend. The cost is that 53,200 merchants would meet a button that five of eight testers misread, in the busiest weeks of their own year, when they are paying distributors fastest and checking least. Part-payments recorded as full settlements would corrupt khata balances, and Singapore would carry the tickets, in the week its team is thinnest.

Option 2: fix Task C and retest, shipping on 2 November. Pune would relabel the button, make part-payment the default, and show the remaining balance before confirmation. Vanita would retest with five new merchants on 28 and 29 October, from 3 pm IST (10:30 am in Berlin once Europe's clocks go back on 25 October), and Pune would cut a second release after the freeze. The cost is ₹6.5 lakh and a week less of the new flow, though the Dubai date still holds and the older flow serves merchants meanwhile.

Option 3: hold the redesign for a full rebuild in January. The upside is a calmer, more thorough redesign of all three tasks. The cost is ₹18 lakh, a missed Dubai pilot and a Diwali spent on the older flow.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly did the sessions show, and what could eight merchants not tell Vishnu? Separate observation from interpretation.
  2. Why did "Settle" fail, and does Exhibit 1 point to a screen problem, a task problem or a participant problem?
  3. How do the stakes in Exhibit 2 change what level of evidence Vishnu should demand before shipping?
  4. Which option would you choose on Thursday, and what would make you change your mind?

7. A note for the learner

Usability testing answers one question: where do real people get stuck, and why? It does so by watching use rather than asking opinions. That frames this decision. The sessions cannot say what share of 1,40,000 merchants will fail; eight people give no rate. Moderated sessions also tend to flatter an interface, since a merchant with a facilitator beside him tries harder than one alone at the counter on a busy afternoon. They can say that a specific word on a specific button produced a specific wrong belief, and that is enough to act on.

A well-reasoned answer therefore treats Task B as having gone smoothly in these sessions, Task A as a small fix and Task C as the finding. It does not average the three: the pooled 62.5 per cent hides a task that failed half the time.

One defensible path is Option 2. The cause is a word and a default, which is cheap to change, the change can be tested in two days with merchants, and the Dubai date and about a week of Diwali survive. Option 1 knowingly ships the observed failure to 53,200 merchants. Option 3 pays ₹11.5 lakh more than Option 2 to avoid a problem that a relabelled button may solve. The retest is not a second sample large enough to prove the fix works; it is a check that the specific misreading has gone. Vishnu would also stage the release to a fraction of merchants on 2 November, and agree in advance that failure of the retest, with two or more of five merchants still misreading the button, sends Task C back to the old flow while the rest ships.

Munafa Technologies: Twelve Sessions and a Board Call

Twelve merchants, a prototype, an hour each. The analytics, the survey and the sessions describe three different companies.

1. Sunday night, Ludhiana

At twenty to ten on Sunday, 15 November 2026, Yoshita Gandotra sat on the floor of her flat in Sarabha Nagar, Ludhiana, with twelve session recordings open and a board pack due at nine. The call was 18:30 IST Monday — afternoon in Berlin, morning in Toronto and New Jersey, night in Singapore.

Gandotra was Vice President, Product at Munafa Technologies Private Limited, a Ludhiana company whose app billed for about a hundred and sixty thousand small Indian merchants a month and, for a minority, arranged a working-capital loan. The board wanted one slide: would the redesign ship, what would it cost, what was it worth.

She had two exhibits that answered and disagreed, a survey that sided with one of them, and a 2022 contract that made the obvious fix the dearest.

2. How Munafa got here

Munafa was founded in 2018 by Yadvinder Grewal and two classmates, as a GST invoicing tool for the hosiery and bicycle-parts traders of Ludhiana's Gill Road. It grew on UPI's volumes and a free tier. By September 2026 it had 4,80,000 registered merchants and 1,62,000 monthly actives — 33.75 per cent of the book. FY2026 revenue was ₹74 crore: ₹41 crore subscriptions, ₹26 crore lending fees and ₹7 crore from one white-label contract in Dubai.

What shaped everything after it was decided in March 2022. With no lending licence and no appetite for balance-sheet risk, Grewal signed a co-lending agreement with Munsif Capital Finance, a Chandigarh non-banking finance company. The terms were generous; Schedule 4 was not. It fixed the sequence and wording of five screens — eligibility, consent, disclosure, offer, acknowledgement — behind sixty days' notice and a joint legal review. Munafa also built the journey on a single WebView shell, frozen in June 2025, which is why nothing on those screens could reflow on a small handset without rebuilding it.

3. The industry around it

Merchant credit in India in 2026 was crowded and heavily supervised. PhonePe, Paytm and Razorpay offered a version of it, Flipkart offered it to its own sellers, and ONDC was making seller financing portable. The plumbing was public: UPI and NPCI for collections, the Account Aggregator framework for statements, the GST Network for turnover.

Supervision tightened twice in 2026, directly on Munafa's screens. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions required a Key Fact Statement — annual percentage rate, all-in charges, recovery contacts — displayed and acknowledged before a borrower accepted; the version Munsif approved in April 2026 ran to fourteen rows. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act required the Account Aggregator notice to itemise purpose and retention rather than collapse into small print, adding a scrolling block above the button. Neither could be removed or summarised away.

Munafa's global exposure came from one contract: Mazaya Retail Group, a Dubai grocery chain, ran Munafa's white-label portal for its vendors at ₹7 crore a year, renewable 31 January 2027, on Munafa's own component library.

Exhibit 1 — What was decided when

Scale. Rail A, 6.5 px per month from Jan 2022 at x=50; rail B, 30 px per month from Jan 2026 at x=450. Within-month markers sit at month start plus (day − 1)/days-in-month of a month's width: 26 Oct at x=744.2, 15 Nov at x=764.0. The rails are not on a common scale.

4. The situation in detail

Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence. Through the first half of 2026 the credit squad believed it knew where applications died: the support queue was thick with tickets about rotated uploads, and turnover proof was the step the field team complained about. In July the squad wrote a redesign brief around document capture.

Yashleen Gauba, who led design from Berlin, pushed back: the brief was treating the loudest complaint as the worst experience, and nobody at Munafa had watched a merchant use the journey. In September the company funded a moderated think-aloud study on a clickable prototype — version three, which reworked the consent and offer layouts but left Schedule 4's wording and order untouched, because it had to. Yashvini Ghuman, a senior researcher in Pune, ran twelve sessions between Monday 26 October and Friday 6 November, seven in Ludhiana and five in Pune, around Diwali on 8 November. Each ran sixty minutes, with a fifteen-minute cap on three tasks: the Account Aggregator consent (A), turnover proof (B), accepting the offer (C).

Exhibit 2 reports what happened; Exhibit 3 the problems behind it. Three things were not what July had assumed. Task B, the document step, was the one most merchants got through. Task C, which nobody had worried about, was completed by 4 of the 11 who attempted it (36.4 per cent). And the three participants with no Munafa account completed nothing at all.

On Monday 9 November, Yagyesh Gumber in Toronto circulated a memo from production data (Exhibit 4): in September, 9,072 of the 12,096 merchants reaching the offer screen accepted — 75.0 per cent, level with turnover proof. On Wednesday a Mohali agency's survey landed (Exhibit 5): 148 of 180 merchants agreed the application was easy to complete (82.2 per cent). By Friday the credit squad had stopped quoting the study and the design team the funnel.

5. The people

Exhibit 6 sketches who reports to whom, and the clock each of them is on.

Yoshita Gandotra, VP Product, Ludhiana, owns the slide and wants the roadmap moved to Task C. Her bonus rides on H2 disbursals. She has not said she approved the July brief.

Yadvinder Grewal, co-founder and CEO, Ludhiana, wants a number and distrusts twelve people. He is circling a Series D and needs the Mazaya renewal clean. He has not said he agreed Schedule 4 himself, unread since.

Yashvini Ghuman, senior researcher, Pune, defends the sessions and wants eight more with merchants who never held an account. Her contract ends in March. She has not volunteered the raters' four disagreements, or that her “balanced sample” slide is silent on tenure.

Yatindra Ghai, head of engineering, Bengaluru, says the shell is the real constraint and any Schedule 4 change eighteen weeks, not eight. Nine of his thirty-four engineers are on credit. He has not said the shell was his own call.

Yashleen Gauba, design lead, Berlin, was right about the July brief and wants the notice served Monday. She is the only senior designer, and has not said a recruiter has her attention.

Yagyesh Gumber, senior data scientist, Toronto, holds that behaviour at scale outranks twelve sessions: 929 of 1,200 merchants shown a simplified fee line accepted, against 900 of 1,200 in control. He owns the funnel dashboards, and his memo body omits that the lift is 1.4 standard errors.

Yadnya Gadhok, customer success lead, Singapore, carries Mazaya and calls any component-library change before 31 January a renewal risk. Her variable pay is that renewal. She has not said two Mazaya vendors asked for the fourteen-row layout.

Yogiraj Gosain, enterprise sales, New Jersey, wants it shipped: he is selling the white-label product to two Gulf groups on “compliance-ready screens”. He has not said neither prospect asked for a usability finding, or that one asked how many merchants finish alone.

Exhibit 6 — Where the decision sits, and the clock it sits on

Reading it. Solid lines are reporting: all six reports hang from Grewal's box, not Gandotra's, which is how the credit squad came to be staffed by Ghai. Dashed boxes are counterparties. Offsets are mid-November 2026, after European clocks changed on 25 October and North American on 1 November.

6. Voices

“Nine of your twelve already had our app. They have accepted an offer before. You have measured habit.” — “The deck says balanced, and it was: six kirana, six small-manufacturing. On tenure it was nine to three, and it is in Exhibit 2's account column.” Yashleen Gauba and Yashvini Ghuman, same thread, 10 November
“My October cell lifted acceptance 2.4 points. That is 1.4 standard errors, and the interval runs from minus one to plus five point eight.” Yagyesh Gumber, memo appendix, 9 November, Toronto
“Thirty-eight per cent of September's acceptances had one of our people in the shop. In Singapore a relationship manager sells this, and nobody pretends the merchant reads the screen. Before you spend a crore on the screen, somebody should say whether it is meant to do this job alone.” Yadnya Gadhok, call notes, 12 November, Singapore
“You have four options on that slide and every one ends in a screen.” Yashleen Gauba, chat, 14 November, 19:12 IST
“Dubai is nine crore and I am not risking it in January.” — “Seven crore. Renewal is 31 January, and you are right about the risk — but get the number right in front of the board.” Yogiraj Gosain and Yadvinder Grewal, call, 13 November
“P4 sat the best part of fifteen minutes on the offer screen, then asked me where the total was. I had to tell her it is not on the screen. She said: then what am I agreeing to.” Yashvini Ghuman, session debrief, 6 November, Ludhiana

7. The options as Gandotra sees them

By Sunday evening she had four lines on a page and a cost against each (Exhibit 7).

Option 1 — ship version three without the Key Fact Statement work. ₹59 lakh, seven weeks, on the 7 January train. It clears A1, A2, B1 and B2 — four of Exhibit 3's seven problems, two of its four severity-3 ones — and touches neither C1 nor C2.

Option 2 — serve the sixty-day notice and rebuild the offer screen. ₹121 lakh, eighteen weeks. Notice served Monday expires 15 January 2027; the build then needs the shell reworked, the credit squad through March. It is the only option addressing C1.

Option 3 — patch the fold and the handoff. ₹20 lakh, three weeks, on the 10 December train: Accept moves above the fold, the handoff gets branded, nothing else.

Option 4 — buy more evidence. ₹35 lakh, eleven weeks: forty unmoderated sessions weighted to merchants with no Munafa account, plus a live A/B on the fee line. It ships nothing.

Gumber's note on the value of fixing the offer screen holds one base throughout: the 12,096 merchants who reached the Key Fact Statement in September, at ₹1,950 of origination fee per acceptance. Two points is 242 acceptances a month, ₹4.72 lakh a month, ₹56.63 lakh a year; five points 605, ₹11.80 lakh, ₹1.42 crore; eight points 968, ₹18.88 lakh, ₹2.27 crore. Against Option 2's ₹121 lakh the paybacks are 25.6, 10.3 and 6.4 months. Nothing in Exhibits 2 or 4 estimates the lift, and the memo says so.
