8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board pack is due 09:00 IST Monday 16 November, the call 18:30 IST the same day. Schedule 4 requires sixty days' notice and a joint legal review before any of the five screens changes; notice served Monday expires 15 January 2027. Mazaya's agreement requires thirty days' notice and a ten-day window on any shared component-library change, and renews 31 January 2027. The Key Fact Statement cannot be shortened, deferred or reordered against acknowledgement; the DPDP notice cannot be collapsed. Release trains before the year-end freeze are 26 November and 10 December, then 7 January. Nine of thirty-four engineers are on credit, the freeze holding since 1 August. Munafa had ₹118 crore of cash at 30 September against ₹6.2 crore a month of burn, just over nineteen months, and the board wants EBITDA breakeven by Q4 FY2028.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibits 2 and 4 disagree about whether merchants can accept an offer. State what each measures, over which population, window and version of the screen — and what would make them comparable.
  2. Exhibit 3's ceiling note has C1 and C2 together touching exactly the seven who failed Task C — the most a severity-3 problem could reach. What does an exact fit like that tell you, and what would it have meant instead if the union had come to five?
  3. The three participants with no Munafa account completed none of the three tasks — one chance in 220, or 0.45 per cent, had the zero-task group fallen at random among twelve. Give two explanations consistent with every figure here, and the evidence that would separate them.
  4. Gumber's October cell lifted acceptance 2.4 percentage points at 1.4 standard errors. What is a result of that strength fit to decide, and what would he have had to design differently to get one that could carry Option 2?
  5. Exhibit 5's survey closed two days before Exhibit 2's first session, over overlapping populations, and the two reach opposite conclusions. If Munafa could fund only one next year, which would you stop paying for, and what does that commit you to about how this company learns?
  6. It is Monday the sixteenth. What does Gandotra do before 09:00, commit to at 18:30, and tell the board she does not know — naming the exhibits she would show and those she would leave out?

At ten past eleven she opened P4's recording again and watched the last four minutes with the sound off: a woman in a kirana in Ludhiana scrolling the fourteen-row table up and down, looking for a number that was not there. Then she opened the funnel and looked at 9,072. Both were made by people she trusted, about the same product, in the same autumn. The Munsif notice sat open in a third tab, the cursor in the date field.
exp20v2-ux.usability.test:
Usability Testing

Where do real people get stuck, and why?

1. A Friday decision at Navasa

On Friday 9 October 2026, Anindya Hazra, the product manager for onboarding at Navasa, had until the evening to decide whether a redesigned "add your landlord" flow would go into the engineering freeze on Monday 19 October. Navasa, a Bengaluru company, lets tenants pay monthly rent by card or UPI (India's real-time bank transfer system) while the landlord receives an ordinary bank transfer. The flow in question was where a tenant enters the landlord's bank details for the first time.

Marketing had committed ₹38 lakh to a campaign starting Monday 26 October, ahead of the 1 November rent date, at a blended cost of about ₹380 per person who starts the flow, or roughly 10,000 starts. In September, 12,400 users had started the existing flow and 8,432 had finished it, a completion rate of 68 per cent. Each percentage point of completion on 10,000 starts is 100 people, or ₹38,000 of acquisition spend rewarded or wasted. Analytics showed that most abandonment happened on the bank-details screen. It had never shown why.

On Tuesday 6 and Wednesday 7 October, Arunima Handique, Navasa's only user researcher, had therefore watched eight tenants attempt the new design on a clickable prototype, while Amlan Haloi, the engineer who would build it, listened in. Five completed the task. Three did not. Was five of eight good enough to ship, and was it even the right number to ask about?

2. The idea

A usability test is a session in which a representative user attempts realistic tasks with a product, or a prototype of it, while someone observes where the user hesitates, errs or fails and, as far as possible, why. A prototype is any artefact, from paper sketches to a clickable mock-up, that behaves enough like the product to be used. The user is usually asked to think aloud, that is, to say what they are looking at, expecting and deciding as they go. A moderator runs the session; a task is the goal given to the participant.

The method exists because designers cannot see their own work as a newcomer does, and interviews capture what people say they would do, which often differs from what they do. Clayton Lewis at IBM described think-aloud for interface design in a 1982 report, drawing on the verbal-protocol research of Herbert Simon and Anders Ericsson. In 1993 Jakob Nielsen and Thomas Landauer modelled why a handful of participants per round exposes most problems, and Steve Krug's 2000 book Don't Make Me Think made the practice something a small team could do in a morning.

Anindya's sentence for the meeting was this:

We are not asking whether eight people like the screen; we are watching where they stop, and working out why.

The idea is narrow on purpose: it finds and ranks problems. It does not measure demand or forecast conversion.

3. How a session actually works

Arunima began by fixing the task: "You have just moved flats and your new landlord's rent is ₹32,000. Set up November rent to him." It named a goal, not a button; a task that says "tap Add Landlord" tests reading, not design. The eight were Bengaluru and Pune renters, aged 24 to 38, paying between ₹18,000 and ₹45,000 a month, none of whom had used Navasa. Recruiting people who match the intended customer is the step practitioners most often leave implicit.

In each 40-minute session she read a script, asked the participant to think aloud, then stayed silent. When a participant froze she asked only neutral questions such as "What are you thinking now?". Help came only after a participant had clearly given up, and a task finished with help counted as not completed unaided. Every stall, wrong tap and misread phrase went into a log with the participant's own words.

Afterwards the log was grouped into distinct usability problems, each rated for impact: 3 if it stopped a participant finishing, 2 if it caused hesitation or recoverable error, 1 if it was cosmetic. This scale is a local convention, not a standard. A fix is a hypothesis until someone is watched using it.

4. The worked example

Figure 2 shows what Arunima saw. Each row is a distinct problem; each column a participant. P1 to P8 label the participants, and "yes" or "no" above them records unaided completion. P2, P5 and P8 never reached the confirmation screen.

ProblemImpactMet itDenominatorWhat was seen
A. Bank-code (IFSC) field368 who attempted the taskParticipants typed the branch name or account number; three of the six never recovered.
B. Re-payment check235 who reached itA ₹1 test deposit was read as a charge or a mistake.
C. Fee on last screen255 who reached itA 1.5 per cent fee (₹480 on ₹32,000) appeared only at the end; all five paused or went back.
D. Button wording118 who attempted the taskOne participant read "Proceed" as "pay now".

Incidences across the grid: 6 + 3 + 5 + 1 = 15, matching the per-participant counts (2, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 2, 1). No problem exceeds its denominator.

The denominators matter. Problem C looks like "5 of 8" but is better read as 5 of 5: everyone who could see the fee screen reacted to it. Problem A is 6 of 8, with three failures. Unaided completion was 5 of 8, or 62.5 per cent, and all eight attempted the task, so the denominator is eight. Dropping the three who failed would report 100 per cent, a false claim.

Because the sample is eight, the rate is imprecise. A 95 per cent Wilson interval, a standard way of bounding a proportion from a small sample, runs from about 31 to 86 per cent. It also cannot be compared with September's 68 per cent, which came from 12,400 real users on the old flow with no moderator present: different people, conditions and design.

How many participants are enough to see a problem at all? Nielsen and Landauer modelled the share of problems found after n participants as 1 − (1 − p)n, where p is the chance that a single participant meets a given problem. Their average across projects was about 0.31. At 0.31, five participants find 1 − 0.695 = 84.4 per cent of problems and six find 89.2 per cent.

Now change one input. Suppose the problems that matter are rarer, as when only tenants renting from a joint-owner couple trip over them, so p is 0.10. Five participants then find 1 − 0.95 = 41.0 per cent and Navasa's eight find 1 − 0.98 = 57.0 per cent. Reaching 85 per cent would take ln 0.15 ÷ ln 0.9 = 18.006, so 19 participants. The "five users" folklore is thus a statement about common problems in a fairly uniform group, not a law. Rare problems need many more people or a chosen subgroup.

5. Nuances that separate users of the vocabulary from practitioners

Watching is not asking

A solution interview or concept test asks people what they think of an idea. A usability test records what they do with it.

Thinking aloud changes behaviour a little

Narrating slows people down and makes them more careful than at home, so timings from a think-aloud session are unreliable, though where people stop remains informative.

Frequency and severity are different axes

Problem D was met once and is trivial. Problem A was met six times and blocked three people. Rank by impact first, then by how many met it among those exposed.

Five is per round, per group, per problem type

Nielsen advised several small rounds with fixes between them. Later studies found some groups of five finding far fewer problems than the average implies, and distinct user types need a few participants each.

A fidelity limit on every prototype

A clickable prototype did not send real money, so participants who saw the ₹1 test deposit were not risking anything. Anxiety about payment is probably understated.

What it cannot tell you

It cannot tell you whether a tenant would choose Navasa over paying by bank transfer, or whether a 1.5 per cent fee is acceptable. Those are questions for interviews, pricing research and live experiments. Before relying on any session, ask who these people were and what was at stake for them.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

In a consumer product like Navasa's, recruitment is easy but motivation is low: a stall that a paid participant overcomes may be fatal in the wild. In B2B products the difficulty reverses: a finance administrator is hard to recruit, testing needs realistic data and several roles, and eight participants may mean eight customers.

A marketplace has at least two audiences. Navasa's tenants and its landlords, who receive the money and must trust it, behave differently and need separate samples; passing with tenants says nothing about landlords. An early-stage company can run five sessions in a week with paper prototypes, and speed beats rigour. A large company adds researchers, panels and unmoderated remote tools handling hundreds of participants; the cost is distance, since the person who needs to see the stall often never watches it.

7. Common mistakes

Leading the participant

Symptom: participants succeed in the lab, then fail in production. Misunderstanding: that a friendly nudge ("did you see the button at the bottom?") helps. Diagnostic: count the moderator's share of words in the transcript; a large share means contaminated data.

Testing colleagues or friends

Symptom: a clean result and a messy launch. Misunderstanding: that any human will do. Diagnostic: compare the screener with actual customer attributes.

Counting votes rather than weighing impact

Symptom: the fix list is dominated by the most-mentioned cosmetic issue, while a blocker seen by two participants waits. Misunderstanding: that more mentions mean more importance. Diagnostic: ask of each item whether it stopped anyone from finishing.

Treating the completion rate as a forecast

Symptom: a launch plan that quotes "62.5 per cent" as the expected conversion. Misunderstanding: that a lab count is a population rate. Diagnostic: ask for the sample size, the interval and whether the comparison figure came from the same conditions.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Navasa's decision has a goal-based task, participants from the real customer base, a log in participants' own words, and every rate shown with its denominator. Findings are ranked by impact, so the meeting begins with the blocker that stopped three of eight, not the loudest opinion. The team sets a pass criterion for the retest before seeing it, for instance that fewer than two of five participants stall on the bank-code field, and they say plainly that the test cannot predict conversion.

9. What Anindya decided

On Friday evening Anindya kept the freeze date and changed the scope. Problem A would be fixed by letting the tenant search the landlord's bank and branch by name, with the code filled in automatically. Problem C would be fixed by moving the fee to the amount screen. Problem B would get a one-line explanation of the ₹1 deposit. She booked five new participants for a retest on Thursday 15 October, four days before the freeze, with the pass criterion written down in advance. Her reasoning was that three failures from one cause, with a clear mechanism, justified a targeted fix; five of eight was not a number to quote to marketing as a forecast. The retest results are not yet in.

Next, study funnel analytics and experimentation: analytics says where people leave and at what scale, an experiment tests whether a fix moved a live rate, and usability testing explains the why between them.

Two questions to sit with. If problem A had been met by 2 of 8 rather than 6 of 8, with all 2 failing, what would you want to know before you decided it was worth fixing? And what kind of participant is missing from a test of eight Bengaluru and Pune renters, and what would you only learn by adding them?
exp40v2-ux.usability.test:
Usability testing: where real people get stuck, and why

Exp40 — UX & Design Collaboration. Watching use instead of asking opinions.

1. Two decisions, seventeen days apart

On Monday 14 September 2026 Bidisha Imam was looking at a slide she did not believe. Imam ran product at Pankhudi Health Technologies in Bengaluru, a consumer app for booking blood tests at home, a category Dr Lal PathLabs and Metropolis lead. The slide reported twelve moderated think-aloud sessions on a prototype of a rebuilt booking flow. One number, in red, said prescription upload completed at 33 per cent. Pankhudi's gate said nothing shipped below 60; four tasks were under it, and engineering had eleven working days before the release train closed.

Imam's objection was not that the number was bad. She could not tell what it was a number of. She asked Bornali Ingti, who ran the sessions, how many participants reached the upload screen. Nine: two ran out of the slot, and a third session was abandoned when the prototype crashed on the patient-details screen. The 33 per cent was four completions over twelve participants; on the nine who attempted it, 44 per cent.

Seventeen days later Bikash Islam faced the opposite problem. Islam led product at Padakshep Technologies in Pune, which sells the handheld screens a warehouse picker reads while walking an aisle. On Thursday 1 October he had a signed go-live at a Bhiwandi site running 46 pickers a shift, a buyer who would never touch the screen, and a design lead, Bhaswati Islary, who wanted eight hours of floor time with fourteen pickers first. His engineering manager said testing was for consumer apps: these users were trained and inducted. Islary's counter was that the pickers did not need convincing. The floor supervisors did.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A usability test has a representative user attempt a realistic task on a working or simulated artefact while an observer records what happens and withholds the help that would make the task succeed. Think-aloud adds a concurrent verbal protocol. It is behavioural, task-anchored, and diagnostic: its output is located causes, not a score.

Two lineages meet here. Ericsson and Simon's Protocol Analysis (1984) held that verbalising short-term memory does not materially disturb the task, provided the instruction is strictly "say what you are thinking". That warrant covers current thought, not explaining. Boren and Ramey's 2000 study found constant violation, with moderators asking "why did you do that?" — a request for the retrospective rationalisation the method exists to avoid.

From engineering economics, Nielsen and Landauer (1993) modelled discovery as a binomial process, and from it came Nielsen's claim that five users suffice. Against it sit Spool and Schroeder's 2001 finding that five were nowhere near enough on large sites, and Faulkner's 2003 study, in which subsets of five drawn from sixty participants recovered 55 to 99 per cent of what the sixty found.

Four positions, by what each would sign. Discount usability signs five participants per round, many rounds, no statistics; it will not sign that a test measures how good a design is. The measurement school, after Sauro and Lewis, signs rates and times with intervals attached, because an uncertainty-free point estimate is a lie; it will not sign five participants for a summative claim. The ethnographic school signs that only field observation is valid. The telemetry school signs that a million sessions show where drop-off happens, and is wrong that watching adds nothing: telemetry locates the cliff, not the cause.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Four decisions made before anyone sits down determine what the data can mean: the task set, the recruitment screen, the prototype's fidelity on the dimension under test, and — usually implicit — the definition of completion. Pankhudi's five tasks ran in fixed order, and that produced Imam's slide: whoever stalled early never reached the later tasks, so those have smaller denominators.

Exhibit 1 — Unaided completion, Pankhudi prototype round 2, twelve participants, fixed task order.

T2 Book tomorrow 8am12650.0%50.0%

"Attempted" counts participants who reached the entry screen with time remaining. The three who missed T4 also missed T5, and one more stopped between them, so 8 is forced by 9 − 1. Pooled on the attempted base, 33 ÷ 53 = 62.3 per cent; the unweighted mean of the five rates is 61.4.

The re-ordering is the point. On the all-12 base the worst four run T4, T5, T2, T3. On the attempted base they run T4, T2, T3, with T5 at 62.5 clearing the gate. The error had not changed the verdict on T4, which fails either way; it had added a fourth task to an eleven-day list.

Imam then asked how confident anyone should be in 44.4 per cent from nine people. The small-sample instrument of choice is the Wilson score interval, whose centre is (x + z²/2) ÷ (n + z²). With x = 4, n = 9 and z = 1.96 (z² = 3.8416), the centre is 5.9208 ÷ 12.8416 = 0.4611. The half-width is (z ÷ (n + z²)) × √(n p̂ q̂ + z²/4) = 0.15263 × √(9 × 0.4444 × 0.5556 + 0.9604) = 0.15263 × √3.18262 = 0.2723. The interval runs 18.9 to 73.3 per cent, fifty-four points wide, with the 60 per cent gate inside it; on the all-12 base it is 13.8 to 60.9, which also contains the gate. A rate at this n is a flag, not a measurement.

The discovery model, and what it claims

Nielsen–Landauer says that if each participant independently has probability p of meeting a given problem, the expected share found by n participants is P(n) = 1 − (1 − p)n. Everything hangs on p, estimable as the fill rate of a problem-by-participant matrix. Ingti's had nineteen problems: fourteen on flows all twelve reached, four on the prescription flow only nine reached, one on the reschedule flow only eight reached. Exposure opportunities are therefore 14 × 12 + 4 × 9 + 8 = 212, not 228. The matrix held 70 filled cells, so p̂ = 70 ÷ 212 = 33.0 per cent; the naive denominator gives 30.7.

Two readings pull opposite ways. At p = 0.33, five participants recover 86.5 per cent of the problem set and twelve recover 99.2, so twelve sessions were a luxury and three rounds of four better science. At p = 0.12, a heterogeneous population's value, five recover 47.2 and twelve recover 78.4.

Worse, a p estimated from found problems is biased upward, because problems nobody hit are absent from the matrix and cannot pull the fill rate down. P(n) estimates the share of problems you would find, not of those that exist.

From observation to fix

Between "a participant struggled" and "here is the change", experts insert a located cause — not "users were confused by upload" but "the Upload control renders in the secondary text style, which participants read as a file-picker" — and a severity score combining frequency with cost.

Exhibit 2 — Pankhudi round 2, ten highest-scoring problems of nineteen. Score = affected × impact.

"Affected" counts participants who hit the problem, including those who then recovered unaided, which is why an impact-3 count can exceed the task's failures. Ceilings: nothing on the prescription flow can exceed 9 affected and nothing on the reschedule flow 8, and 70 cells sit inside 212 exposure opportunities. P-02 is the single highest-scoring problem at 24; two pairs tie exactly, P-04 with P-15 at 12 and P-18 with P-06 at 3.

Ingti's first draft said ten of twelve participants hit P-07. Only nine reached that flow, so ten exceeds the ceiling exposure allows and the figure was impossible whatever the rest of the table said; the true count was seven. By raw count P-02 leads P-07, eight to seven; by hit rate on the exposed base, P-07 at 77.8 per cent leads P-02 at 66.7. Which ordering is right is a judgement, not arithmetic.

4. When the claim holds, and when it misleads

The task must be one the participant would want to do, or you are measuring instruction-following. Pankhudi passes: Ingti recruited people who had booked a home blood test within ninety days. Padakshep passes more strongly — a picker resolving a short-pick is doing their job. It fails on seeded enterprise sandboxes, where nobody knows what a plausible answer looks like.

The prototype must be faithful on the dimension under test. Fidelity is not global: a paper sketch tests information architecture well and perceived performance not at all. Pankhudi's was faithful on labelling, unfaithful on latency and the camera, which is why a session died at the image picker. Padakshep's test fails this in the lab and passes on the floor: a handheld read walking, in a glove, is a different artefact.

The behaviour must be observable within a session. Testing sees first use and early learning, not the habits of a user in month six. T5 sits at that edge: rescheduling really happens next morning, under time pressure.

The population must be reachable in the numbers the design requires. One coherent segment can live on p near 0.3 and small rounds. Several segments with different mental models mean a low effective p per segment, and need rounds per segment rather than participants pooled.

The method actively misleads in three cases. Where the question is desirability rather than operability, a participant who completes flawlessly and would never pay yields a false green light. Where friction is intended — a confirmation step, a regulatory disclosure — a test that reads hesitation as defect optimises the safeguard away. And where the real failure sits outside the screen: a scanner that takes 1.8 seconds to wake is not a UI defect, and a UI test will find UI problems reliably while staying silent about it.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Two-sided products break the single-participant session. A marketplace task is a pair — a buyer requests, a seller responds — and watching one side measures half a loop. Mature practice runs paired sessions, two participants acting on one object in near-real time, at roughly three times the scheduling cost.

Regulated products invert the relation between testing and compliance. In medical devices usability work is not optional: standards practice requires a validation study with representative users on production-equivalent hardware, pass criteria fixed in advance. Pankhudi sits adjacent — health data under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, samples to NABL-accredited labs — so a participant who skips consent unread may require the screen to be made slower.

In hardware-plus-software, Padakshep's case, the seam between device and application is owned by neither team. When a scan fails, neither picker nor observer can tell whether barcode, firmware, network or software is at fault. Experts instrument the seam first, so a recording splits into device time and application time.

AI-native products are genuinely unsettled. A test assumes the artefact is the same for every participant; with a generative feature it is not, so a failure may belong to the interface, to the model on that sample, or to the prompt. Practice scripts fixed model responses for interface questions and accepts live variability only for the interaction loop. Nobody has a settled method for attributing failure between surface and model.

At the organisational seam the stated practice is a research function serving product teams; the observed practice, past a few hundred people, is that capacity is rationed by whoever shouts loudest, and the teams with the best data ran their own sessions badly rather than waiting six weeks.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

The denominator is the finding. A competent practitioner reports a completion rate; an expert reports the attrition that produced it. The tell is a report where every task has the same n. The obvious reading, that a smaller denominator weakens the finding, is backwards: those who never arrived are the evidence about the upstream task.

Hesitation is data; self-report about hesitation is not. The expert records the pause, the back-navigation, the cursor drift, and ignores the participant's theory of why. The tell is a report quoting the answer to "why did you do that?" as a cause. The Ericsson–Simon warrant covers current thought, so that cause is a confabulation.

A problem found by one participant can outrank one found by six. Frequency and severity are different axes and their product is a convenience, not a truth. The tell is a queue sorted strictly by count. One participant who lost ₹1,180 to a silent address overwrite outweighs six who found a label odd.

The moderator's help is the measurement. Every assist converts a failure into a completion. The tell is a report with no record of assists. Experts pre-commit to a timestamped escalation ladder, so "completed unaided" is auditable.

Recruiting is where most tests are lost. A bad screener delivers professional participants who know what an observer wants. The tell is participants who narrate fluently and never get properly stuck. Tightening the screener often worsens it; better to recruit through the product's own channels.

Five is a parameter, not a number. The expert says five users at this p, and can say where that p came from. The tell is five-participant rounds for every question regardless of heterogeneity. The obvious reading of Faulkner, that five is unreliable so run more, is half right: better is more rounds of five, since her variance is across samples, which iteration averages out.

The fix is a hypothesis, not a conclusion. A located cause suggests a change, and the change needs testing, because designs fail in new ways. The tell is a round-two report that does not re-test round one's fixes. Pankhudi's P-11 fix, defaulting the slot grid to today, created a new problem: same-day slots operations could not staff.

Watching is cheap; deciding what to watch is expensive. A session's marginal information is governed by a task set fixed weeks earlier. The tell is a team that debates sample size for an hour and task wording for ten minutes. More sessions buy certainty only inside the space the tasks define.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

Consumer products are closest to the textbook form: first use matters, recruitment is easy, and the real constraint is heterogeneity. In B2B and enterprise the buyer is not the user, so a finding has no automatic route to priority; Padakshep's data must first be translated into supervisor-visible seconds. Platforms and marketplaces differ for the paired-task reason above. In hardware the environment is part of the artefact. In AI products only the model-mediated loop is new.

By stage, what changes is what you may conclude. Before product-market fit, testing is cheap and usually the wrong instrument, because the binding constraint is whether anyone wants the thing. At early scale it is a high-return discovery practice. At maturity it shifts to defending against regressions. Claims that the technique changes by stage are mostly false.

8. Three worked examples

Pankhudi, round 2. Twelve sessions, nineteen problems, 70 matrix cells, p̂ = 33.0 per cent. After the correction the fix list held three gate-failing tasks rather than four, and engineering shipped P-02, P-07 and P-11, the only three impact-3 problems.

Padakshep, Bhiwandi. Islary got her eight hours. Fourteen pickers resolved short-pick exceptions on both screens, within-subjects, order counterbalanced. Mean time fell from 94 to 71 seconds: a difference of 23 with a paired standard deviation of 31, so the standard error is 31 ÷ √14 = 8.29 seconds and the 95 per cent interval, at t(13) = 2.160, is 23 ± 17.9 seconds.

The interval carried through at full transfer: the 5.1 s bound yields 1,307.5 picker-hours and ₹2.48 lakh a year, the 40.9 s bound 10,486 hours and ₹19.92 lakh. Lab time does not transfer to the floor one-for-one, so Islam planned on 40 per cent — ₹4.48 lakh, inside a like-for-like scaled interval of ₹0.99 lakh to ₹7.97 lakh. The range is the claim, not the point estimate.

The round that failed, February 2026. Pankhudi's first search-as-you-type tested at 92 per cent unaided completion on a prototype whose stub responded in under 0.2 seconds. In production, p95 latency on that path was 4.1 seconds, and field analytics showed 54 per cent of users who started a search reached a booking. Calling this a 38-point collapse was wrong: 92 per cent was unaided completion on a scripted task, 54 per cent funnel conversion over all sessions including abandoned browsing. The real finding was worse — the premise that results appear as you type had never been tested at the latency it would run at. Recovery took a latency-faithful prototype with a 4.1-second delay, on which completion was 61 per cent.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

The wrong denominator. Sign: every task has the same n. Question: how many reached this task's entry screen with time left? Caught late it costs a mis-ordered queue — at Pankhudi, a fourth task added to an eleven-day list.

Moderator rescue. Sign: unexpectedly high completion and warm recordings. Question: show me the assist log with timestamps. Caught late, a design certified usable fails on users with no moderator.

Confirmation testing. Sign: the test is booked after the design is locked and the deck says "validate". Question: what result would change the design, and who may act on it? Costly, because the evidence exists and is ignored.

Fidelity mismatch. Sign: the prototype is faster or better-populated than the product. Question: what does this design assume about speed or network, and is it present? Caught late, it is the February round.

Severity inflation. Sign: thirty problems, twenty-two marked high. Question: what would this cost the user if it happened every time? Caught late, engineering stops reading the list.

Round-one-only. Sign: one research date per release. Question: when do we test the fixes? Caught late, regressions are found by operations rather than research.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The live disagreement is whether small-sample usability data should carry numbers at all. The qualitative position at its strongest: a usability test is a problem-finding instrument, and attaching a completion rate to nine participants invites the error Pankhudi nearly made. It rests on Molich's evidence that independent teams find disjoint problem sets, making the denominator of "all problems" unknowable. For this to be wrong, practitioners would have to hold a number loosely.

The measurement position at its strongest: refusing to quantify does not remove the quantity, it hides it. Someone will decide whether the design is good enough, and without an interval they will decide on whichever session they watched. Sauro and Lewis argue that small-sample intervals are wide but honest; on that reasoning the 18.9 to 73.3 per cent computed above beats a confident anecdote. For this to be wrong, intervals would have to be routinely misread as point estimates.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four ways. They spend preparation effort on the task set and the screener rather than the script. They state denominators unprompted, and can say who is missing from each. They separate observation from inference — "seven of the nine exposed hit the Upload problem" is observation, "the control reads as a file-picker" is inference. And they treat round one's output as hypotheses with a re-test date.

12. The decisions

Imam shipped the three impact-3 fixes rather than working the whole four-task list. More consequentially, she struck the 60 per cent gate and replaced it with a rule that no impact-3 problem affecting more than a third of exposed participants ships — a statement about problems rather than samples, and computable at n = 9.

Islam ran the floor sessions and took ₹4.48 lakh, not ₹11.20 lakh, to the operator's supply-chain vice-president, with the interval scaled to the same 40 per cent transfer assumption, ₹0.99 lakh to ₹7.97 lakh. He held the go-live date: the conservative number was large enough to win the argument. Whether holding it was right is still argued at Padakshep.

  1. Imam abandoned the numeric gate rather than run more sessions. What would have to be true for thirty more sessions to be the better response?
  2. Exhibit 2 ranks P-02 above P-07 by count and below it by rate. Which should drive the fix queue, and what evidence would settle it?
  3. Islam's case rests on a 40 per cent transfer from lab seconds to floor seconds. What measurement after go-live would test that?

13. Going deeper

Solution interviews and concept tests
Answers whether anyone wants the thing — which a usability test cannot.
Wireframes, mockups, prototypes
Fidelity binds what a test can conclude; unlocks which dimension to make faithful.
UX fundamentals for PMs
The vocabulary to state a located cause rather than a symptom.
Usability heuristics
An expert review finds many of the same problems far cheaper.
Information architecture and navigation
A common class of usability failure is structural, not visual.
User flows and task analysis
Where the task set comes from; get it wrong and no sample size rescues the round.
Design systems and components
Explains P-07: a component's default style carried a meaning nobody chose.
Content design and microcopy
Pankhudi's P-09 is wording, not layout — the cheapest class of fix.
case40v1-ux.heuristics:
Galla Securities: Ten Heuristics and Nine Weeks

A Bengaluru investing app has a design review, a usability study, a support queue and an experiment. They do not agree, and nine build weeks remain.

1. Sunday night, Bengaluru

It had rained since four o'clock, and Nikhat Yamdagni had been at the dining table since the power came back. In front of her were four columns in a ruled notebook, one for each way the next nine weeks could be spent. On Monday 19 October 2026 at 18:30 IST — the one hour in which Bengaluru, Pune, Berlin, Singapore and New Jersey are all awake — she had to choose one.

Galla Securities Private Limited had 58.00 lakh registered accounts and a problem it had been describing confidently, and wrongly, since January. In April it paid ₹17.5 lakh for an expert review of its investing flows against Jakob Nielsen's ten usability heuristics, and got back seventy-eight logged problems, twenty-nine of them major or catastrophic, and a deck that Naunihal Yasrotia, the chief executive, called the most useful thing design had produced in two years. A usability study, a support audit and an A/B test have since each said something different about where customers were losing their way. Nikhat could not get them to agree, and on Monday had to act as though they did.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Galla was founded in 2019 in Bengaluru by Naunihal and two classmates to do one narrow thing: let a salaried person in a tier-2 city start a ₹500 monthly SIP in four minutes on a mid-range Android phone. It became a SEBI-registered broker in 2021 and an AMFI-registered mutual fund distributor, held client securities with CDSL, and collected instalments through UPI AutoPay mandates. In FY2025-26 it reported revenue of ₹118 crore, of which ₹41 crore came from a business nobody had planned: licensing Galla's front-end to institutions abroad.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken in March 2023: facing a cash crunch, the founders chose one React Native codebase and one in-house component library, the Galla Kit, over separate native apps. In September 2023, when Gharnata Investments DMCC of Dubai signed to white-label the app for Gulf-based NRI investors buying Indian equities under the RBI's Portfolio Investment Scheme, the same economy applied: Gharnata got a theme, not a fork. It is why Galla can serve a ₹9.2 crore-a-year client with four engineers, and why Galla cannot change a button in Nagpur without telling Dubai first.

3. The industry

Zerodha and Groww hold the imagination of the Indian retail investor; Angel One and Paytm Money compete on the first-time user; PhonePe and Jio have distribution Galla will never have. The regulatory floor keeps rising in ways that are expensive for interfaces: SEBI's risk-disclosure and nominee requirements, two-factor authentication on every order, and the DPDP Act's consent notices each add a screen, and each screen is a place to drop out. The exchanges' Muhurat session on Diwali, Sunday 8 November 2026, anchors a festival fortnight in which Galla books its heaviest new-account volume and freezes all releases from 2 to 12 November.

Abroad the exposure runs two ways. Gharnata must re-certify the white-label app with its own auditors whenever the interface materially changes, and Niketan Yachhru in New Jersey is three weeks from signing Glenhaven Advisors LLC, an NRI-focused investment adviser, to a ₹8.4 crore three-year licence. Glenhaven's procurement does not ask about heuristics. It asks for a WCAG 2.1 AA conformance report, a different document produced by a different method.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In January 2026 the quarterly funnel review produced the number that set everything in motion: of 89.40 lakh opens of the order ticket in October–December 2025, 33.97 lakh — 38.0 per cent — ended without a submitted order. The order ticket was therefore the problem, and in March Niharika Yakhmi, Galla's design director in Berlin, commissioned Greifbar Nutzerlabor GmbH: four evaluators, two hours each, independently, against the ten heuristics, on the English build of release 7.4 on a reference Android handset (Exhibit 1, delivered 24 April; Figure 1).

In June two things happened. A usability study of twelve first-time investors, recruited in Nagpur and Indore for ₹6.8 lakh, was fielded from 8 to 12 June (Exhibit 2). On 19 June an engineer in Pune fixed a defect Nabarun Yugral, Galla's data scientist in Toronto, had chased since April: every sheet rendered by the shared OrderSheet container — order ticket, SIP amount, add-funds, UPI mandate — had emitted the same open event since release 6.9.

Nabarun re-cut the quarter from server logs. Of those 89.40 lakh opens, 23.25 lakh had not been the order ticket at all; 12.96 lakh of that subset, 55.7 per cent, were abandoned — mostly, but not only, mandate sheets. Strip all three sheets out and the quarter's order-ticket abandonment was 21.01 lakh of 66.15 lakh opens, or 31.8 per cent. The clean July–September figure is 15.41 lakh of 72.00 lakh, or 21.4 per cent. Of the 16.6 points of apparent improvement since the baseline quarter, 6.2 are taxonomy. Nobody at Galla can account for the other 10.4; Nabarun puts the August experiment's own contribution at under half a point, in writing.

Two further beliefs have not survived. The Gharnata app is a theme, not the fork the team assumed, and clause 9.4 gives Gharnata 45 days' notice of any material interface change. And the Hindi and Marathi strings the January roadmap listed as complete cover 61 per cent of those in the investing flows; the digit grouping was never localised.

5. The people

Nikhat Yamdagni, senior product manager, Bengaluru, owns the investing flows and Monday's decision. Her January promotion review names activation as her metric. She is not saying that she scoped the April review herself, in two lines, without asking what the 38 per cent counted.

Naunihal Yasrotia, co-founder and chief executive, wants the twenty-nine severity 3–4 items shipped: a numbered list is something a board can be shown, and his February Series C assumes the B2B line compounds. He is not saying that an investor has asked why a ₹41 crore licensing business still calls itself a consumer app.

Niharika Yakhmi, design director, Berlin, commissioned the review and was one of its four evaluators. She argues that heuristics are the only review at Galla that is not somebody's taste. She is not saying that her own ratings were the highest of the four on seven of the ten heuristics.

Neelkanth Yadhwal, engineering manager, Pune, has six engineers and nine build weeks. He wants the mandate flow rebuilt because it is what his on-call rota wakes for. He is not saying that it means touching the shared container he has wanted to replace since 2024.

Nabarun Yugral, senior data scientist, Toronto, found the instrumentation defect and will not sign a document containing the 38 per cent. He wants a powered test on first-time investors first, and is not saying that it needs eleven weeks of traffic he cannot get by 31 December.

Neeti Yotra, customer success lead, Singapore, carries Gharnata and the Gulf accounts. She calls Galla's own 48 per cent a recruiting artefact. She is not saying that Gharnata has twice asked her, informally, what a fork off the shared codebase would cost.

Niketan Yachhru, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey, needs the conformance report dated before 15 December or Glenhaven slips to April. He says he is agnostic about the consumer work, and is not saying that his commission on the licence exceeds the entire nine-week plan.

6. Exhibits

The study's single severity 4 item arose on task 3, for 7 of the 10 attempting it: four finished only after the moderator read out the bank's error text, which is information from outside the app, three abandoned, and the three unassisted finishers were on banks where it did not arise. A severity 3 item arose on task 4 for 8 of 12 — five finished unassisted after cancelling and re-entering, three after the moderator pointed at the on-screen cancel control; both of that task's abandonments came at a later step.

7. Voices

"Twenty-nine severity three and four items, numbered, with screenshots. That is not an opinion, it is a list. We have had it since April and shipped four of them."

Niharika Yakhmi, design review call, 2 October 2026

"Taste in a lab coat. Three of four evaluators work for the agency that sold us the review, the fourth is our design director, and they scored the English build on a handset no customer owns. Meanwhile 8,210 contacts came in about mandates failing or not showing, in ninety days, and the review never opened that screen."

Neelkanth Yadhwal, same call

"Gharnata's own panel put task success at 71 per cent. Ours says 48. Twelve people in Nagpur and Indore is an anecdote with a spreadsheet."

Neeti Yotra, email to Nikhat, 6 October 2026

"If Gharnata counts prompted completions as successes, which we have never been shown, our own figure is 46 of 58, or 79.3 per cent. Neither number is comparable to the other: different tasks, different panel, and a definition of success we do not have. And the mandates line in E-114, Niharika, is plus 0.05 per hundred users, interval minus 0.08 to plus 0.18. It includes zero. Please stop calling it a lift."

Nabarun Yugral, reply-all, 13 October 2026

"I don't need the consumer app to be good this quarter. I need a conformance report dated before 15 December. If we are rebuilding the mandate screen instead, say so on Monday and I will tell Glenhaven April."

Niketan Yachhru, chat to Nikhat, 16 October 2026

"Board on the 26th. I want one slide: what we found, what we fixed, what it was worth. Nikhat, do not bring me four options."

Naunihal Yasrotia, voice note, Saturday 17 October 2026

8. The options as Nikhat sees them

Her four columns are, in her shorthand, the review, the queue, the language and the contract. Each fits inside the 43 person-weeks of Figure 2 — 16, 27, 20 and 16 — and each is a pairing of asks from Exhibit 5.

The review. A and E: the confirmation and undo step, which the review logged under error prevention, plus the Kit pass — 16 person-weeks, inside capacity. It gives Naunihal his slide and Niharika her credibility, and ships the change E-114 measured a revenue cost for.

The queue. B and C: rebuild the mandate flow and the failed-instalment screen, 27 person-weeks, aimed at 13,330 of Exhibit 3's contacts — 32.4 per cent — and at the task the study found worst. It is also what Neelkanth has wanted since 2024, and it means touching the container that produced bad numbers from January 2025 to June 2026.

The language. D with E: Hindi and Marathi across the flows, and the digit grouping, 20 person-weeks. The review was conducted in English; the moderator's notes record the problem four times.

The contract. F and G: WCAG conformance and the Gharnata pack, 16 person-weeks, protecting ₹2.8 crore a year of new licence and ₹9.2 crore a year of existing, and leaving the consumer app untouched until February. Niketan's commission is not in Exhibit 5, and neither is the unminuted possibility that Gharnata would rather be forked.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Clause 9.4 requires 45 days' notice of a material interface change: anything live for Gharnata on 31 December must be notified by Monday 16 November, four weeks from the decision, so the design freezes before most of it is built. Missing a committed milestone triggers a service credit of 12 per cent of one quarter's fee — ₹27.6 lakh against a quarterly ₹2.30 crore. Glenhaven's report must be dated before 15 December. Releases are closed from 2 to 12 November. SEBI's two-factor requirement and the DPDP consent notice cannot be removed to shorten the flow, whatever any review says about minimalism. There are six engineers, 43 person-weeks, 72 asked for, and no budget for the gap. Nabarun's powered test needs eleven weeks of traffic.

10. Sunday, 23:40

The rain had stopped. Nikhat turned the notebook sideways and wrote, across the four columns, the only sentence of the evening that was not a number: we found seventy-eight problems in a screen that was never the problem. She could not decide whether it was the beginning of her Monday argument or the thing she most needed not to say in front of five offices and a board meeting on the 26th. Her phone lit with Naunihal's second voice note. She did not open it.

Questions for discussion

  1. On the evidence in Exhibits 1 to 3, where is Galla losing first-time investors, and what evidence that is not on the page would you most want?
  2. Exhibit 1 logs 78 problems; Exhibit 2 observes 12 abandonments in 58 attempts; Exhibit 3 counts 41,100 contacts. What does each instrument miss, and which could have found the mandate sheet?
  3. Severity in Exhibit 1 is a median of four ratings, three by the agency's own evaluators. If Galla scored production frequency against impact instead, which workstreams in Exhibit 5 would move?
  4. Niharika and Nabarun read Exhibit 4 differently. Which population does each speak for, and what would an experiment that spoke for Exhibit 2's users look like, given that Nabarun says it needs eleven weeks?
  5. Of the 16.6 points by which order-ticket abandonment appears to have improved since the October–December 2025 baseline, 6.2 are taxonomy. What explains the other 10.4, and how would you tell the candidates apart before 16 November?
  6. It is Monday 19 October, 18:30 IST, and the five offices are on the call. What does Nikhat put in front of them, what does she stop doing, and what does she tell the board on the 26th about whether the ₹17.5 lakh review was worth it?
case20v1-ux.heuristics:
Ekrang Khata: Checking the Reminder Flow Before Diwali

A decision case on usability heuristics

1. Opening

At 9:40 on Monday 12 October 2026, Manpreet Virk shut the door of a glass meeting room in Ekrang's Gurugram office and read the beta report for the third time. Virk was group product manager for Ekrang Khata, a ledger app used by kirana owners across northern India. By the end of Tuesday she owed Mandeep Vasudeva, head of engineering in Pune, one answer: which of three plans the next sprint would be built around. Engineering would freeze the build on Friday 23 October. The new Udhaar Wapsi reminder feature was promised to the board for Monday 2 November, six days before Diwali, when shopkeepers settle their year's credit. The designers thought the screens were finished. The beta numbers suggested otherwise, and Virk could not yet tell a matter of taste from a fault. "Everyone in this building has an opinion about those screens," she told her deputy. "I need something better than opinions."

2. Company background

Ekrang was founded in 2019 in Ludhiana by two former bank officers who noticed that their neighbourhood grocer kept customers' credit in a school notebook. The app replaced the notebook: a merchant records what each customer owes and collects through a UPI QR code. By March 2026 it had 2.1 lakh monthly active merchants in about 1,100 towns and FY26 revenue of ₹26 crore, mostly from payment-collection services. About 18,000 merchants paid for a ₹199-a-month Pro plan.

The rivals are familiar. Khatabook and OkCredit own the ledger habit, while PhonePe for Business and Paytm bundle soundboxes and settlement. Ekrang's bet was that the merchant's real problem is not recording credit but recovering it. Udhaar Wapsi would send each debtor a polite WhatsApp message carrying a UPI payment link. Because the messages use customers' phone numbers, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act applied, and NPCI's limits on UPI collect requests shaped the design. The plan assumed 30,000 additional Pro merchants by the end of November, and the board had already pencilled the revenue into its quarterly forecast. Merchants are mostly in their forties, run the app on mid-range Android phones with patchy 4G, and switch to Hindi or Punjabi labels within minutes of installing.

3. The situation

A 19-day beta ran from 21 September to 9 October with 4,000 invited merchants. Exhibit 1 shows the funnel. Merchants opened the feature readily, but 1,040 of the 2,600 who did never created a reminder. The data scientist in Toronto, nine and a half hours behind Gurugram, found the exits clustered on the customer-picker screen, though she could not say why. Figure 1 shows how little calendar remained.

Figure 1. Key dates, 12 October to 23 November 2026. Scale: 15 px per day from 12 October.

Maninder Vij, who leads customer success from Singapore, forwarded a harder signal. Of the 1,092 merchants who sent reminders, 71 (6.5 per cent) complained that a message had reached a customer they had marked as disputed. A Jaipur merchant wrote that one such message arrived during a quarrel over a returned order. In Berlin, three and a half hours behind Gurugram until the clocks change on 25 October, Mehak Vadehra's design team had passed the flow through critique by five senior designers, and she read the funnel as a question of merchant education. "We tested the screens with colleagues for two weeks," she said on the Friday call, which ran at 6:30 in her evening and 10:00 at night in Gurugram. "Shopkeepers will learn it the way they learned the QR code."

On Thursday 8 October Virk and two colleagues walked the flow independently against Nielsen's ten heuristics, rating each problem from 0 to 4 for severity. Exhibit 2 gives the result. 4. The people

Manpreet Virk, Gurugram, owns the launch and the revenue target. She wants a decision she can defend to the board without apologising to merchants. She has shipped features on instinct before and was twice lucky.

Mehak Vadehra, design lead in Berlin, built the flow. She wants it shipped and is wary of checklists that turn critique into box-ticking. Her team spent two months on the flow, and she does not want strangers rating it.

Mandeep Vasudeva, head of engineering in Pune, wants a clean freeze on 23 October. Every change after that date, he says, costs a sprint, and his engineers in Pune and Bengaluru are already stretched by festival-season leave.

Maninder Vij, customer success in Singapore, two and a half hours ahead of Gurugram, wants no reminder to reach a disputed customer, because his team answers the complaints, usually in Hindi, by phone, after the merchant has already apologised to the customer.

5. The options

Option A: ship as signed off. The critique already happened, the freeze holds and the launch date is kept. Cost today is nothing. The downside is that Exhibit 2's severity-4 problem reaches Diwali-week customers, and the beta suggests about one sender in fifteen would complain.

Option B: a structured heuristic evaluation. Four independent reviewers, two of them external, rate the three core flows against all ten heuristics over three working days, then merge their lists. Fixes at severity 3 or above go in before the freeze. It costs ₹1.2 lakh for the review, but it cannot show whether merchants will succeed with the flow. Because reviewers work from their own judgement, results depend on who is chosen.

Option C: a moderated usability test. Ten merchants in Ludhiana and Jaipur attempt real tasks over three weeks from 19 October, with a Punjabi and Hindi moderator. It yields direct evidence and exposes problems reviewers miss, but it moves launch to 23 November, after Diwali.

Exhibit 3 sets the three side by side. The deferred revenue figure assumes all 30,000 planned additional Pro merchants would have paid from launch day, so it is a ceiling.

Exhibit 3. The three options compared

Deferred revenue: 30,000 new merchants × ₹199 × 21/30 of a month = ₹41.79 lakh. Severity 3+ fixes for B and C reuse Exhibit 2's pilot figure; a fuller review may find more.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 establish, and what can it not tell Virk about why merchants leave?
  2. Is each finding in Exhibit 2 filed under the right heuristic, and why should the severity 4 item outrank the ₹4.5 lakh efficiency fix?
  3. What would Options B and C each learn that the other would not?
  4. Which option should Virk choose by Tuesday evening, and what evidence would change your mind?

7. A note for the learner

Nielsen's ten heuristics answer one question: how do we review a design systematically instead of by taste? Each heuristic is a named, general rule of good interface behaviour, such as showing system status or preventing errors. Reviewers who work independently, rate severity and then merge their lists find far more than any single reviewer, who typically catches only a fraction. Heuristic review, devised by Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich, finds violations of known principles cheaply. It does not show whether users succeed, which only observed use can.

A well-reasoned answer separates three things the case blurs: whether a design breaks rules (a review question), whether users complete tasks (a testing question) and whether the idea is wanted (a market question). Exhibit 1 raises all three, and only the first is cheap to answer before the freeze.

One defensible path is Option B, plus a small follow-on. Four independent reviewers keep the author from marking her own work, which answers Virk's worry about opinions, though it cuts against Vadehra's wish to avoid strangers rating her work; the severity scale gives Vasudeva a cut line. Fix the four items rated 3 or worse for ₹8.4 lakh, defer the ₹4.5 lakh efficiency item, and launch on 2 November. The reviewers' list also becomes a shared vocabulary: Vadehra and Virk can argue about "error prevention" rather than about whose taste prevails. Then, after Diwali, test the customer-picker screen with five merchants, because that is where the funnel leaks and no heuristic explains why. Option A ships a known severity-4 defect into the busiest week, and the 71 beta complaints already show it is not hypothetical. Option C buys certainty at a cost of up to ₹41.8 lakh in deferred revenue, plus ₹5.3 lakh more in review cost than B, for evidence B largely supplies in three days.
exp40v2-ux.heuristics:
Usability heuristics: reviewing a design systematically instead of by taste

A short list of general principles, applied independently by a handful of inspectors, is still the cheapest way to find usability problems — and among the most misused instruments in product development.

1 Two rooms, two weeks apart

On Monday 28 September 2026, in Ilaaj Health Cloud's Bengaluru office, Rupsha Bordoloi was reading a spreadsheet with 93 rows in it. Ilaaj sells clinical software to hospital groups, and the previous week five people had independently inspected its new medication-reconciliation module: two Ilaaj designers, a product manager and two external consultants. Each worked alone and wrote down everything that struck them as a usability problem. Bordoloi had a release gate on Friday 9 October, after which a 1,400-bed hospital group in Pune would discharge patients through the module. The spreadsheet was 93 claims of unknown quality, and her job was to decide which were true.

Fifteen days later, Ranadeep Barkataki had the opposite problem. Barkataki runs product at Imlee, a consumer money app with 1.8 crore registered users and 42 lakh monthly actives, whose 1 September assistant answers questions about a household's spending and acts on them. Before launch, four reviewers inspected it against a standard heuristic list: 31 candidates, 22 accepted, 16 fixed. None described what happened next. In September, 496 of 1,24,000 assistant-initiated actions executed against the wrong payee or amount: 0.40 per cent. On Tuesday 13 October, Barkataki had to decide whether heuristic review stayed in Imlee's gate.

The same method, honestly applied, served one of them well and failed the other. Understanding why is the whole of this topic.

2 The idea, and who disagrees about it

Heuristic evaluation is a procedure, not a list. A small number of inspectors examine an interface independently, each judging it against a short set of general usability principles and reporting problems as a triple: where it occurs, which principle it offends, how bad it is. Three things are confused with it: a heuristic is a reviewer's memory aid, deliberately few and abstract; a guideline set is a reference of hundreds of recommendations; a standard is a criterion with a pass/fail rule, such as W3C's WCAG 2.2. Heuristics are highest in generality and lowest in enforceability, which is why they make a good conversation and a bad gate.

Rolf Molich and Jakob Nielsen set out nine principles in Communications of the ACM in March 1990; Nielsen and Molich followed with a method paper at CHI that year. Nielsen revised the set at CHI 1994, deriving the familiar ten by factor-analysing a corpus of real usability problems, and it was written up in Usability Inspection Methods, the 1994 collection he edited with Robert Mack. The problem was economic: a laboratory study then cost more than most projects could justify. Nielsen called the alternative discount usability.

Those ten are the industry's lingua franca, and the objective is to use them as a review checklist — grouped, not recited. Orientation: the interface says what state it is in, speaks the user's vocabulary, and shows the options rather than requiring them remembered. Agency: the user can leave, undo and work at their own pace, and nothing irreversible happens through a one-way door. Error economics: prevent what can be prevented, make the rest legible, keep recovery cheap, documentation last. Restraint: every element competes for attention, and consistency with the platform and with itself frees that attention for the task. The four cover all ten of Nielsen's items; the grouping is this page's, the content his.

Five schools disagree about what the method is for; the test is which proposition each signs. The discount school (Molich, Nielsen): three to five trained inspectors with a short list find most of the problems worth fixing, cheaply enough to run before the design is decided — but never substituting for watching users. The criteria school, Bastien and Scapin's INRIA ergonomic criteria of 1993: operational definitions raise agreement between evaluators, precision before memorability. The task-theory school behind the cognitive walkthrough of Polson, Lewis, Rieman and Wharton: evaluation must be anchored in a named task and a theory of exploratory learning, never a static screen. The measurement school — Gray and Salzman's 1998 critique, Hertzum and Jacobsen on the evaluator effect, Molich's Comparative Usability Evaluation studies: no published experiment establishes that one inspection method finds more real problems than another, so findings are never a release criterion. The compliance school — WCAG, platform guidelines, IEC 62366: only a pass/fail criterion belongs in a gate, and a finding is not a defect.

3 Mechanics, and the arithmetic underneath

Practitioners describe inspection, consolidation and severity rating; the implicit steps decide the outcome. Experts inspect tasks, not screens, and walk each twice: once to learn the flow, once to inspect it. They keep each evaluator's findings separately, because the per-evaluator record is the only thing that later says how much of the problem population has been seen. They attach a consequence to every finding, since one without a consequence cannot be triaged. And they triage with a domain expert, because an inspector's judgement is a hypothesis about a user they are not.

Ilaaj's review followed that shape. The 93 rows were issue statements, not problems; de-duplicating left 66 distinct candidates. In a two-hour triage with a ward sister and a clinical pharmacologist, 47 of the 66 candidates (71 per cent) were accepted as real problems in the hospital's working context and 19 rejected, mostly conventions the inspectors had read as inconsistencies. Those 47 accounted for 72 detections, the figure that makes the method quantitative.

The formal treatment comes from Nielsen and Thomas Landauer's INTERCHI '93 paper, which models discovery as independent sampling from a fixed population. If an interface holds N problems and the average evaluator finds a fraction λ of them, the number found by i independent evaluators is Found(i) = N × (1 − (1 − λ)i). Pooling the studies available to them they reported an average λ near 0.31 — the origin of the five-evaluator rule of thumb.

Ilaaj could estimate its own λ, because it had kept per-evaluator records. With 47 real problems and 72 detections across five evaluators, λ̂ = 72 ÷ (5 × 47) = 72 ÷ 235 = 0.3064 — almost exactly the pooled literature figure. Substituting back, 1 − 0.69365 = 1 − 0.1605 = 0.8395, so five evaluators should have found 84 per cent of the population; dividing the 47 found by 0.8395 gives a true population near 56, and roughly nine problems nobody saw. Reaching 95 per cent needs ln(0.05) ÷ ln(0.6936) = 8.19 — nine evaluators, not five.

Detection events = problems × evaluators flagging them (32×1 + 9×2 + 3×3 + 2×4 + 1×5 = 72), so λ̂ = 72 ÷ 235 = 0.3064.

Exhibit 1 carries the uncomfortable result: 32 of the 47 real problems — 68 per cent — were reported by exactly one evaluator, and one by all five. This is the evaluator effect documented by Hertzum and Jacobsen, and Molich's CUE studies found the same between professional teams. A manager who fixes only what two or more reviewers flagged discards roughly two- thirds of the real findings, and Exhibit 2 shows that severity barely protects against it.

Severity is routinely done badly. Nielsen's scheme combines how often a problem is met, what it costs, and whether it persists once known, into one 0-to-4 rating — a judgement, not the mean of its inputs. One Ilaaj finding, ward drug abbreviations differing from the paper chart, scored 4, 3 and 3 on those inputs, a mean of 3.33, and was set to severity 2 because that chart is withdrawn in the same release. Such overrides are why clinicians sit in the room.

The economics follow from the model and are less obvious than the folklore suggests. Ilaaj priced a round at ₹0.60 lakh of fixed cost plus ₹0.30 lakh per evaluator, and valued each problem fixed before release at ₹0.85 lakh from its own support history.

But the ratio is the wrong objective when the budget is not binding. Three if you maximise return per rupee, eleven if you maximise problems found at a profit — and the answer swings on the ₹0.85 lakh estimate and on how many found problems get fixed.

4 When it works, and when it misleads

Three conditions, stated as testable claims. First, a convention exists to measure the design against. It holds for Ilaaj's application shell, not its clinical content, where the 19 rejected candidates clustered; and for Imlee's ledger screens, not an assistant with no settled interaction grammar. Second, the failure mode is visible in the artefact at rest. Ilaaj's tab-clearing defect is visible to anyone who opens two tabs; Imlee's wrong-payee executions are a property of a distribution of model outputs, of which an inspector sees one draw. Third, a false positive costs less than a missed problem. Bordoloi, with a week of triage capacity, could afford to be wrong 19 times; Barkataki, with engineering committed, could not. The method misleads when used to certify: a single reviewer misses roughly seven problems in ten, so a short report says little about what remains.

5 Hard edges: platforms, regulation, hardware, AI

In a multi-product company one of the commonest findings — "inconsistent with the rest of the suite" — has no owner. It belongs to the design-system team, who did not commission the review, and arrives as a cross-charge, not a bug. Mature companies route it into the system's backlog with a severity and allow divergence where a documented exception exists: they say they enforce the system; what they keep is a register of exceptions.

On two-sided products the asymmetry is structural: a reviewer can role-play a buyer and almost never a seller, whose work is an occupation with its own accounting, so the detection rate differs by side and nobody notices. In regulated hardware the gap is formal: IEC 62366 wants a documented use-related risk analysis tracing hazards to mitigations, so review is an input to the risk file, not the file. Several standard principles are silent on hardware's dominant failure modes, having been derived from desktop software. And on AI-native surfaces independence survives but the target does not: each evaluator sees a different realisation of the product.

6 Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The denominator you cannot see. λ̂ comes from the problems the panel found, so it cannot see the ones nobody found — and with n evaluators it has a floor of 1 ÷ n, since every counted problem was found at least once. Tell: a four-person panel reporting λ near 0.25 measures nothing.

False positives are the expensive half. Ilaaj's 19 rejected candidates cost two clinicians two hours; the same 19 sent straight to a backlog would have cost engineering weeks. Tell: usability tickets with a higher won't-fix rate than the rest of the backlog.

The list is a recall aid, not a taxonomy of the product. It stops a reviewer noticing only what they habitually notice. Tell: roughly one finding per heuristic, evenly spread — real interfaces are lumpy, so an even spread means someone worked the list instead of the task.

Consistency is a property of a corpus. Nobody can judge it from one screen; it needs the other screens, the platform conventions and the user's prior products. Tell: "inconsistent" findings naming no second location.

Expert users invert two of the families. Orientation and restraint both assume a new user; a ward sister doing forty reconciliations a shift wants density and memorised positions. Tell: a reviewer calling a professional screen cluttered while its users have muscle memory.

The method reviews the artefact it is shown. Problems between screens — a wait, a handoff, a form filled from a document in another room — are invisible. Tell: every finding anchored to one screen, none spanning an interval of time.

Independence is the mechanism. A group walkthrough is a different, worse method: the first speaker anchors the rest and the per-evaluator record disappears. Tell: a consolidated report with no counts of who found what — without Exhibit 1, Ilaaj would have had no λ.

Agreement is not accuracy. Treating multiple reports as corroboration selects for problems easy to see, which correlates with a frequently visited screen, not with severity. Tell: a rule feeding "flagged by" counts into severity.

7 How this differs by product type and stage

Less than practitioners claim, in one respect: error economics applies identically everywhere, because the cost of an unrecoverable mistake does not care about the market. The differences sit in three places. Who can review: on consumer products almost any careful inspector is a plausible proxy for the user; on B2B and enterprise products the inspector is not, and the review is worthless without a domain expert in triage. Whether a convention exists: consumer mobile has dense platform conventions, so consistency findings are well founded, while a novel enterprise workflow or an assistant has none and such findings are invented. What a false positive costs: on a marketplace, a change made for one side's reviewer can damage the other side's economics, so triage must seat both. By stage what changes is the gate, not the method: a seed-stage team runs it weekly on sketches; a scaled company puts it in a release checklist, the most expensive moment to learn anything.

8 Three worked cases

Ilaaj — the method working as designed. Five evaluators, 93 statements, 66 candidates, 47 real problems, λ̂ = 0.3064, nine estimated unseen. Eighteen fixed before the 9 October release — all 14 rated 3 or 4, plus four cheap cosmetic items — and 29 deferred. The round cost ₹2.10 lakh and bought 47 findings nobody would otherwise have had before go-live.

Imlee — the method failing. The pre-launch review found 31 candidates, accepted 22, fixed 16 and named nothing resembling the wrong-payee class. In September, 496 of 1,24,000 assistant actions executed wrongly — 0.40 per cent — at a cost of ₹7.19 lakh in support resolution (496 cases at ₹1,450), on top of ₹18.60 lakh of misdirected payment to trace and reverse (496 at an average ₹3,750). The heuristics ask whether the interface communicates; here the inference was sometimes wrong and the interface communicated it beautifully, and a well-worded confirmation of the wrong payee violates no principle on the list. The 30 September recovery restated payee and amount as parsed and opened a reversal window; in the twelve days to 12 October, 58 of 53,400 actions executed wrongly — 0.11 per cent, 73 per cent below the September rate. Barkataki had meanwhile re-run the review, 5 to 9 October, with seven evaluators: 46 real problems, 53 detections, λ̂ = 53 ÷ 322 = 0.165 — barely above the 1 ÷ 7 = 0.143 floor seven evaluators impose, with 40 of the 46 (87 per cent) reported by exactly one evaluator. At that λ, seven evaluators cover 71.6 per cent, implying a population near 64 and 18 unseen; 95 per cent would take 17 reviewers — not a review but a study.

Ilaka Instruments — the scope error. Ilaka makes milk-chilling units for dairy co-operative collection centres, with a touchscreen controller now on 1,250 units across 310 centres. A four-person review found 24 problems; field observation at nine centres found 11, seven of which appeared nowhere in the desk review, while 20 of the 24 desk findings never arose in the field. The desk review had been reviewing a different artefact: a screen in an office, not one in sunlight under a wet glove.

9 Failure modes and their early warnings

Review as certification. Sign: it sits in a release checklist with a pass/fail column. Diagnostic: what result would have stopped the release? Late cost: a gate that cannot fail. No triage. Sign: findings reach the backlog carrying a reviewer's severity. Diagnostic: who here has done this job for a living? Late cost: a sprint on conventions the users preferred. Group inspection. Sign: one shared document. Diagnostic: how many evaluators found finding 14? Late cost: no coverage estimate for that round. Corroboration ranking. Sign: a "flagged by" count feeding priority. Diagnostic: the severity mix of single-reviewer findings? Late cost: two of the three catastrophic problems would have shipped, as Exhibit 2 shows. Scope drift. Sign: no finding spans two screens or a wait. Diagnostic: which task did each evaluator perform, end to end? Late cost: the expensive problems stay in the field.

10 Where experts genuinely disagree

Discovery or assurance? The discount position is that inspection generates candidates cheaply and early and its error rate is tolerable because triage is cheap; it rests on the cost ratio against laboratory studies. The measurement position is that no published experiment establishes the comparative claims, so inspection may inform but never assure. The first fails if triage is expensive or absent, as in most organisations; the second fails if the method's value lies in hypotheses rather than validity.

Does the list do the work, or the reviewer? One camp holds the ten items are an engine that makes a reviewer notice what they habitually miss; the other that domain experience predicts a good review and the list is scaffolding one outgrows. The evaluator effect favours the second: if the list drove the findings, agreement would be higher. The first fails if reviewers with the list do no better than those without; the second if experienced reviewers using no list match their coverage.

Do heuristics transfer to generative interfaces? One position: nothing has changed, since the principles concern communication and a probabilistic system must still communicate. The other: the unit of evaluation has moved from interface to behaviour, so what is needed is a consequence inventory — every action the system can take, ranked by reversibility and money at risk. Imlee's numbers favour the second, but are one product.

Principal papers. Nielsen, "Enhancing the explanatory power of usability heuristics", CHI 1994; Nielsen and Landauer, "A mathematical model of the finding of usability problems", INTERCHI '93; Gray and Salzman, "Damaged Merchandise?", Human–Computer Interaction 13(3), 1998; Hertzum and Jacobsen, "The evaluator effect", Int. J. Human-Computer Interaction 13(4), 2001.

11 What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs the review and circulates the report. Someone who has internalised it sets panel size from a stated value per problem, not a folklore number; keeps the per-evaluator record, without which there is no coverage estimate; never lets an inspector's severity reach a backlog without a domain expert's override; and names what the review cannot see — the nine unseen problems at Ilaaj, the eighteen at Imlee — so that an absence of findings is never mistaken for an absence of problems.

12 What each of them decided

Bordoloi shipped on 9 October 2026 with 18 of the 47 problems fixed, changing the gate rather than the schedule. Heuristic findings at Ilaaj are now formally candidates, not defects; the gate is clinician triage plus two observed reconciliations on a real ward; and the review moves to the sketch stage of the next module, where the ₹0.85 lakh per problem is still recoverable. She funded nine evaluators rather than the three or eleven the value calculation supports, because nine reaches 95 per cent coverage and a dosing module is where unseen problems are least tolerable.

Barkataki, on 13 October 2026, took heuristic review out of the assistant's gate and kept it for Imlee's deterministic screens, where the method's assumptions hold. In its place went a consequence inventory: every action the assistant can take, ranked by reversibility and rupees at risk, with confirmation-as-parsed and a reversal window above a threshold. He kept the ten as the vocabulary his designers critique in, and out of the sign-off.

  2. Imlee's λ̂ of 0.165 sat two points above its own floor. On what grounds, if any, is that measurement worth paying for?
  3. A mean severity of 3.33 was overridden to 2 because a paper chart is being withdrawn. What rule makes such overrides legitimate rather than convenient?
