Usability Heuristics: Reviewing a Design Without Relying on Taste

A working guide for product managers, built around one decision at a Kolkata software company.

1. A design nobody could fault

On Monday 12 October 2026, Pritha Adhikari, the product manager for invoicing at Hilsa Books, opened a design file she had waited three weeks to see. Hilsa Books is a Kolkata company whose app lets shopkeepers write GST invoices and send them on WhatsApp. About 58,000 shops used the send flow each week, pushing roughly 2,40,000 invoices through it. In the current version, 3.8 per cent of sends were followed within two minutes by the same invoice sent again. That is 9,120 a week, each a customer receiving the message twice.

Pranab Acharya, the lead designer, had redrawn the flow, and it looked good. That was what worried her. The release was fixed for Thursday 22 October, because the Diwali billing season in early November is when shops send most of their invoices. Pallab Auddy, the engineering lead in Pune, wanted to begin building on Tuesday. A moderated test with shopkeepers could not start before 3 November.

Pritha could approve the design because everyone liked it, delay until November, or find a disciplined way to judge it in three days. She chose the third: a heuristic review, five people working separately on 13 and 14 October against a shared rubric. This page follows what the method is, what it found, and what it could not tell her.

2. The idea

A heuristic is a rule of thumb: a general guide that works most of the time without proof in each case. A usability heuristic is such a rule about interfaces, for example “people should be able to see what the system is doing.” A heuristic evaluation is a review in which several trained people inspect an interface alone, note every place it breaks one of those rules, and pool the notes afterwards. No end users take part, which makes it fast, cheap and different from a usability test.

The method comes from Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich, who published it in 1990. It was invented because usability testing was thorough but slow, so most teams skipped it. Their first list had nine rules. In 1994 Nielsen analysed 249 real usability problems against several candidate rule sets and merged the best performers into the ten most people now mean by “Nielsen’s heuristics.” The Nielsen Norman Group still publishes them; read that text rather than any summary, including this one.

The ten fall into families that are easier to hold than the ten. Some concern telling the person where they are: the system shows its status, speaks in the shopkeeper’s own words, and keeps its labels consistent. Some concern keeping the person in charge: undo, exits, and shortcuts for experts. Some concern preventing and repairing mistakes. The rest concern economy: recognising rather than remembering, and leaving out what is not needed. Pritha could say in a meeting, without sounding glib: “This does not predict what users will do; it finds where the design breaks a rule users are known to rely on, before we pay to ship it.”

3. How it actually works

Descriptions usually mention only the middle stages; the first and last decide whether the review is useful.

Frame. A review of “the app” produces vague notes. Pritha scoped it to one task, a shopkeeper creating a GST invoice and sending it, on a mid-range Android phone, the device most users own. She also fixed the rubric: Nielsen’s ten on one page, each with an example from the app.

Walk alone. Each evaluator went through the flow twice: once for the overall feel, once screen by screen, asking whether each element broke a rule. Reviewers who confer first converge, and the method’s strength, that different people notice different faults, is lost.

Log. Every finding was recorded as what happens, which rule it breaks, and a severity from 0 to 4. The scale is Nielsen’s: 0 is not a problem, 1 cosmetic, 2 minor, 3 major, 4 a catastrophe to fix before release. Severity weighs frequency, impact and whether users can learn their way past it.

Merge, rank, decide. Only now did the five meet. They collapsed duplicates, ranked by severity with weekly volume as tie-breaker, and sorted each item into fix now, defer, or test with users. The review ends in a decision, not a score.

4. A worked example, line by line

The evaluators were Pritha, Pranab, Pallab and two support agents who handle shopkeeper calls. They logged 8, 5, 9, 7 and 6 findings: 35 in all, 7.0 on average. After merging, 21 distinct problems remained, because many were found more than once. Table 1 shows the overlap.

Thirteen of the 21 were found by exactly one person. Had Pritha reviewed alone she would have found 8, which is 38 per cent of the merged list, unaware of the rest. Nielsen and Thomas Landauer expressed this in 1993: the share found by n independent evaluators is 1 − (1 − λ)n, where λ is the chance that one evaluator finds any given problem. Across the projects they studied the average λ was about 0.31 across all projects they studied (about 0.34 for heuristic evaluations alone). It is a model, assuming every problem is equally easy to spot.

At λ = 0.31 the shares are 31, 52, 67, 77 and 84 per cent for one to five evaluators, so each added person contributes 31, 21, 15, 10 and 7 points. Five evaluators at an assumed ₹9,000 a day, fully loaded, cost ₹45,000.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Review is not usability testing

A test watches real users and measures what they do; a review applies rules and predicts where they may stumble. It will flag things users never trip on and miss things they do. Nor is it an accessibility audit against a standard such as WCAG, or an A/B experiment.

Heuristics are not design principles

Principles, such as Don Norman’s emphasis on discoverability and feedback in The Design of Everyday Things, or Ben Shneiderman’s eight golden rules, guide a designer making something. Nielsen’s list suits an inspector examining something already made.

The rules conflict

Minimalism argues for hiding the confirmation text; keeping the user informed argues for showing it. A review surfaces the conflict; judgement and testing settle it.

Severity is opinion, so average it

Have evaluators rate independently and take the mean; a two-point gap is a conversation.

It cannot say whether to build the thing

A compliant invoice flow can still solve a problem shopkeepers do not have. A review judges execution, not demand.

It reflects the evaluators’ world

Reviewers in Kolkata and Pune share assumptions about literacy and devices. The “challan” finding came from a support agent.

Before relying on it

Who were the evaluators, and how independent? Was the scope one task or the whole app? What would we do differently if the review is wrong?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

Table 4. Where the review sharpens and where it misleads.

Hilsa Books is B2B with a consumer-like audience: shopkeepers use a phone between customers, so first-use clarity matters. A large firm’s danger is ritual; a start-up’s is assuming five friendly colleagues are representative.

7. Common mistakes

Table 5. Four common mistakes in heuristic review.
Symptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of Pritha’s week has a one-task scope, a one-page rubric, five independent walkthroughs and a merged list with the overlap shown, as in Table 1. Severity is rated separately and averaged. The report states the evaluators’ limits and gives a range for unseen problems. Every finding links to a rule, a screen and a weekly volume. The meeting ends with three lists, fix now, defer and test, each with an owner.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On Thursday 15 October, Pritha chose. The three problems rated 3 or 4 would be fixed before the 22 October release: a clear delivered confirmation, a labelled toggle on the discount field, and an undo for deleted drafts. Pallab estimated six engineer-days. The two severity-2 items would wait, and the unlabelled icon would be tested, not assumed. She booked five moderated sessions for the week of 3 November, because the roughly six unseen problems (plausibly four to ten) in Table 3 were what a review cannot find. Her reasoning: the review bought a better release for ₹45,000, not certainty.

To go further, learn how usability testing is run, then how to weigh severity against business metrics. Both begin where this method stops.

Two questions to sit with. If your team could afford only three evaluators, which three would you choose, and what would each know that the others do not? And think of a design you recently approved on taste: which family of rules did it most likely break, and how would you have found out?

Sources: J. Nielsen and R. Molich, “Heuristic evaluation of user interfaces,” CHI 1990; R. Molich and J. Nielsen, “Improving a human-computer dialogue,” Communications of the ACM, 1990; J. Nielsen, “Enhancing the explanatory power of usability heuristics,” CHI 1994; T. Landauer and J. Nielsen, “A mathematical model of the finding of usability problems,” INTERCHI 1993; J. Nielsen, Usability Engineering, 1993. Hilsa Books and everyone and every figure attached to it are fictional.
case40v1-ux.critique:
Discovery & Design · UX & Design Collaboration

Bandobast Technologies: One Screen, Four Options

A Bengaluru field-service software company has three weeks of pilot data, one usability study, a contract clause and seven people who agree on none of it.

1. Sunday night

At 22:40 on Sunday, 8 November 2026, Jaskirat Randhawa was sitting on the floor of her flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, a laptop on a stool and, beside it, a ₹9,000 Android handset with 2 GB of memory, issued in September so that she could see what a technician in Hubballi sees. It had taken 4.8 seconds to open the app.

On the laptop were three documents. The first was her own one-page brief from February: one screen, one scroll, no back button. The second was the revised proposal Jinia Rakhra had sent from Berlin, splitting that one screen into two and asking for fourteen weeks. The third was the slide Randhawa was due to present at 09:30 the next morning, which said the new job card was 19.7 per cent faster and recommended a full rollout on 1 December.

A message had arrived at 22:35 from Toronto, where it was 12:05 on Sunday afternoon. Jhumpa Riar had re-run the reopen numbers a third way; the gap had got worse. Randhawa had not replied. Eleven days later, on Thursday 19 November, she had twelve minutes at the board meeting, between the GST e-invoicing update and the Gulf pipeline. She had not decided what they would say.

2. The company and the annexe

Bandobast Technologies was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Jarnail Rayat, who had run after-sales operations for an air-conditioner distributor, reconciling job sheets by WhatsApp photograph. Bandobast Field gave the technician a phone app and the franchisee a dashboard: assignment, route, parts, customer OTP, UPI collection, warranty exception. By October 2026 it carried 2,14,000 technicians across 19 states. Revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was ₹96 crore; annual recurring revenue on 1 October 2026 was ₹118 crore.

The decision that constrains November was taken in March 2024, when Bandobast signed Annexe 4 to win Bidaya Facilities Services, a Dubai facilities group. Bidaya had printed 4,000 procedure cards and trained 2,800 technicians against screenshots of the job card, and wanted that investment protected: any change to the job-card screen required 60 days' notice and Bidaya's user-acceptance sign-off, and Bandobast would reimburse retraining caused by vendor-initiated interface changes, capped at ₹40 lakh.

Annexe 4 also required a mirrored Arabic layout built from the same components as the English one. That is why Bandobast Base, the design system, was built in 2024 around a strict rule of one task per screen: mirroring is tractable when a screen holds one job and intractable when it holds four. Jinia Rakhra was hired in Berlin to build Base. Her fully loaded cost is about ₹96 lakh a year against ₹34 lakh for a senior designer in Bengaluru — roughly 2.8 times, a ratio nobody has forgotten.

3. The industry

Field-service software in India sits between two sorts of competitor. Salesforce Field Service and the global suites sell to large captive service arms; Zoho and Freshworks sell horizontal products bought on a card. Bandobast's wedge was the technician's phone: cheap handsets, patchy data, three languages, and a workforce that turns over fast enough that any screen needing training is a screen that fails.

Three external forces press on the job card itself. UPI collection at the doorstep, cleared through NPCI's rails, made the app the payment instrument and raised the cost of a mis-tap to the price of the part. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act obliges a consent notice before a technician reads a customer's number for the OTP step; that work starts on 1 December. GST e-invoicing changes land on 1 January 2027. Jio and Airtel reworked their prepaid plans in September; franchisees migrated circle by circle.

Abroad, the Gulf is Bandobast's only non-India revenue of any size, and Bidaya is almost all of it: ₹14.2 crore a year, just over 12 per cent of ARR. Jaiveer Rohilla's North American pipeline — three deals worth ₹9.6 crore, ₹4.1 crore of it forecast to close in the quarter ending March 2027 — is the growth story the board has seen twice.

4. What happened, and what was wrong

In January, a renewal review showed technicians abandoning job cards part-way. The four-screen flow was blamed, and Randhawa's brief followed on 10 February. In August, re-reading the raw export, Riar found that of 11,480 abandonment events logged that January, 7,118 — 62.0 per cent — were on one field, the serial-number scan. The remaining 4,362 are not located by screen. Nobody has revisited the brief.

Between January and June the fortnightly critique worked through components (Exhibit 4). On 18 June, Jogesh Rattan's team in Pune began building the one-screen card from the brief. Rakhra objected in writing that it broke Base's one-task-per-screen rule and would not mirror; the objection sits in a thread nobody closed. Jorawar Rehal, the design head, was on leave for most of July. On 4 August, critique #12 reviewed the card; at 10:00 IST that Tuesday it was 06:30 in Berlin.

The lab study ran 2–5 September in Jaipur and Coimbatore (Exhibit 1) and produced the 19.7 per cent. The pilot opened on 28 September in four circles, 23,540 technicians, 11.0 per cent of the base. On 1 October those circles moved to a new data plan. On 20 October Jumana Ruprai escalated ticket volumes from Singapore (Exhibit 3). On 26 October Riar's telemetry pull landed (Exhibit 2), with the device mix in Exhibit 6. On 30 October Rakhra sent the two-screen proposal. On 3 November Rohilla demonstrated the new card at a conference in Chicago. On 5 November legal confirmed that Annexe 4 covers any change to that screen, not only a material redesign: 60 days from Monday is 8 January 2027.

5. The people

Jaskirat Randhawa, 34, vice-president of product, holds that the one-screen card is right and the pilot circles are the problem. The February brief is hers, as is the 1 December date she gave the board in August. She has not said that the brief arrived with the screens already drawn, or that Rehal's team has not had a blank page since.

Jorawar Rehal, 41, design head, has four designers for eleven surfaces. He wants to ship: the critique ran, decisions were recorded, and his FY28 headcount case rests on design being seen to deliver. He has not said how long the card was on screen at #12, or who else had seen it before he signed.

Jinia Rakhra, 37, staff product designer in Berlin, wants the two-screen split and fourteen weeks. Base is her work; the one-screen card breaks its central rule and will not mirror into Arabic for Bidaya. She has not said that her contract ends in March, or that she knows exactly what she costs relative to Bengaluru.

Jogesh Rattan, 38, engineering manager in Pune, has nine engineers, six on this. He wants to ship because fourteen weeks is time he loses to the consent-notice work on 1 December. He has not said that his team built the card from the brief without a design hand-off, or that the Base deviation was never documented.

Jhumpa Riar, 31, data scientist in Toronto, thinks the field signal is real and badly confounded, and wants four more weeks of pilot. She put the 19.7 per cent in the board pack herself and now wants it withdrawn. She has not said she never saw the lab protocol before the number was quoted.

Jumana Ruprai, 36, customer-success lead in Singapore, wants a rollback. Her renewal numbers carry the four pilot franchisee groups, two of which have asked for credits. She has not said how partial her ticket data is: her desk runs 09:00 to 21:00 Singapore time, and anything in India after 18:30 IST reaches the brand's call centre instead.

Jaiveer Rohilla, 45, sales head in New Jersey, wants the card everywhere, Bidaya included, with retraining paid out of the renewal. He demonstrated it in Chicago on 3 November. He has not said that he told two prospects it ships on 1 December.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Three thousand two hundred and ninety-one more reopened jobs. That is the number. Everything else is interpretation.”Rohilla, on Exhibit 2, 27 October
“It is not the number. The pilot closed 29,700 fewer jobs than the control. At the control's own rate the pilot would have reopened 14,036, so the excess is 4,078, not 3,291 — and as a rate it is 29.1 per cent worse. Your figure is smaller than the truth.”Riar, replying forty minutes later
“We review every week. It is just not written down. Writing it down was never the job.”Rattan, on the gap in Exhibit 4
“Nobody has reviewed that card. They reviewed five components, one at a time, and the card is what is left when you staple them together.”Rakhra, 2 November
“I signed #12. I had been back from leave six days with eleven surfaces behind it. Ask me whether we reviewed the card or the components and you will get different answers.”Rehal, 6 November
“All four of your options end with a screen and a date. So would mine, if you asked me the way you asked in February.”Rakhra, 6 November, 18:10 Berlin
“Do not bring me a design argument on the nineteenth. Bring me a number and what it cost.”Rayat, to Randhawa, 4 November

8. The options as Randhawa sees them

A. Ship as built on 1 December, to the whole base except Bidaya's estate, where no notice is served and v8.6 stays. ₹31.2 lakh (Exhibit 5), and two live variants of the job card with no end date, which Rattan costs as a second support queue and test matrix. Rohilla's two prospects get their date.

B. Take Rakhra's split and ship two screens in mid-February. ₹90.6 lakh, and it assumes Base can carry a two-screen variant of the flow its components were written for; nobody has opened Base to check, and Rakhra's contract ends in March. The 1 December slot passes to the consent-notice work, which Rattan says will take it anyway.

C. Roll the pilot back to v8.6 and re-run the research as a field diary study through December, deciding in January. ₹15.9 lakh, the cheapest column in Exhibit 5, and the re-run would be commissioned from the same vendor.

D. Ship everywhere including Bidaya, serve the 60-day notice on Monday so the Dubai estate converts on 8 January, and pay the ₹32.2 lakh retraining inside Exhibit 5's ₹67.2 lakh total, in the renewal conversation that closes on 31 January. Bidaya's user-acceptance testing is run by Ruprai's desk, two people, in a week that also holds the GST change.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The go/no-go is at 09:30 on Monday 9 November, because the release train for 1 December closes code on 14 November. Annexe 4 gives Bidaya 60 days and a sign-off; served on Monday, that lands on 8 January 2027. Four of Rattan's nine engineers move to the consent-notice work on 1 December and the GST e-invoicing change takes the rest from 1 January. The Berlin role is frozen, so Rakhra's fourteen weeks are Rakhra's alone. The retraining cap is ₹40 lakh; the Bidaya renewal decision is 31 January; ₹4.1 crore of Rohilla's pipeline falls in the quarter that contains it. The board meets on 19 November.

At 23:50 Randhawa picked up the ₹9,000 handset and opened the new card again. The parts field was where she had asked for it to be, in February, in a document she had written in an afternoon. The card took 4.8 seconds to load and it fitted on one screen, and she could not tell, holding it, whether the thing in her hand was the right design measured badly or the wrong design measured kindly. The slide still said 19.7 per cent. She had until half past nine.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly does the 19.7 per cent in Exhibit 1 measure, over whom, and under what definition of completion? What would you need added before repeating the figure to the board?
  2. Exhibits 2, 3 and 6 describe the same three weeks. Which of the pilot's worse numbers survive once device tier and the 1 October plan change are allowed for, and which cannot be separated at all here?
  3. On the warranty-exception task Exhibit 1 shows 143 seconds against 164, and 6 of 9 completing against 4 of 9, on nine technicians an arm; Exhibit 2 shows 1.18 exceptions raised per 100 jobs against 1.90. Give two readings of that pair that lead to opposite decisions, and name the measurement that would separate them.
  4. Rehal, Rakhra and Rattan each describe a different critique process. What would have to be true for each account to be accurate, and what does the way Exhibit 4 is compiled prevent you from knowing?
  5. Annexe 4 won a contract now worth ₹14.2 crore a year. Using Exhibit 5 and anything else here, price what that clause has cost Bandobast since, and say who inside the company should have been in the room when it was signed.
  6. It is 09:30 on Monday 9 November. What does Randhawa decide, what does she stop doing, and to whom? Then write the twelve minutes she gives the board on 19 November, including the sentence saying what she still does not know.
exp20v2-ux.critique:
Design critique and collaboration

How a product manager can improve a designer's work without writing it for them, and without waving it through.

1. A payment screen, two proposals

On Tuesday 22 September 2026, Kaberi Sarkar, a senior product manager at Chorui, opened a message from her engineering lead, Kallol Sarmah. Chorui is a Kolkata-founded app for booking homestays and small hotels across eastern and north-eastern India. The message held a link and one line: "Koyel's payment screen is ready for review. Are we building hers, or the one you marked up?"

Both existed because of one number. In the four weeks to Sunday 13 September, an average of 40,000 sessions a week reached Chorui's payment screen, and 62 per cent of them ended in a completed booking. Each completed booking earned Chorui a 10 per cent commission on an average booking value of ₹1,850, or ₹185. Two weeks earlier Kaberi had annotated a screenshot: make the Pay button larger, make it orange, lift it above the fold. Koyel Saikia, the product designer in Guwahati who owned the screen, had answered with something else: collapse six form fields into two and put UPI first.

Funnel input (four weeks to 13 September 2026)Value
Sessions reaching the payment screen, weekly average40,000
Share of those sessions ending in a completed booking62%
Completed bookings per week (40,000 × 62%)24,800
Commission per completed booking (10% of ₹1,850)₹185
Weekly commission (24,800 × ₹185)₹45,88,000

Completion is measured against sessions that reached the payment screen, not against all app visitors. UPI is India's instant bank-to-bank payment system.

Engineering had room in the next sprint for one of the two. The review was set for Thursday 24 September at 11:00. If Kaberi simply chose her own version, Koyel would learn that her analysis was decorative, and the next problem would arrive already solved by someone who had not examined it. If she praised Koyel's version without testing it, Chorui would spend three weeks on a redesign nobody had held against the number that justified it.

2. The idea

Design critique is a structured conversation in which people judge a piece of design against what it is meant to achieve, and say why, so the designer can improve it. Three terms are worth fixing. The objective is the outcome the design exists to produce, such as more completed payments. A constraint is a fact the solution must respect, such as a payment partner's rules. A preference is a reaction that depends on taste and cannot be traced to either.

The practice is old. Architecture and art schools have held studio "crits" since at least the nineteenth-century École des Beaux-Arts, and the Bauhaus carried the habit into design. Choreographer Liz Lerman formalised a version in the 1990s, her Critical Response Process, in which the maker asks questions before the audience offers opinions. Aaron Irizarry and Adam Connor's Discussing Design (2015) is a well-known statement of the software version. It exists because opinions about visual work are cheap, and without a shared standard the most senior opinion wins.

The sentence Kaberi could say in the meeting without sounding glib was this: "Tell me what the screen is for, and I will tell you whether I think it does that and why; how it does it is yours."

Figure 1 shows the division. The left column is information the designer rarely has in full: what the business needs, what the evidence says, what cannot move. The right column is craft the manager rarely has. The middle is the only place the two meet, and it carries observations and questions, not instructions. Kaberi's orange-button markup crossed the line: it handed Koyel a solution before either of them had agreed on the problem.

3. How it works, step by step

A well-run critique has five steps.

In framing, the designer says what the screen is for and for whom, in a sentence. Koyel's was: "A first-time guest on a mid-range Android phone should be able to pay in under a minute without re-typing anything the app already knows."

In observing, reviewers describe before they judge. Kaberi's observation was: "The billing address is the third of six fields, above the payment methods." In relating, she tied it to evidence. Kunja Saha, Chorui's researcher, had reviewed 15 recordings of abandoned payments she had selected as typical, and in 9 of them the guest stopped at the billing-address field. That is a sample chosen by a person, not a random one, so it supports a hypothesis and does not measure a rate.

In asking, she posed a question: "Does the billing address need to be asked before payment at all?" The table shows the translation.

As first writtenAs critique
"Make the Pay button orange and bigger.""I see a grey button of the same weight as 'Back'. Guests who hesitate here may not know which action completes the booking. Is it clear enough?"
"Cut the address field.""The address is asked before the payment methods, and 9 of 15 sampled abandonments stopped there. Is it needed before payment?"
"UPI should be first.""The payment methods sit below all six fields. What do we lose if the most-used method appears first?"

The last step is the one managers most often forget to protect. The designer decides. She may accept the point, answer it with a constraint the manager did not know, or answer it with a solution nobody had imagined.

4. A worked example

Before the review, the team wrote down what each proposal was expected to do. These were guesses made before any test, not results. Kaberi's markup (call it B) was expected to lift completion from 62 to 63 per cent. Koyel's reflow (call it A) was expected to reach 66 per cent. Everything below uses the 40,000 weekly sessions and the ₹185 commission from section 1.

OptionAssumed completionBookings a weekGain on todayWeekly gain
Today62%24,8000₹0
B, larger orange button63%25,200400₹74,000
A, reflow, as predicted66%26,4001,600₹2,96,000
A, cautious second pass63.5%25,400600₹1,11,000

Bookings = 40,000 × completion rate. Gain = bookings minus 24,800. Weekly gain = gain × ₹185. Gains are weekly commission, before any cost of building.

The first pass is easy to follow. A's predicted 66 per cent gives 26,400 bookings, 1,600 more than today, worth 1,600 × ₹185 = ₹2,96,000 a week. B gives 400 more, worth ₹74,000. A is four times B.

The second pass changes one input: the lift for A. Koyel herself said 66 per cent rested on a single comparison with a competitor's checkout, so Kaberi asked what happens if the reflow reaches only 63.5 per cent. Bookings fall to 25,400, a gain of 600, worth ₹1,11,000. A is still ahead of B, but by 1.5 times, not four, and the choice now deserves a real test.

Writing the guesses down turned a dispute about taste into an argument about one number, 66 per cent, and that is something a critique and a prototype test can address.

5. Nuances that separate users from the vocabulary

Critique is not approval, and it is not a vote

A meeting that ends with "any objections?" is a sign-off ritual. A critique produces information the designer can use.

Objective, constraint and preference are different kinds of comment

"This slows the guest down" is traceable to the objective. "The payment partner requires an address" is a constraint. "I don't like orange" is a preference. Only the first two should change the design on their own authority; teams that cannot sort comments this way drift towards the preference of whoever ranks highest.

Having a view is not dictating

The test is where the comment points. A comment that describes an effect leaves the designer free. A comment that names a colour, a size or a position removes the choice. A manager with a solution in mind should offer it once, labelled as a hypothesis.

Critique is not usability testing

Colleagues reviewing a mock-up predict user behaviour; they do not observe it. Critique cannot tell you whether a guest in Siliguri on a patchy connection will finish paying.

Fidelity should match the question

A sketch invites comments on the idea. A polished screen invites comments on the polish. If the open question is whether to ask for an address at all, show a rough flow.

The designer may critique the brief

Collaboration runs both ways. If Koyel says the objective is wrong, because completion matters less than refund requests, that is critique of the product manager's work and deserves the same discipline in return.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

In a consumer product such as Chorui's guest app, objectives are about behaviour at volume, and the 40,000-session funnel gives critique something to measure against. In a B2B product, say software for hotel owners, the users are few and expert, so the critique is better anchored in a conversation with three or four of them than in a funnel, and the designer needs the manager to bring the workflow, not the click rate.

In a marketplace, one screen serves two sides whose interests partly conflict. A payment screen that reassures the guest might expose the host to more cancellations. The objective must name which side the design is for.

Scale changes the ritual. In an early-stage company critique happens at a desk, and the risk is that it never becomes explicit. In a large company, formal reviews with many attendees are common, and the risk is the opposite: too many opinions and no clear owner.

7. Common mistakes

Solutioneering. The symptom is that screens converge on the manager's sketch and the designer stops presenting alternatives. The misunderstanding is that specificity helps. The cheapest diagnostic: strike every colour, size and position from your comment. If nothing is left, you had a preference, not a critique.

Abdication. The symptom is "looks good, ship it" and a launch nobody can connect to a goal. The misunderstanding is that respecting craft means withholding judgement. The diagnostic: ask the designer to state the objective in one sentence, and then try yourself. If the two sentences differ, you have found the real problem.

Critique by committee. The symptom is a review with nine attendees and forty comments, most contradictory. The misunderstanding is that more voices means better coverage. The diagnostic is to count how many comments name the objective. Few of them doing so suggests the framing step was skipped.

8. What good looks like

Picture the same Thursday handled well. Koyel opens with her one-sentence objective. Kunja shares the 15 recordings and states their limits. Kaberi gives three observations, each tied to the objective, and two questions. Kallol, the engineer, adds a constraint: the address field is required by the payment partner for card payments but not for UPI. The meeting does not choose between A and B. It leaves with a sharper question, namely whether to drop the address for UPI and move it after payment for cards, and with the guessed completion figures written beside the designs.

Koyel leaves with more information than she arrived with, and she keeps the decision.

9. What Kaberi decided

She did not choose A or B on Thursday 24 September. She withdrew her markup, wrote the objective at the top of the review document, and asked Koyel to prototype A with the address dropped for UPI and moved after payment for cards. She also asked Kunja to test it against today's screen with a small group of guests before engineering committed three weeks. Her reasoning was that the 66 per cent guess was the weakest link in the case for A, and a small test of whether guests stall less is cheap.

To go further, read about how research findings become design decisions, and about handoffs among research, design and product. Critique tests a design against its objective; those topics show how the objective is built from evidence.

Two questions to sit with. Think of the last piece of design feedback you gave. Would it still make sense with every colour, size and position removed? And if you had to write down, before the next review, the number you expect the design to move, would you be willing to be held to it?
case20v1-ux.critique:
Aaina Homes: Fixing the Booking Flow

A case on design critique and collaboration

1. Opening

On the evening of Monday 19 October 2026, Ishmeet Puri sat in Aaina Homes' Indiranagar office in Bengaluru with two documents open side by side. One was a twelve-slide redesign of the company's booking flow, sent from Berlin that morning by Ishleen Pannu, the senior product designer. The other was Ishmeet's own page of notes, headed "What I would change", with eleven screen-by-screen annotations. She had not sent it to anyone.

Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November. The last app release before the festival would leave on Thursday 29 October, and on Thursday 22 October Ishmeet had to tell the festive-readiness call what the booking flow would look like on the 29 October train. She had three days to decide what to change, and how to work with a designer who was three and a half hours behind her and did not yet know she had doubts.

2. Company background

Aaina Homes, founded in Bengaluru in 2018, sells home-cleaning and repair services through an app: deep cleaning of kitchens and bathrooms, AC servicing, sofa and carpet shampooing. A customer books a professional for a visit of two to four hours. Aaina keeps 20 per cent of the booking value and pays the remainder to the independent professional. By September it served nine cities through about 4,100 professionals and had raised ₹140 crore over three rounds.

Its rivals are better known. Urban Company leads the category; Pronto and Snabbit have pushed quick home help in the metros; Justdial still sends many customers to local providers. Customers pay by UPI, mostly through PhonePe and Google Pay, on a Razorpay gateway. Because addresses and phone numbers fall under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, Aaina's lawyers had advised asking for them only when needed.

In the 30 days to 15 October, 2,40,000 sessions began a booking and 87,480 completed one, at an average booking value of ₹2,000 (Exhibit 1). Product and engineering numbered 22 people in Bengaluru and Pune, plus two remote colleagues: Ishleen in Berlin, hired in 2022, and Ikjot in Toronto.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 shows three large leaks: the home-details screen loses a fifth of users, and the slot and payment steps each lose a quarter. Ishmeet's instinct, written in her notes, was to cut steps: delete the home-details screen and move the slot picker to the front. Ikjot Purewal, the data scientist in Toronto, had already warned her that the home-details screen collects the bedroom and bathroom counts on which every price depends. Without it Aaina could show no price at all.

Ishleen's redesign did something else. It put a single bedroom selector and a price estimate on the service card, ahead of the slot, and merged address and payment onto one screen. It rested on September interviews in Bengaluru and Pune and on a moderated test of a clickable prototype (Exhibit 2, lower table). Ipsa Phull, who ran customer success from Singapore, had coded 150 chats from customers who left at the slot step (Exhibit 2, upper table). The largest reason was price, not the slot; a third of those who wrote in found no slot they wanted, which no layout could fix.

The calendar mattered as much as the evidence. Ishleen's working day ended at 22:00 Bengaluru time, so anything Ishmeet sent later waited in Berlin's inbox overnight and arrived as an instruction, with no conversation around it. Her message had closed, "Happy to walk through the thinking whenever useful." Ishmeet read it as an offer and a warning. Ishwinder Pabla, the engineering lead in Pune, put the full redesign at six weeks for five engineers. Ishleen, asked separately, said four weeks, assuming the existing component library. Neither had seen the other's number.

4. The people

Ishleen Pannu, senior product designer, Berlin. She wants the booking flow rebuilt around the price, and she wants to be asked what problem a screen solves before being told how it should look. Her last two projects were reshaped by stakeholder markups, and she said so.

Ishwinder Pabla, engineering lead, Pune. He wants a scope that fits a release train and no festive-week incidents. He distrusts any design he sees only after it is "done".

Ikjot Purewal, data scientist, Toronto. He wants any change shipped behind a flag so it can be measured. Toronto is 9.5 hours behind India until 1 November, so his working day opens in Bengaluru's early evening, and live debate with him is possible only after 18:30 IST.

Ipsa Phull, customer success lead, Singapore. She wants the customer's own words heard in the room, and she wants slot supply treated as an operations problem, not a design one.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 3. The three options compared

Option C is 4 engineer-weeks before Diwali and 24 after, built over five weeks from 16 November, the first Monday after a week to read flag results post-Diwali. Design time excluded.

Timeline scale: 30 px per day from 19 October. Option B reaches customers on 7 December, off this chart.

6. The options

Option A: send the markup. Ishmeet converts her eleven annotations into a specification, Ishleen draws it to the letter, and Pune ships it on 29 October. The upside is certainty and a release before Diwali. The cost is that the spec removes the home-details screen the price depends on, tests nothing, and tells Ishleen her research was optional. Her interviews are evidence the markup never consults.

Option B: approve the redesign as drawn. Ishmeet trusts the specialist and signs off. The upside is a coherent flow built by the person who understands it best. The cost is that it ships on 7 December, after Diwali, so the festive peak runs on the flow Exhibit 1 describes; the four-week and six-week estimates stay unreconciled; and nobody has examined why a third of the chats came from customers wanting slots Aaina cannot supply.

Option C: brief, critique, phase. Ishmeet withholds her markup and writes a one-page brief instead: the outcome (more completed bookings), the evidence, the fixed constraints (UPI, DPDP-compliant address timing, the 29 October train) and what is open. A structured critique follows on Wednesday 21 October, at 20:30 in Bengaluru, 17:00 in Berlin, 11:00 in Toronto and 23:00 in Singapore. Before Diwali, only the price-on-card element ships, behind a flag; the rest is built afterwards. The upside is a measured gain and a working relationship. She names Ishleen as owner of the solution and defines success as the slot-step rate in Exhibit 1, now 75.0 per cent. The cost is a smaller festive win, a full redesign eleven days after Option B, and a decision that may look timid to the leadership call.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. In Exhibit 1 the home-details and slot steps each lose 48,000 sessions. What else would you need to know before choosing between them as the target?
  2. Exhibit 2 gives a reason for leaving, not a cause. What does each of the four reasons imply for who should act, designer or not?
  3. Ishmeet's markup and Ishleen's redesign both claim to reduce friction. What would each need to show before you would accept it?
  4. Which option would you choose, and what would you say to Ishleen first?

8. A note for the learner

Design critique is product critique at screen level. The PM's job is to say what the screen must achieve and for whom, to react to the designer's work as a user would, and to leave the solution to the person trained to find it. Dictating pixels fails because the PM holds one hypothesis and no craft; abdicating fails because the designer lacks the commercial and engineering context to prioritise.

One defensible path is Option C. Its reasoning runs through the exhibits. Price visibility is the largest stated reason (44.0 per cent) and sits at the centre of Ishleen's design, so that element deserves to go first. If the slot-step rate rose five points, from 75.0 to 80.0 per cent, that gain would, at current volume, lift confirmed bookings in a 30-day period from 87,480 to 93,312, which is 5,832 more, worth ₹116.64 lakh of booking value and ₹23.33 lakh to Aaina per 30 days. Four engineer-weeks cost ₹2.0 lakh, once. Ipsa's 34.0 per cent should go to operations. The prototype result, four people in twenty, is encouraging but too thin to justify skipping the flag Ikjot wants.

The brief is the instrument: it fixes the outcome and constraints and states what is open, so the critique can test the work against them rather than against taste. In the critique, Ishmeet speaks last, begins with the outcome, and frames reactions as observations rather than fixes. She also reconciles the two estimates on the call. The test of the approach is that Ishleen leaves it owning the solution.
exp40v2-ux.critique:
Design critique and collaboration

Discovery & Design › UX & Design Collaboration · near-expert reading

1. Two rooms, three weeks before a freeze

In Bengaluru on Tuesday 6 October 2026, Labanya Talukdar asked her design lead a question she knew she should not ask. Talukdar is vice-president of product at Dinchari, a money-habits app with 2.1 million monthly actives. Lavleen Tahbildar, her principal designer, had brought a redesigned streak-setup screen — the one 42,000 new users a week pass through, and the entry to Dinchari's paid tier. Talukdar wanted a single-tap default; Tahbildar wanted the three-field version she had drawn. Completion sits at 61.0 per cent; Talukdar thought her variant worth a point or more, Tahbildar a few tenths.

On Friday 9 October, Lekhraj Tamuli met the same problem in another shape in Pune. Tamuli is vice-president of product at Damru Yard Systems, which sells warehouse execution software and the rugged handhelds it runs on: 41 depots live across three logistics customers, about 1,400 handheld users. On 22 September five people inspected the nine-screen putaway flow and returned 41 distinct problems, and the tooling freeze for the next handheld revision falls on 30 October. Tamuli cannot run an experiment — there is no traffic to split, only depots and training rosters — and cannot get a usability session into a night shift before the freeze.

Both face the question this page is about: what does a product manager contribute to a design decision, and by what mechanism, such that the contribution neither dictates pixels nor abdicates? The answer argued here is narrower than the usual advice about tone. Critique is a detection instrument with a measurable yield and cost, and the product manager's distinctive input is consequence — the problem, the constraint, the price of being wrong.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A design critique is a time-boxed, non-binding examination of an unfinished artefact against a stated goal, whose output is information for the person holding the pen. A design review is a binding decision taken by a named owner at a known time. The two are routinely held in one meeting, and that conflation causes several of the failures in section 9. Critique produces information; review spends it.

The history is older than software. It descends from the Beaux-Arts atelier and the Bauhaus preliminary course, where unfinished work was examined in public. Donald Schön's work on reflective practice in the early 1980s gave the studio crit its theory: the critic's job is to surface the frame the designer is working inside, not to substitute their own. Horst Rittel's wicked problems explain why such inspection cannot be specified away; Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich's heuristic evaluation of 1990 industrialised it, showing that trained reviewers find defects at a measurable rate. Ed Catmull's account of Pixar's Braintrust supplied the governance rule: candour mandatory, authority absent, the director decides.

What the practice solves is economic. Design decisions are taken under evidence scarcity, and the cost of finding a defect rises at every stage of commitment, about fifty times in all between concept and full release. Critique is the cheapest detector because it is pointed at something unfinished. Four schools disagree about what follows.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice has a shape whose steps mostly go unmentioned. First, the session is named against a decision: what is decided, by whom, when. Second, the locked constraints are declared — Dinchari's streak screen cannot add a server round-trip and cannot change the legal-reviewed paid-tier copy. Third, the author frames: what she is confident about, what she is unsure about, what she wants answered. Fourth, written before spoken, which removes the anchoring of whoever outranks the room. Fifth, the sentence form, every item expressible as problem — evidence — consequence; an item that cannot be is logged as a preference, permitted but budgeted.

The quantitative treatment, borrowed from inspection methods, tells a product manager how many reviewers to invite and when to stop. If each reviewer independently detects a given problem with probability λ, the share of the problem population found by n independent reviewers is 1 − (1 − λ)n. Damru's inspection gives a measured λ: five inspectors found 14, 12, 11, 9 and 7 problems — 53 findings, a mean of 10.6 each — against a union of 41 distinct problems.

Taking λ as 10.6 ÷ 41 = 0.259, five inspectors should have found 77.7 per cent of the population, implying 41 ÷ 0.777, or about 53 problems. Here is the trap: λ was measured against the found set, not the population. Re-deriving it against 53 gives 10.6 ÷ 53 = 0.20, at which five inspectors find only 67.2 per cent and the implied population rises to about 61. The estimate climbs with each iteration — and a capture-recapture bound on the same table, 41 + 29² ÷ (2 × 12), lands nearer 76 — so Tamuli uses the curve for marginal returns only, and treats those as a floor.

Two second-order effects are routinely missed. Raising detection raises the queue: a session that finds more problems hands the author more carried work, so a team that measures critique by items raised will drown. And the model assumes reviewers sharing a λ, which Damru's spread — 14 findings against 7 — refutes. A reviewer duplicating an existing lens buys almost nothing, so composition matters more than size.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as testable claims. Claim one: critique pays when the cost of discovery rises steeply with commitment. It holds overwhelmingly for Damru, where a defect found in Figma costs five hours and the same defect found after a 41-depot release costs about 248 on Damru's model (section 8); it holds weakly for a copy string Dinchari can change by remote config. Claim two: critique pays when the question cannot be measured inside a useful window. Dinchari sees 42,000 new users a week on the screen, 21,000 per arm. Detecting a 1.5-point absolute lift on a 61.0 per cent baseline at 80 per cent power and 5 per cent significance needs about 16 × 0.61 × 0.39 ÷ 0.015², or 16,917 per arm — six days. The 0.4-point difference Tahbildar expects needs 237,900 per arm, or 11.3 weeks. Claim three: critique pays when a reviewer holds information the author cannot get — the paid-tier entry rate, the support cost of a confusing state, the promise made to a customer. Where no such information is held, the items are preferences and should be labelled so.

Critique actively misleads in three situations. When a stochastic system is shown as a static screenshot, the room critiques a sample of one. When reviewers do not resemble the users — nine Bengaluru designers judging a Hindi-first first-run flow for a first-time smartphone owner — critique converges on confident, wrong answers, and faster as the room gets more senior. And on small-effect questions of preference it manufactures certainty; the right output there is a logged disagreement and a named decider.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

In multi-product companies critique quietly becomes governance. Where three products share a design system, "use the standard bottom sheet" is not feedback about a screen but a request to spend the system's budget, and the tell is that nobody present can settle it. In two-sided and marketplace products the supply side is under-critiqued: the consumer app gets most of the design team, the partner console one person. Damru seated a depot supervisor for that reason, and he found nine problems, three of which nobody else saw.

In regulated products the wording is often not the team's to change, so critique moves to placement, sequence and comprehension: not whether the disclosure is clear, but whether a user who has read it can still complete the task safely, and the written log doubles as an audit artefact. In hardware-plus-software the asymmetry is brutal — Damru's handheld trigger position locks at the 30 October freeze while the screen above it can change monthly — so critique is ordered by reversibility. In AI-native features the artefact is a distribution, not a screen: Dinchari sampled 40 generated summaries, and 7 of the 40 (17.5 per cent) carried a figure that did not match the user's ledger, which turned the critique into "what does the screen do in the 7".

At the seams, what mature companies do differs from what they say. They say critique is open and non-binding; in practice they protect it with two devices rarely written down — an invitation list held by the design lead, and a convention that the most senior person speaks last. Dinchari's session has a standing list of six plus a contract designer who joins from Berlin at 6:00 pm IST, 2:30 pm there while central Europe is on summer time and 1:30 pm after 25 October. Opening the room to all comers produces not candour but section 8's third example.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Directive feedback is lossy, not rude. The standard objection to "make the button blue" is that it disrespects the designer; the expert objection is informational — it discards the problem that generated it, so the designer cannot answer a problem she was never told. The tell is compliance followed by recurrence two sessions later.

The product manager's contribution is consequence. In a healthy log the PM's items are the ones carrying numbers: a support volume, a revenue dependency, a commitment date. A PM whose items look like a designer's supplies a second opinion on form while withholding the only input nobody else had.

A critique with a decision in it stops being a critique. The mechanism is behavioural: once the room can mandate, authors bring finished work, because unfinished work is dangerous. The tell is maturity — if the earliest version anyone outside the designer sees is already clickable, critique has been lost.

Unanimity is a warning sign. Five reviewers naming the same three problems means salience is driving detection rather than coverage; Damru's healthy session had only 12 of 41 problems seen twice. The obvious reading inverts the statistics: agreement measures redundancy of lenses, not severity.

"Make it consistent" has a price. Consistency with the system is a real good and also a cost, and the expert asks what the inconsistent option would save. Damru's non-standard confirm screen would have cost 6 hours; the compliant rebuild cost 34. A critique that never prices consistency always chooses it, and is sometimes wrong.

You cannot critique a screen whose job you cannot state. When a session spends twenty minutes reconstructing the goal, the brief failed and the items will contradict each other. The tell is two reviewers disagreeing about what success means rather than about the design.

The best output is a question, not an instruction. "Would a first-time user know the streak can be edited later?" survives contact with alternatives; "add a tooltip" does not. Converting an opinion back into its question exposes where there was no question, only taste.

Silence from engineering is a schedule risk. Engineers who say nothing are not endorsing the design; they are waiting for the spec. The diagnostic is to ask for the cheapest version of what is on screen, before the review.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products volume makes some questions measurable, so critique narrows to what instruments cannot see: embarrassment, trust, the first ninety seconds. In B2B and enterprise the buyer is not the user, so a critique without someone who has watched the user work is a room of proxies; Damru seats a customer's supervisor, at some cost in candour. In platform products the surface is documentation, console and error text. In marketplaces the asymmetry above dominates; in hardware the freeze date reorders everything; in AI products critique shifts to the failure distribution.

By stage: at seed, critique is two people and a whiteboard and the characteristic failure is formalising it. At Dinchari's stage — nine designers, six product managers — the ritual starts paying. At scale the risk inverts: critique ossifies into compliance review against a system, and the question becomes who may deviate. What does not change is the sentence form, which works identically on a consumer onboarding screen and a firmware error state.

8. Three worked examples

Dinchari's streak screen, August to September. Six sessions on one flow. The ledger below measures the shape of the feedback rather than its volume.

Of the 142 items, only 9 (6.3 per cent) framed a question an experiment could settle inside four weeks. Four weeks at 21,000 per arm per week is 84,000 per arm, which resolves absolute effects of about 0.67 points or larger; everything smaller was judgement in a data costume.

Damru, and whether to add a sixth inspector. From the curve, moving from five inspectors to six raises coverage from 77.7 to 83.4 per cent, a gain of 5.7 points, which against a population of 53 is about 3 new problems; under the conservative λ of 0.20 the gain is 6.6 points against 61, or about 4. A sixth inspector costs Damru roughly 6 hours including consolidation. A problem caught at critique costs 5 hours and the same problem caught after build costs 43, so the sixth inspector pays if there is even a 16 per cent chance that one of those problems would otherwise have survived to the built stage — the break-even for a single problem, nearer 4 to 5 per cent if three or four arrive.

Where it failed: Dinchari's open critique, April to June 2026. Wanting more candour, Talukdar opened the session to anyone and gave it decision power; attendance reached fourteen. One session on 12 May logged 41 items; 7 of the 9 sessions that quarter ended with a change mandated in the room, and the streak screen was redesigned three times in nine weeks. Completion moved from 63.4 per cent to 61.0 per cent — a before-and-after on a screen whose copy also changed twice, so Dinchari treats the 2.4-point fall as a signal, not an estimate. The deeper damage was not measurable: Tahbildar stopped bringing sketches and brought finished prototypes. The recovery, from July, split the forum — critique non-binding on Tuesday, a named decider on Thursday — required items in writing, and kept the ledger. The directive share fell from 64.5 per cent to 16.7 per cent.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

Critique theatre. Feedback is collected and nothing decided. Warning: the carried-forward column rises instead of falling — Dinchari's stood at 24 after the first session and at 4 by the last. Diagnostic: which decision does today's session feed, and who takes it? Caught late, the ritual loses credibility.

Pixel dictation. Warning: solution-framed share above roughly 60 per cent, as on 4 August. Diagnostic: what problem would that change solve, and how would we know it had? Caught late, designers stop generating alternatives, which process cannot buy back.

Abdication. The product manager contributes nothing until the engineering estimate lands. Warning: no item in the log carries a number. Diagnostic: what did the PM know that nobody else in the room did? Caught late, it costs the 34 engineering hours above, repeatedly.

Seniority anchoring. Warning: the most senior person speaks first and later items cluster on their framing. Diagnostic: compare the written notes with the discussion — if only the spoken items survive, the room is not reading its own evidence.

Over-inspection. Warning: the marginal inspector contributes fewer than two new problems, which the two models of section 3 put past the eighth reviewer and past the tenth. Diagnostic: track new problems per added reviewer, not problems per reviewer. The cost is queue noise crowding out severe items.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The candour-without-authority position holds that any decision right inside a critique destroys it, resting on evidence from direction-led creative organisations and the information-loss argument above. It is wrong where no review forum exists, in which case non-binding critique produces an unbounded queue and the loudest stakeholder wins anyway, later and less visibly.

The accountable-taste position holds that coherence comes from one person with judgement who also carries the metric, and that aggregating preferences produces mush; its evidence is the observable coherence of taste-led products. It is wrong when the owner's taste is uncorrelated with the population served — enterprise operators, non-metro users, assistive-technology users — because no loop runs from taste to outcome.

The evidence-first position holds that argument about anything measurable is waste. It is correct and underused at Dinchari's traffic, and fails on arithmetic rather than principle: 11.3 weeks for a 0.4-point effect, and no randomisation across Damru's 41 depots. For it to be generally right, effect sizes would have to be larger, or experiments far cheaper.

The inspection position holds that codified heuristics make critique nearly objective, resting on three decades of measurable discovery rates. It is wrong in two ways shown above: λ varies twofold across inspectors, and heuristics rank problems by type rather than cost, so an inspection-led process fixes a cheap defect and misses an expensive one.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves visibly differently in one session. They arrive with the decision and its date written down. They say what is locked before anyone draws. Their items carry numbers and little else, and a preference they catch themselves holding is named as one and allowed to lose. They ask for the cheapest version before the best one. Most tellingly, they lose arguments in public, which buys the right to be believed on the item they do not yield.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On 13 October Talukdar shipped Tahbildar's three-field version. Her reasoning was not deference: her item carried no number nobody else had, and the difference under argument sat near 0.4 points, which her own traffic would take 11.3 weeks of a single test to resolve. She converted it into the question that generated it — would a first-time user know the streak can be edited later? — and into an instrumented event. Tamuli, on 9 October, added a sixth inspector for 6 hours, refused to let inspection stand in for the night-shift observation he cannot schedule, and reordered the 41 problems by reversibility: the four touching the handheld's physical controls move ahead of the 30 October freeze, the rest after it. Neither decision has an outcome yet.

Discussion questions. First: Talukdar's ledger improved on every measure it tracks between the first session and the last, while completion did not recover to 63.4 per cent — on what grounds should she keep the ritual? Second: Tamuli's sixth inspector is justified by a curve whose parameter he has shown to be unstable; what would you measure to defend that decision? Third: if a product manager's only legitimate contribution is consequence, what should one do on believing a design is bad while able to attach no number to it?

13. Going deeper

  • UX fundamentals for PMs — the principles an item must cite.
  • Product critique — the same discipline above screen level.
  • Design–research–PM handoffs — fixes who owns an item between sessions.
  • Translating research into design decisions — makes the evidence half usable.
  • Usability heuristics — the vocabulary behind inspection, and section 3's λ.
  • Information architecture and navigation — most recurring items are structural.
  • User flows and task analysis — lets critique argue about the path, not the screenshot.
  • Usability testing — the instrument critique cannot replace.
  • Design systems and components — prices "make it consistent".
  • Content design and microcopy — the cheapest high-yield critique surface.
case40v1-ux.onboarding:
Indian School of Business · Case study

Imkaan Systems: Eleven Screens to the First Bill

Four ways to raise activation, two exhibits that disagree about which channel works, and 1.1 points nobody can explain. The board meets on Monday.

1. Pune, Sunday night

At twenty to ten on the night of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Ravneet Bhambri sat at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, a board deck open on one laptop and a dashboard on the other. The lights were still up opposite; Diwali had fallen the previous Sunday. The board of Imkaan Systems Private Limited met at half past nine the next morning in Bengaluru, and Bhambri, its senior director of product, owned the slide titled Activation.

The number on it was 18.8 per cent: the share of merchants who opened a self-serve account on Imkaan Shop in October and went on to take a customer payment through it. In September it had been 23.4 per cent. Beneath it sat the 61.2 per cent recorded by merchants onboarded in person by Rashpal Bhasin's field agents, in September and October alike.

Ronita Basnotra's note had landed the previous evening from Toronto and had made Bhasin's composition argument harder to hold, though not impossible. It had also left Bhambri something harder to put on a slide: of the 4.6 points lost, 3.5 were explained and 1.1 were not. Her phone held a voice note from a hardware merchant in Ludhiana, now played four times.

2. The company: a wizard and a parity clause

Imkaan Systems was founded in Pune in March 2019 by Rohanpreet Bedi and two colleagues from a payments gateway, as a credit-ledger app for small retailers. Imkaan Shop, the billing product, followed in 2020: an Android app that printed a GST-compliant invoice, tracked stock and collected over UPI.

The decision that shapes today was taken in August 2021. Imkaan had won its first distribution deal, with a Nagpur staples distributor whose retailers needed invoices carrying HSN codes from the first bill. Rather than keep two paths, the team built Setup 2.0: one mandatory sequence of ten screens, implemented as a server-driven step graph the engineers call SetupGraph, in which a catalogue had to exist before a bill could be raised. In March 2023 that sequence was written into a contract. Ittehaad Wholesale Markets LLC of Dubai signed for 9,200 outlets at ₹14.6 crore a year, and Clause 7.4 requires the setup sequence to be identical and auditable across all tenants, with ₹18 lakh of service credits for every month the go-live slips.

A Series C of ₹520 crore followed in January 2025. By October 2026 Imkaan had onboarded 11.4 lakh merchants, of whom 3,20,000 paid an average ₹240 a month — ₹7.68 crore of monthly recurring revenue, against FY26 revenue of ₹76 crore. On 1 October 2026 the wizard became eleven screens. Figure 1 sets out those decisions.

Figure 1. Imkaan Systems: decisions that constrain the November 2026 choice.

Scale: linear in calendar months, 1 January 2019 at the left tick and one year spanning 90 pixels; a marker's date is (x − 70) ÷ 7.5 months after January 2019.

3. The industry: billing is free, trust is not

Nothing Imkaan sells is scarce. Khatabook, Vyapar and myBillBook offer free or near-free billing tiers; Tally and Marg ERP hold the accountant's end; PhonePe, Paytm and BharatPe bundle billing behind a counter soundbox; Razorpay and Pine Labs come from payments. UPI, built by NPCI, carries the transaction at zero merchant discount rate, so nobody earns on the payment. Revenue comes from subscription, and subscription from habit.

Three forces press on the merchant. GST e-invoicing obligations have ratcheted down the turnover scale, so billing software is now a compliance instrument as much as a convenience. The DPDP Act of 2023 obliges Imkaan to record consent for the customer data a merchant uploads. And quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — has taken the fastest-moving lines out of the kirana basket, making retailers readier to try software and less willing to pay.

Roughly 46 per cent of Imkaan's self-serve installs are on Android devices with less than 3 GB of memory, where the catalogue importer is slow enough to be abandoned. And Ittehaad's outlets must satisfy the Emirates' phased e-invoicing programme, one reason Clause 7.4 was drafted so tightly.

4. What happened, and what it was taken to mean

Before October the funnel was stable: the July cohort activated at 23.4 per cent, 5,112 merchants of 21,850 accounts, and September repeated it (Exhibit 1).

On Thursday, 1 October 2026, Imkaan inserted a screen. Counsel had advised that Imkaan should know a merchant's turnover band and registration type before issuing the first invoice template. Bhambri approved it in a twenty-minute call, as a thirty-second question, and it shipped without a holdback group: every account from 1 October saw eleven screens.

By the third week of October the dashboard showed two things, both on cohorts whose fourteen-day windows had not closed. The new screen was completed by 85.0 per cent of merchants who reached it; and the first-bill rate — the share who, having seeded a catalogue, went on to raise a bill — was running near 71 per cent against September's 75.0. In the review of Tuesday, 20 October, Bhasin put the decline down to the festive cohort: more pharmacies, more tyre-kickers, a denominator whose composition had changed.

Basnotra's full-cohort analysis reached the team on Saturday, 14 November, on Exhibit 1's extract. The trade mix of the two cohorts was identical to one decimal (Exhibit 4) — but at account creation, three steps above the stage the first-bill rate is measured on, and nobody has split the catalogue-seeded stage itself by trade. Applying September's four step rates to October's cohort with the new screen's 85.0 per cent inserted gives 23.4 × 0.850 = 19.9 per cent, against an actual 18.8. Taking the screen first, it accounts for 3.5 of the 4.6 points lost and the remaining 1.1 is the first-bill rate falling from 75.0 to 71.0 — a move far outside sampling error, the standard error of the difference over 12,480 and 10,750 accounts being 0.6 points — for which no mechanism has been proposed.

Two other beliefs have weakened. On Friday, 6 November, the same counsel said orally that the test could equally be run at the first invoice rather than at signup; a written opinion has been asked for and has not arrived. And the 2021 premise that a merchant needs a catalogue before billing is contradicted by Imkaan's instrumentation: 99,200 of the 3,20,000 paying merchants, 31.0 per cent, raise over four-fifths of their bills against a free-text line.

5. The people

Ravneet Bhambri, senior director of product, Pune. Holds that a merchant must be able to bill on day one and that compliance belongs after value. Activation is her headline objective. She has not told the board that she approved the October screen in a twenty-minute call, with no holdback.

Rohanpreet Bedi, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Wants Dubai live on 11 January, because the Ittehaad reference anchors a Series D conversation planned for 2027. He has not said the lead investor's interest is conditioned on it.

Rashpal Bhasin, president of field distribution, Ludhiana. Argues that Tier-2 and Tier-3 merchants will never self-onboard: agents, not screens. His headcount is the plan's largest discretionary line, and he has not circulated the field audit of his agents operating the merchant's phone.

Rimple Bhullar, director of engineering, platform, Bengaluru. Estimates ten to fourteen weeks to make SetupGraph's step order configurable per tenant, and will not commit to less. Her squad of nine also owes Ittehaad its tenant work, and she has not read the ordering module since 2023.

Ronita Basnotra, staff data scientist, Toronto. Holds that the 1.1 unexplained points must be understood first, since any option will be credited or blamed for them. Rebuilding credibility after a forecast miss, she does not foreground Exhibit 4's referrer model.

Rajbir Batra, head of customer success, Singapore. Wants the flow shortened on cost: 38 per cent of October's tickets carried the setup tag, and cost per merchant is his metric. He has not mentioned that the tag was redefined in August.

Ravdeep Bhogal, principal product designer, Berlin. Argues for progressive disclosure: one screen to the first bill, catalogue by photograph, compliance deferred to day seven. He wants his five-month prototype shipped, and does not volunteer that six merchants have seen it, all in Pune, on one handset.

Rehmat Bakshi, head of international sales, New Jersey. Says Clause 7.4 is renegotiable because Ittehaad's operations team is itself unhappy with eleven screens. His commission rides on the Dubai renewal, and he has already told their chief operating officer that a shorter flow is coming in January.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Look who walked in during the festive weeks. Chemists, and people who downloaded on an offer. Seventy-five down to seventy-one is the mix, not the product.”
