“The mix did not change: kirana 44.0 and 44.0, pharmacy 12.5 and 12.5, on 24,000 and 24,320 accounts. That is at account creation; nobody has split the catalogue-seeded stage by trade, so I cannot rule the mix out there. But 23.4 times 0.850 is 19.9; we came in at 18.8. The screen cost 3.5 points. Something else cost 1.1, and I cannot say what.”

Ronita Basnotra, #activation, Saturday 14 November, 7.35 p.m. IST (9.05 a.m. Toronto).

“Eleven screens before a man can take ₹40 for a packet of screws. Let him bill. Ask his turnover band on day seven, when he has a reason to answer.”

Ravdeep Bhogal, product chat, Tuesday 10 November, 2.05 p.m. IST (9.35 a.m. Berlin).

“The order is not a flag, Ravdeep. The invoice template is built from the catalogue, and the declaration now decides which template. Ten to fourteen weeks if you want it per tenant.”

Rimple Bhullar, same thread, 2.19 p.m.

“There is a tenant flag. We used it for the Ittehaad pilot in August. Somebody should read the code before we buy a quarter of engineering.”

Ravdeep Bhogal, same thread, 2.26 p.m. No reply was posted.

“Their COO wants six screens, not eleven. Do not let a contract we can amend decide a product question — and do not let January slip, because that I cannot amend.”

Rehmat Bakshi, voice note to Bedi, 14 November, 9.50 p.m. IST (11.20 a.m. New Jersey).

“Context before Monday: we activated 7,848 merchants in October against a plan of 7,600. We beat the plan in the quarter that matters.”

Rohanpreet Bedi, email to the board list, Sunday 15 November, 8.05 a.m. IST.

Total activations fell 4.0 per cent, from September's 8,176 to October's 7,848. The blended activation rate went from 29.0 per cent (8,176 of 28,180 accounts) to 26.5 (7,848 of 29,660), each pooled across the channels' different windows. The October plan was 7,600; the agent count was 212 against September's 168.

8. The options as Bhambri sees them

A. Defer the declaration. Move the eleventh screen to day seven, triggered at the first invoice above the e-invoicing threshold. Four engineers, three weeks, ₹10.2 lakh at a loaded ₹3.4 lakh per engineer-month. Removing the 85.0 per cent screen and holding October's other four rates compounds to 0.22152, or 5,387 activations on October's cohort — 807 more than the 4,580 achieved. It puts the sequence out of parity with Ittehaad's, and the written opinion has not arrived.

B. Buy activation with agents. Hire 120 more field agents: five weeks from offer puts a first visit near 21 December, so 3.3 productive agent-months to the end of March. At October's 15.4 activations per agent-month that is 6,098 activations for ₹182.16 lakh, ₹2,987 each — spread over the window, not on one month's cohort — at a cost the plan assumes holds as the channel grows by more than half, in a channel whose July retention was 44.0 per cent against self-serve's 71.5.

C. Rebuild SetupGraph. Make step order configurable per tenant: nine engineers for twelve weeks, ₹91.8 lakh at the same rate, and the squad the Dubai go-live depends on. It alone leaves Clause 7.4 untouched while letting India and Dubai differ, and delivers nothing this quarter — unless Bhogal is right about the flag, in which case the question is an afternoon of code reading.

D. Fix the catalogue instead. Leave the sequence alone and attack the largest single loss, the 65.0 per cent catalogue step, with photograph-based import of a supplier invoice. Taking it to 80.0 per cent and holding everything else compounds to 0.23174, or 5,636 activations — 1,056 more than actual, against Option A's 807 on the same cohort. The 15-point improvement is an assumption, and 31.0 per cent of all paying merchants already raise most of their bills against a free-text line.

Bhambri's summary for the board carries the four options in that order and no recommendation. The slide after it is blank except for its heading, What we have not measured.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 9.30 a.m. on Monday, 16 November 2026. Ittehaad's user-acceptance freeze is 18 December and its go-live 11 January 2027, with ₹18 lakh a month in service credits beyond that; amending Clause 7.4 needs Ittehaad's own board, which next sits on 7 January. Imkaan held ₹196 crore of cash on 31 October against a net burn of ₹13.0 crore a month, about fifteen months, and Bedi will not approve both B and C. There is one platform squad of nine. Consent under the DPDP Act cannot be deferred, whatever happens to the turnover question. Agent hiring runs five weeks. And the festive season, roughly a third of the year's new merchants, closes this month.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 measure, over which denominators and windows? What would you add to it before acting on the 4.6-point fall?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 point in opposite directions about the agent channel. What would you measure, and over what period, to compare them like for like?
  3. Basnotra has explained 3.5 of the 4.6 points and not 1.1. What are the candidate mechanisms, and what evidence would separate them?
  4. Exhibit 5's participants came from agent referral lists, and two of fourteen were on low-memory handsets against 46 per cent of the base. How far does that limit its use as evidence about self-serve onboarding?
  5. What is the unit of analysis in each option, and what alternative unit would a different reading of Exhibits 1, 3 and 5 suggest?
  6. What should Bhambri do on Monday morning, and what exactly should she say to the board — what would she commit to, what would she refuse, and what would she tell them she does not know?

11.52 p.m.

She played the voice note once more. The merchant in Ludhiana was patient about it: he had downloaded the app on a Tuesday, been asked for his turnover band, called his accountant, been asked for a product code he had never heard of, and put the phone down. On the Friday he bought a competitor's soundbox from an agent who did it all for him. Bhambri typed a message to Bedi, read it, deleted it. Outside, the last lights came down.
exp40v2-ux.onboarding:
Onboarding and first-run design

How fast can a new user get to value, and what is actually in the way?

1. Two decisions, nine days apart

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Tuhin Dastidar, vice-president of product at Kutumb Finvest, a Bengaluru discount broker, had a funnel on one screen and a media plan on the other. The funnel covered every first-time app open from installs between Monday 1 June and Sunday 28 June 2026, each user followed fourteen days from their own first open, the last observation on 12 July. Of 61,200 first opens, 8,338 placed a first order. The media plan proposed ₹9.4 crore over the December quarter to buy four times the June install volume.

Dastidar's objection was the multiplier, not the spend. If the flow converted first opens into first orders at 13.6 per cent, four times the installs bought four times the same leakage — and the leak sat where Kutumb had least control: the regulated identity sequence of permanent account number, Aadhaar-based electronic know-your-customer through DigiLocker, e-signature and liveness check, closing with a depository confirmation from CDSL. His design lead's remedy — let a new user build a watchlist and set a price alert first, and move the gate to after that first value moment — had already run on a slice of July and August traffic, reported in section 8. Compliance had no objection to a general rollout. Growth did, because the test had visibly depressed the PAN-validation rate, the metric the company watched.

Nine days later, 1,500 kilometres north-west, Trina Debnath faced the same question in different clothes. Debnath is head of product at Keshar Retail Systems, an Ahmedabad company selling pharmacy chains a billing and reorder system — an Android app, a thermal label printer and a scanner, on a per-outlet monthly licence. Keshar had signed 148 outlets across eleven chains in the quarter to 30 June 2026. Measured thirty days after each outlet's own go-live date, the last on Wednesday 9 September, 71 were billing at the level Keshar called live: twenty invoices a day for five consecutive days. That is 48.0 per cent of outlets already paid for. A 240-outlet chain was due to roll out in the December quarter, and Keshar's eleven-person implementation team could not hand-hold 240 go-lives. Debnath had to decide whether a guided first invoice could replace the human at the counter.

The two decisions are one decision: in both, the instinct to remove steps collided with the instinct that some steps are why the product works at all.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define onboarding as the designed path from a user's first encounter with a product to their first instance of the value it exists to deliver, and first-run design as the part of that path walked before the user has any accumulated state or habit to lean on. The governing quantity is time to first value; the governing constraint is that willingness to invest effort falls with effort already spent without payoff.

Three traditions converged on it. John Carroll's minimal-manual work at IBM in the 1980s established that users do not read first and act second — they act, fail, and read only to repair the failure. The usability-heuristics tradition, Jakob Nielsen's ten heuristics of 1994 among them, contributed recognition over recall and the demand that a system reveal its state. And progressive disclosure, now cited loosely, originally meant something narrow: show the options serving the common case and defer the rest behind a deliberate act, so the novice sees a simpler system at no cost to the expert.

Three schools now disagree substantively, not terminologically. The frictionless school holds that every step before first value is a tax: it will sign the proposition that any field not required for the first unit of value should be collected later, and not the proposition that effort can itself be productive. The commitment school, from enterprise implementation practice, holds that certain effort is load-bearing — a user who imports data or invites a colleague has built something to come back for. It will sign the claim that setup effort predicts retention, and not the claim that the effort merely selects users who would have retained anyway. The situated school, strongest among those who have shipped to field users, holds that both argue about the wrong object: the constraint is rarely the interface but the user's circumstances — a shared handset, a weak cell at the back of the shop, a document not in the room. It will sign neither side's claim that step count is the main lever.

3. Mechanics: the funnel, and what its denominators are

Expert practice defines the cohort before the metric, because almost every onboarding argument that goes wrong goes wrong on a denominator. The funnel below is one cohort: all 61,200 first-time app opens from installs between 1 and 28 June 2026, each followed fourteen days from that user's own first open. Every rate shown is pooled — one numerator over one denominator for the whole cohort — not a mean of weekly or per-source rates, which is a different and usually larger number.

Read the geometry, not the shape. The depository confirmation holds 96.0 per cent and the e-sign pair 85.0 per cent; four steps lose heavily — mobile verification at 77.0 per cent, PAN at 75.0 per cent of the 47,124 who verified a mobile number, the eKYC handoff at 70.0 per cent of the 35,343 who validated a PAN, and funding at 59.0 per cent of the 20,188 accounts opened. In absolute users the ranking differs: 14,076 lost at mobile verification, 11,781 at PAN, 10,603 at eKYC, 8,276 at funding, the seven losses summing to 52,862, which is 61,200 less 8,338. Experts argue from the absolute column, because that is what a fix recovers.

Then the discipline the funnel enforces. Kutumb's August board deck described the identity flow as converting "about 40 per cent of installs". It does not. The same window recorded 78,400 installs, of which 61,200 produced a first open — 78.1 per cent. Against installs, eKYC completion is 24,740 of 78,400, or 31.6 per cent, and activation 8,338 of 78,400, or 10.6 per cent. The 40.4 per cent figure is a share of first opens, and the base moves implied cost per activated user by a quarter.

The second discipline is pooling. Tapati Duarah, Kutumb's product analyst, split the eKYC step by acquisition source.

Aadhaar eKYC completion by acquisition source, among the 35,343 users of the June 2026 cohort who validated a PAN. Rows are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

The final row is pooled: 24,740 divided by 35,343. The unweighted mean of the three source rates is 70.7 per cent. The gap is small here only because the largest source is among the worst; average a small excellent channel with a large poor one and the two can differ by several points. A deck quoting one while a model uses the other is the commonest quiet error in this material.

The formal treatment is under-applied. Write activation as the product of step rates, a = ∏ si. Because they multiply, the marginal value of a point at step i scales with a / si. Five points at funding gives 20,188 × 0.05 = 1,009 more funded accounts, of which 70.0 per cent order: 706 more activated users. Five points at e-sign gives 24,740 × 0.05 = 1,237 more e-signs, but each must survive 96.0, 59.0 and 70.0 per cent — 39.6 per cent survival — yielding 490. The same five points are worth 706 activated users at one step and 490 at the other, a gap of 44 per cent.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as testable claims. One: a first unit of value exists that is deliverable without the deferred step. True at Kutumb — a watchlist and a price alert are useful to someone with no account — false at Keshar, because a billing system not given an outlet's opening stock cannot print a correct invoice. Two: deferral does not transfer the cost to someone else. Here the signs reverse: Kutumb's deferred gate stays inside the app, while Keshar's deferred stock-loading lands on a pharmacist at a counter with customers waiting. Three: the retained population is not selected by the effort itself. Almost nobody tests this, the hinge of section 10.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. Where value is irreducibly delayed — a credit decision underwritten overnight — minimising steps optimises a quantity the user never experiences, and the real work is designing the wait. Where the user is not the buyer, as in most of Keshar's accounts, the person whose effort you minimise is not the one who decides renewal. And where the blocker is external: 1,557 of the 4,717 preload-partner users who validated a PAN never finished eKYC, 33.0 per cent, most attributed by Duarah to an Aadhaar-linked mobile number no longer matching the handset in the user's hand.

5. Hard edge cases

In a multi-product company the first run belongs to the account, and the second product inherits the first one's onboarding. Kutumb's mutual-fund tab ships only to users who have cleared eKYC, so its first-run metrics look superb and compare with nothing; the honest treatment reports two funnels with separate counts.

In two-sided products first run must survive an empty other side, and the defensible move is real but unmatched inventory rather than fabricated activity. In regulated products steps cannot be deferred, only re-ordered. In hardware-plus-software, first run spans a courier, a power socket, a pairing and a label roll: Keshar's software funnel begins at a point 22 of its 148 outlets had not reached within seven days. Cohort shape matters too — the 71 activated outlets fall in nine of the eleven chains, the two with none being the smallest at four and six outlets, so on the 138 outlets in those nine the rate is 51.4 per cent, not 48.0.

In AI-native products first run carries an extra job, calibration: a user whose first prompt fails concludes the product cannot do the thing. At the organisational seams, onboarding is owned by whoever holds the metric. Mature companies describe a cross-functional squad; what they have is growth owning the funnel's top, a core team owning everything past activation, and nobody owning the handoff.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

Activation is a definition, not a measurement. The tell-tale sign is a rate that improved in the quarter its definition was revised. Keshar's bar is defensible, and was chosen while the board was watching the number it produced. An expert puts the definition and its last revision date on the same slide as the rate.

Step rates and absolute losses rank differently. The obvious reading is to fix the worst-converting step; the expert multiplies the gap by the traffic reaching it. Kutumb's funding step converts worst at 59.0 per cent but loses 8,276 users, while mobile verification converts at 77.0 per cent and loses 14,076, so a modest fix upstream outweighs a heroic one downstream.

Deferring a step changes who reaches it. The tell-tale sign is a step rate that rises on a shrunken denominator, as Kutumb's eKYC rate does in section 8, while an earlier rate falls because a step was inserted in front of it. Two mechanisms, routinely reported as one, and the most common way a good onboarding change is killed by its own dashboard.

Effort that produces an artefact differs from effort that produces nothing. Importing contacts or loading opening stock leaves the user owning something; a six-field form leaves nothing. Experts ask whether the user ends the step holding an object, and keep artefact-producing steps even when they convert badly.

The first run has a memory the designer does not share. Most teams test on a fresh install and good connectivity. The tell-tale sign is abandonment concentrated in sessions that are not the user's first — someone who stopped at eKYC on Tuesday, returned Thursday, and found the flow restarted from the top.

Progressive disclosure is about the common case, not about hiding. The obvious reading, that fewer visible options is always better, makes the expert path undiscoverable. The original claim was narrower: default to what most users need, keeping the rest reachable by a deliberate act. The tell-tale sign of the misreading is a support queue in which experienced users ask where a feature went.

Time to first value is a distribution, not an average. Among the 8,338 June-cohort users who ordered inside fourteen days, the median time from first open to first order was 4.2 days and the mean 6.9, dragged out by a tail that funded only after a salary credit. A flow tuned to the median is tuned for the user who least needs help; the mean moves when you fix the tail.

Support tickets per activated user is an onboarding metric. A flow that raises activation and raises tickets per hundred activated users has moved cost, not removed it. The tell-tale sign is support asking for headcount one release after a growth win; “success brings volume” hides a rise in the rate per user.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products first run is a solo act under time pressure and step count matters. In B2B and enterprise it is a project with named humans and the unit is the account: Keshar's eleven chains each have a head office that must agree before any outlet moves, so a flow that delights the counter operator while leaving head office uninformed stalls. On platforms and marketplaces the two sides need separate first runs with separate value definitions; conflating them yields an activation metric nobody can act on. In hardware first run starts before the software and is measured in days, because a courier is in the loop. For AI products it must teach capability boundaries — the one place where adding a step, a worked example the user edits, beats removing one.

By stage what changes is who absorbs the failure. At seed stage a founder onboards each account, so defects stay invisible; at growth stage the patching capacity runs out and they surface at once, which is what Keshar faced; at scale first run is load-bearing for revenue, so teams ship around it rather than through it.

8. Three worked examples

Kutumb: the step rate falls and the outcome rises

Kutumb ran the two orderings above on first opens between Monday 13 July and Sunday 9 August 2026, 30,000 per arm, followed fourteen days, last observation 23 August. Mobile verification was identical in both arms at 77.0 per cent, or 23,100 users. In the control, 17,325 of those 23,100 validated a PAN — 75.0 per cent — and 12,128 of the 17,325 finished eKYC, 70.0 per cent. In the treatment, 19,635 built a watchlist, 85.0 per cent of the same 23,100, and only 16,401 validated a PAN: 71.0 per cent, four points worse on the metric growth watched. But 12,793 of those 16,401 finished eKYC, 78.0 per cent, so completed eKYCs rose from 12,128 to 12,793, up 5.5 per cent. Apply the June cohort's downstream rates to both arms — 85.0, 96.0, 59.0 and 70.0 per cent, a 33.7 per cent yield — and first orders rise from 4,087 to 4,311, or 13.6 to 14.4 per cent of first opens, a relative gain of 5.5 per cent. Note what moved and what did not. The PAN rate fell because 3,465 of the 23,100, 15.0 per cent, dropped at the inserted watchlist step and never reached PAN; both PAN rates sit over that same 23,100, so no composition effect can explain it. The eKYC rate rose because its denominator shrank from 17,325 to 16,401, a more selected group.

Keshar: moving work off the counter

Keshar pre-loaded opening stock from the chain's own goods-receipt invoices of the preceding ninety days instead of asking a pharmacist to count shelves. It applied to 62 outlets signed in July 2026, live between Monday 20 July and Monday 31 August, measured at day thirty, last observation 30 September. Of the 62, 55 had hardware delivered and the printer paired inside seven days — 88.7 per cent, against 85.1 for the 148-outlet cohort. Of those 55, 49 loaded opening stock: 89.1 per cent against 82.5 on the same base earlier. Of those 49, 36 cleared the twenty-invoice bar, 73.5 per cent against 68.3; and 36 of 62 signed outlets reached it, 58.1 per cent against 48.0. Debnath's written caveat: the July cohort skews to two larger chains with in-house IT, so the comparison is like-for-like on measure, bar and window, not on account mix.

Kuhasa Labs: the activation win that was a loss

Kuhasa Labs, a Pune company whose assistant drafts commercial contracts, required users to connect a document repository before producing anything. On first opens between Monday 4 May and Sunday 31 May 2026, followed twenty-eight days to 28 June, the control's 14,000 first opens produced 4,774 activations — a first generated draft — 34.1 per cent. The treatment replaced that step with a demo workspace: 7,252 activations, 51.8 per cent.

Retention told the other story. Of the control's 4,774 activated users, 1,957 were still active on day twenty-eight — 41.0 per cent. Of the treatment's 7,252, only 1,639 were: 22.6 per cent. Normalised on the base both arms share, the control retained 139.8 per thousand first opens and the treatment 117.1, a fall of 22.7 per thousand, or 16.2 per cent. Support cost moved the same way: 296 onboarding tickets from the control's 4,774 activated users, 6.2 per hundred, against 827 from the treatment's 7,252, or 11.4, because a user whose first draft came from demo documents found the gap late. Titir Dalui, the product manager, put the step back in a better place — the demo workspace stayed, and the repository connection became a gate on the second draft. That arm ran later, on a separate non-concurrent cohort of first opens from Monday 6 July to Sunday 2 August, followed to 30 August, with no random assignment against the May arms. It activated 6,846 of 14,000 — 48.9 per cent — and retained 2,410 at day twenty-eight, 35.2 per cent: 172.1 per thousand first opens against the May control's 139.8.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Optimising a step without watching the outcome. Warning: step rates reported weekly, activation monthly. Ask: what is this rate's denominator, and did its composition change? Caught late, a team spends two quarters raising a number that never moves revenue.

Removing load-bearing effort. Warning: activation and day-28 retention moving in opposite directions, as at Kuhasa. Ask: does the user end this step owning something? Caught late, the cost is a whole cohort — the damage appears only after the retention window closes.

Treating an external blocker as an interface problem. Warning: transcripts naming a document, a mobile number or a network rather than a screen. Ask: of those failing here, what share could have succeeded with any interface? Kutumb's preload cohort is the case.

Confusing the user with the buyer. Warning: healthy per-seat activation, flat renewal. Ask: has anyone who signs the invoice seen the product work? Keshar's version was stark — head office users at only seven of its eleven chains, 63.6 per cent, had logged in by day thirty.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The live disagreement is whether setup effort causes retention or merely selects users who would have retained anyway. Steelmanned, the causal position runs: a user who has imported data and invited a colleague has switching costs and a reason to return. Its evidence is Kuhasa's recovery arm, where restoring the connection step was followed by 172.1 day-28 retained users per thousand against the demo arm's 117.1 — an equal-sized but later and non-concurrent cohort, which is what weakens it. Steelmanned, the selection position runs: the effort is a filter, and the recovery arm improved because the demo workspace taught the user what to connect, not because connecting did anything — so the right move is always a cheaper filter. For the causal position to be wrong you would need a design that holds the filter constant and removes the effort, and still sees retention hold. For the selection position to be wrong you would need the mirror image: random assignment to effort inside an already-filtered population. Neither experiment is common.

A second disagreement is sharper: whether time to first value should be the measure at all. The dissent holds that first value is trivially manufactured — Kuhasa's demo workspace is the proof — and that the honest metric is time to habitual value, measurable only retrospectively and so unable to steer a weekly release. Measuring both and shipping on neither alone is a truce, not a resolution.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a list of steps to remove. Someone who has internalised it asks what the first unit of value is, who the user is at that moment, and what the denominator of the rate on the slide actually is. They state the activation definition and its last revision date unprompted, separate step rates from absolute losses before proposing work, defend an expensive step that produces an artefact, and say when a rate is pooled. And they treat the resumed session and the empty state as design surface.

12. The decisions

On Friday 25 September 2026 Dastidar committed to the value-first ordering, with two conditions in the ticket: the PAN-validation rate would be retired as a headline metric in favour of completed eKYCs per thousand first opens, and the December media plan would be costed on the install base at the control flow's 10.6 per cent activation — deliberately conservative — rather than on first opens. Debnath's decision was narrower than her team wanted — pre-loaded opening stock for every new outlet, a guided first invoice for the counter operator, and no cut to implementation staffing until the 240-outlet rollout produced its own day-thirty numbers, because 62 outlets skewed to two IT-capable chains was not evidence about the rest.

1. What does Kutumb lose by no longer watching the PAN-validation rate, and what would have to go wrong for that to matter?

2. Kuhasa's recovery arm came out above its control, in a later cohort. What single further arm would settle section 10's argument?

3. Who should own Keshar's activation bar, and what would you change about it before the 240-outlet rollout?

13. Going deeper

User flows and task analysis — how to see a step you did not design. Activation and onboarding optimisation — the experimental machinery behind section 8. Device setup and provisioning — Keshar's first seven days. UX fundamentals for PMs — how to referee a design argument. Usability heuristics — the source of recognition over recall. Information architecture and navigation — what a user finds afterwards decides whether onboarding worked. Usability testing — the only way to see the resumed session. Design systems and components — why a consistent first run costs less. Content design and microcopy — where a deferred step is explained or resented.
exp20v2-ux.onboarding:
Onboarding and First-Run Design

Discovery & Design, UX & Design Collaboration. How fast can a new user get to value, and what is in the way?

1. A Monday review

On Monday 12 October 2026, Sudeshna Chowdhury, head of product at Joyjatra Wealth, put a single funnel on the screen of a Kolkata meeting room. Joyjatra sells a mobile app for systematic investment plans (SIPs): a standing instruction that moves a fixed sum, often as little as ₹500, from a bank account into a mutual fund every month. The September cohort had been generous. Between 1 and 30 September the company had paid for 100,000 installs at ₹180 each, a spend of ₹1.8 crore. Only 16,524 of those people had finished the one thing the company needed from them: a live SIP.

Subhadip Chakraborty, the engineering manager, had a ready answer. The steps were not optional. Regulation requires an investor's identity to be verified before an investment is accepted, and each step existed for a reason. Sayan Chaki, the design lead, disagreed with the framing rather than the facts. Nobody, he pointed out, had asked when a new user first saw any evidence that the app was worth the trouble.

The stakes were concrete. Joyjatra's finance team estimated that each activated user returned about ₹1,000 of first-year contribution, meaning revenue net of variable cost. At 16,524 users that was ₹165.24 lakh against ₹180 lakh of acquisition spend: a loss of ₹14.76 lakh on a single month of marketing, repeated every month the funnel stayed as it was. Chowdhury's task was to decide what to change, and how to know whether the change had worked.

2. The idea

Onboarding is everything that happens between a person's first contact with a product and the moment they receive its value for the first time. First-run design is the deliberate shaping of that stretch: which screens appear, in what order, asking for what. It exists because most products demand effort before they pay anything back, and effort kills most attempts.

Two older ideas sit underneath it. The first is time to value, the elapsed time from first open to the first useful outcome, a phrase now common across software. The second is progressive disclosure: show only what the next decision needs, and defer the rest until it is wanted. It traces to 1980s interface research, such as the "training wheels" study by Carroll and Carrithers (1984), which disabled advanced functions for novices; Jakob Nielsen popularised the name in the 1990s.

The sentence Chowdhury could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: ask for each thing only when the user can see why it is needed, and show the reward before the last of the paperwork.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics begin with a choice that practitioners often leave implicit: defining the value moment, the single event that proves the product has delivered. For Joyjatra it is a live SIP, not an account. Everything before that event is cost; everything after is the product. The team then lists every step on the path and classes each as required before value (a verified phone number), required but movable (identity checks could in principle follow a first look at the product, provided the law permits investing only after them) or not required at all (a long questionnaire about risk appetite and income that nothing downstream uses).

Each step is then measured as a conditional conversion rate: of the people who reached this step, the share who passed it. These rates multiply into the overall rate, which is why a funnel is a chain rather than a menu. Timing each stage by its median separates steps that lose people from steps that merely delay them.

Each user at step 5 has already survived four ordeals, which is why losing one there costs more than losing a stranger at step 1: the acquisition spend is the same, but the attention invested is greater.

4. A worked example

Joyjatra's team recorded, for each step, how many people entered, the conditional rate, and the median time those who passed spent on it. The overall rate is the product of the rates: 0.72 × 0.75 × 0.68 × 0.75 × 0.60 = 0.16524, or 16,524 of 100,000.

Table 1. Joyjatra funnel, 1–30 September 2026
StepEnteringConditional ratePassingMedian seconds
1 Phone and OTP100,00072%72,00045
2 PAN entry72,00075%54,00060
3 Aadhaar eKYC54,00068%36,720150
4 Bank link36,72075%27,540120
5 First SIP mandate27,54060%16,524150
Overall (pooled)100,00016.52%16,524525 (sum of step medians)

Rates are conditional on reaching the step; the denominator for each conditional rate is that step's Entering count; for the overall rate it is the 100,000 installs. PAN is the Permanent Account Number issued by the tax authority; eKYC is identity verification done electronically; the SIP mandate is an automatic monthly debit approved through UPI. The 525 seconds adds the medians, which is not the median of total time.

Now change one input. The team chose step 3 not because it loses the most people (step 1 does, with 28,000) but because it is the only step where pre-filling is technically available: details already given at PAN entry could be reused. Suppose that pre-filling lifts its rate from 68% to 78%, an illustrative gain rather than a forecast, while nothing else moves. The product becomes 0.72 × 0.75 × 0.78 × 0.75 × 0.60 = 0.18954. The same 100,000 installs, and the same ₹180 lakh, now yield 18,954 activated users.

Table 2. Second pass: step 3 improved from 68% to 78%
MeasureBaselineScenarioChange
Activated users16,52418,954+2,430
Overall conversion16.52%18.95%+2.43 points
Acquisition spend (₹ lakh)180.00180.000.00
Spend per activated user (₹)1,089950−139
First-year contribution at ₹1,000 each (₹ lakh)165.24189.54+24.30
Contribution minus spend (₹ lakh)−14.76+9.54+24.30

Spend per activated user is ₹180 lakh divided by activated users, rounded to the rupee. The ₹1,000 contribution is an assumption supplied by finance and applies to every activated user alike.

A ten-point gain on one step turned a ₹14.76 lakh monthly loss into a ₹9.54 lakh profit, because the whole chain scales together: a 14.7% relative gain at any one step (78 over 68) is a 14.7% gain in activated users. The arithmetic assumes the extra completers are as valuable as the existing ones, which is a claim about people.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Activation is a definition, not a measurement

Someone chose that a live SIP counts. Choose "PAN entered" and the funnel looks over three times as healthy (54,000 against 16,524) while nothing improves. A good definition is an event that predicts the user is still there months later; the test is to compare retention of those who did it against those who did not.

Required is not the same as early

Subhadip's objection conflated two things. A step can be mandatory yet movable. The legal question is what must precede an investment, not what must precede a look around. Sequencing is the designer's real lever, because it changes when effort is spent without removing anything.

Progressive disclosure defers; it does not hide

Deferred items must still arrive when needed and be findable before then. Hide a setting entirely and the user who needs it concludes the product lacks it.

Drop-off says where, never why

The funnel flags steps; it cannot say why. At step 3 it cannot say whether users distrust the request, lack their Aadhaar-linked phone, or hit a failed OTP. Session recordings, support tickets and five conversations with people who quit are the cheap way to find out.

Check the denominator

The overall rate above uses installs. Count only people who opened the app and step 1 improves while nothing real has. Compare cohorts only on a like-for-like base, and split by acquisition channel, because a cheap channel may bring users who never intended to invest.

Sums of medians are not medians of sums

The true median journey, which includes waiting for a bank to approve a mandate, will differ, and the long tail is where a few users spend days. Report percentiles for the journey itself.

Optimising completers can degrade the base

Easing a step admits people who would previously have left, and they may be less committed. Judge a change by activated users and by their retention afterwards, not by the step it touched.

6. How it differs by product and by stage

Table 3. Where the value moment sits
Product typeValue momentDistinctive difficulty
ConsumerFirst useful result, minutesZero patience; every extra field costs users
B2BTeam using it on real data, days or weeksBuyer, administrator and user differ; setup needs integration and permissions
MarketplaceFirst completed transactionTwo sides to onboard; supply must exist before demand arrives

In consumer products, as at Joyjatra, minutes matter and the design question is sequencing. In B2B the person who signs the contract is rarely the person who must change habits, so onboarding becomes a project with human help, checklists and an assigned owner; time to value is measured in weeks and the funnel is a handful of accounts rather than thousands of users. In a marketplace, a newcomer on the demand side finds an empty shelf if supply was onboarded badly, so the sides are onboarded in a deliberate order.

Stage matters too. An early company can run five interviews a week and fix the flow by hand; a large one needs instrumentation and holdout tests because no individual sees enough users. Large companies inherit legal reviews that make steps immovable, so their gains come from sequencing and pre-filling.

7. Common mistakes

Counting sign-ups as success. The symptom is a growing user count beside a flat revenue line. The misunderstanding is that arrival equals value. The cheapest diagnostic is to compare ninety-day retention of those who reached the value moment with those who did not.

Replacing design with a tour. The symptom is a five-tooltip walkthrough that nearly everyone taps through with no change downstream. The misunderstanding is that explaining friction removes it. Run the tour against a holdout group that does not see it.

Fixing the largest drop first. The symptom is repeated redesigns of whichever step looks worst on the funnel while the overall rate barely moves. The misunderstanding is that worst-looking means most recoverable: a loss there may be a legitimate filter. Interview ten people who quit there before drawing anything.

Averaging across channels. The symptom is an overall rate that rises after a campaign ends. The misunderstanding is that the funnel is one population. Split the same table by acquisition source.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of the Monday review begins with the definition of activation, written on one line and agreed by finance. The funnel arrives with its denominators and with timing for every step. The team has classified each step as required, movable or removable, and has listened to ten people who quit. The proposal changes the fewest things that test one idea: here, moving a no-commitment SIP simulator ahead of the identity checks. It names what would count as success and failure before launch, and who will read the result.

9. Closing

Chowdhury declined to rebuild the flow. She approved a seven-day, two-arm test starting Monday 19 October 2026: half of new installs see the current order, half the proposed one, assigned at random. The 18.95% from section 4 is not a forecast of the reorder; it serves as an illustrative minimum detectable effect, the smallest lift worth paying to detect. To detect a rise from 16.52% to 18.95% with 80% power at the 5% significance level, each arm needs roughly 3,900 installs. At about 3,300 installs a day, two arms would reach that in under three days, but she chose a full week to cover weekday and weekend behaviour, about 11,550 installs per arm. The primary measure is activated users per install, with ninety-day retention tracked afterwards as the guard against hollow wins.

Her reasoning was that the funnel is evidence of where users leave but not of why, and that a reordering was cheap to build, reversible, and aimed squarely at the question Sayan had raised. To go deeper, read next on activation and onboarding optimisation, which turns this funnel into a measurement system, and on device setup and provisioning, where onboarding must cross hardware.

1. If the identity checks must precede any investment, what is the strongest argument that a preview of value, shown before them, still belongs ahead of them?

2. Which of your own product's steps are required, which are only early, and what would you have to believe to move each one?
case20v1-ux.onboarding:
Haazir: Eleven Screens Before the First Attendance

A teaching case on onboarding and first-run design

1. Opening

On Friday 16 October 2026, Preeti Arora sat in Haazir's office in HSR Layout, Bengaluru, watching a screen recording of a salon owner in Ludhiana abandon the app. He had typed his shop's name, chosen Punjabi, photographed his PAN card twice because the first picture blurred, and been asked to link a bank account. At that step he put the phone down. The recording lasted four minutes forty seconds, and he had not marked one employee present, which was the only reason he had downloaded Haazir.

Arora, Haazir's head of product, had until Friday 23 October to commit the team to one of three plans. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, and the company expected 27,000 new businesses to sign up between 2 and 29 November. Whatever she chose would be the first thing they met.

2. Company background

Haazir Technologies was founded in Bengaluru in 2020 by two former hotel managers tired of paper muster rolls. The app lets a small employer, typically a salon, clinic, workshop or shop with eight to forty staff, mark daily attendance, record salary advances and, since 2023, pay salaries by UPI. The company has 74 employees and about 4.1 lakh registered businesses, concentrated in cities such as Ludhiana, Surat, Coimbatore and Indore. Most owners hold entry-level Android phones and read Hindi, Punjabi, Gujarati or Tamil.

Haazir earns when a business runs payroll through it: the partner bank charges a fee and Haazir keeps a share. Finance models an average contribution of ₹1,800 per business over the six months after its first salary payment, and a paid sign-up costs about ₹140. Competitors set expectations. Khatabook and OkCredit taught the same owners that a bookkeeping app can help within a minute; Zoho Payroll and RazorpayX Payroll serve larger firms with finance staff. Because payouts move money under RBI rules, the partner bank requires PAN and bank-account verification before any salary is released.

3. The situation

The onboarding flow was designed in 2023, when payouts launched, and it grew by accretion. A new owner crosses eleven screens before reaching the home page: OTP, language, business profile, staff estimate, PAN entry, PAN photograph, bank account, penny-drop confirmation, consent, plan choice and a tutorial carousel. Only then can she add employees and mark attendance.

Exhibit 1 follows the 18,000 August sign-ups in the control flow, beside a 1,800 pilot. The largest loss comes at verification: of 15,300 who completed their profile, 9,180 were verified, a drop of 6,120, or 34.0 per cent of all sign-ups. In the end 6,610 marked attendance, 36.7 per cent, and 2,644, or 14.7 per cent, paid a first salary.

Exhibit 1. August sign-ups: control flow and pilot flow
Milestone (within 30 days)Control% of sign-upsPilot% of sign-ups
Signed up18,000100.01,800100.0
Business profile completed15,30085.01,53085.0
PAN and bank verified9,18051.074441.3
Staff added8,26245.91,37776.5
First attendance marked6,61036.71,23968.8
First salary paid2,64414.737220.7

Source: Haazir product analytics. Pilot sign-ups were a random one in eleven of August's 19,800 and are excluded from control. Control verifies before adding staff; the pilot asks for verification only when an owner first tries to pay, so its rows are not in sequence.

Piyush Arneja's team ran that pilot through August. In the pilot, owners added staff and marked attendance first, and PAN and bank details were requested only at the first payout. Exhibit 1 shows 68.8 per cent marking attendance, against 36.7 per cent, and 20.7 per cent paying a salary against 14.7 per cent. The partner bank had agreed that attendance records need no verification.

The team sees the choice from different clocks. In Pune, engineering has a code freeze from Tuesday 3 November, so anything touching the flow must ship by Friday 30 October. Berlin is 3.5 hours behind Bengaluru until the clocks change on 25 October, and Toronto 9.5 (10.5 from 1 November), so Piyush overlaps Bengaluru's working day only in its evening; his questions usually arrive overnight and are answered the next afternoon.

None of this is new to Arora. In July the pricing team asked for a plan-comparison screen, and in August compliance asked for a second consent screen. Each request was reasonable alone, and nobody owned the sum. The pilot was the first time anyone had tested removing a step instead of adding one.

4. The people

Parminder Atwal, engineering manager in Pune, leads nine engineers. He can harden the pilot code in a week if told on 23 October, but fears that a change near the payout path could stall salaries in the festive week. He prefers anything smaller.

Paulina Aulakh, senior designer in Berlin, drew the pilot. She wants a complete first-run redesign, with Punjabi and Tamil copy and a sample shop that lets owners rehearse before entering real data. That needs six weeks and would land after Diwali. She argues that a half-measure leaves a poor flow looking finished, and that owners who read Punjabi or Tamil are the ones most punished by English-only verification screens.

Piyush Arneja, data scientist in Toronto, ran the pilot. He reads it as a signal rather than proof: 1,800 businesses, one month, two months before the festive season. He asks that any rollout keep a 10 per cent holdout on the old flow.

Their weekly call is Thursday 22 October at 5:30 pm IST, which is 2:00 pm in Berlin and 8:00 am in Toronto.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 above gives the funnel and the pilot. Exhibit 2 sets the calendar. The decision on 23 October leaves one working week, 26 to 30 October, before the freeze, so the choice is between what fits in five days and what does not. Monday 2 November is the only slack day, and it is also the first day of the forecast window. Paulina's six-week redesign, started on 26 October, would end in early December, after the window has closed. Exhibit 3, in the next section, prices the three options.

6. The options

Option A: re-sequence the flow. Roll the pilot flow to all new sign-ups on Friday 30 October, deferring PAN and bank checks until the first payout. It costs eight engineer-weeks at ₹60,000 (₹4.8 lakh) and two designer-weeks at ₹1.5 lakh (₹3.0 lakh), or ₹7.8 lakh. Applying the pilot's rate of 372 per 1,800 to 27,000 sign-ups gives 5,580 salary-paying businesses, 1,614 above baseline. It uses little of Paulina's design, leans on a one-month pilot, and changes the screens that precede every payout, which is where Parminder's worry lies.

Option B: rescue the stalled. Leave the flow alone and have the support team telephone every owner who completes a profile but stalls before verification, at ₹60 a call. Of the forecast 27,000, 9,180 (34 per cent) would stall between profile and verification, costing ₹5.5 lakh. If one in four is rescued, 2,295 reach verification, and by the control flow's later rates (90, 80 and 40 per cent) 661 pay a salary. It is quick and safe, and needs no release. But every owner who stalled has already had the bad experience, and the calls reach people only after they have decided the app is hard.

Option C: buy more sign-ups. Spend the same ₹7.8 lakh on advertising at ₹140 a sign-up, giving about 5,571 businesses, of whom the control rate yields 818 paying. It needs no engineering, and sends more owners into the same eleven screens. Haazir's marketing team could start it on Monday, and could also stop it if the funnel changed.

Exhibit 3. The three options compared for the November cohort
OptionCost (₹ lakh)Extra salary-paying businessesValue at ₹1,800 (₹ lakh)Value less cost (₹ lakh)
A. Re-sequence7.81,61429.121.3
B. Rescue calls5.566111.96.4
C. Buy sign-ups7.881814.76.9

Baseline: 27,000 sign-ups at the control rate, 2,644 per 18,000, gives 3,966 salary-paying businesses. The rescue rate of one in four in B is a management assumption; A uses the pilot's measured rate.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Where in Exhibit 1 do owners leave, and what is a recovered owner worth in rupees?
  2. Why might the pilot's lift differ for November's 27,000 sign-ups, and what would you check before relying on it?
  3. What does Option A give up compared with Paulina's redesign, and how should Parminder's freeze shape the choice?
  4. Which option would you approve on 23 October, and what would you ask Piyush to measure afterwards?

8. A note for the learner

The lens is time to value. A new owner has come to mark attendance, so every screen that is not attendance must justify itself. Progressive disclosure asks for what the next step needs and no more: the bank needs PAN before paying, not before recording who came to work. A well-reasoned answer locates the loss in the funnel, checks that the pilot was randomised, and compares the options on the same rupees.

One defensible path is Option A, shipped on 30 October to all new sign-ups, with weekly rates read against the August control so the lift is measured rather than assumed. A 10 per cent holdout, as Piyush asks, would cleanly isolate the effect but give up about ₹2.9 lakh of it (161 businesses), so the path takes the cheaper comparison. The pilot's 6.0-point gap in first-salary rate is about six times the 1.0-point standard error of the difference between the two arms. Even if the true lift were half the pilot's, 807 extra businesses would return ₹14.5 lakh, a net ₹6.7 lakh, close to Option C's ₹6.9 lakh, while a true lift as large as the pilot's would net ₹21.3 lakh. The downside is bounded and the upside is large. Paulina's Punjabi and Tamil copy and sample shop follow in January, and calls like Option B can serve owners stuck at the first payout.

Discovery & Design · UX & Design Collaboration

Vayam Credit Technologies: The Words in the Loan

An Indian lending-service provider rewrote 180 strings of its app — labels, errors, empty states, disclosures — and cannot agree what the rewrite did.

1. Wednesday night, 14 October 2026

The copy review had ended ninety minutes earlier and Gitashree Mahanta was still in the eighth-floor room on Lavelle Road in Bengaluru, because going home meant deciding something. On the whiteboard, in her own hand, were two lines from a Slack thread the previous afternoon. Rewrite cost us ₹24 lakh in four weeks. Under it: Rewrite saved us ₹23.7 lakh in four weeks. Both came from inside her own company, from the same window.

On Friday at 18:00 IST the code for release v4.33 froze. Whatever words were in that build would be on roughly six lakh phones by the last week of October, through Dhanteras and Diwali on 8 November. They were the labels on a loan application, forty-four error messages, nine empty states, and the thirty-eight strings of consent and Key Fact Statement text that the Reserve Bank's digital-lending framework and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act had made into regulated artefacts.

At 21:30 she had a call with Berlin, Toronto and Singapore (Figure B) — 18:00 for Gitesh Mondal, noon for Gyanendra Munshi, midnight for Gopesh Malakar. On Monday she owed Gunajit Medhi a recommendation for the board.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2022

Vayam Credit Technologies Private Limited was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by Gunajit Medhi, a payments engineer from Guwahati. It does not lend: it sources, services and collects, while the loans sit with Vaarahi Finserv Limited, an RBI-registered non-banking financial company. Tickets run from ₹5,000 to ₹60,000 over three to twelve months, repaid by UPI Autopay mandates, and Vayam earns 3.4 per cent of principal disbursed. In the year to 31 March 2026 it earned ₹28.6 crore, ₹4.3 crore of it from white-labelling its flow, and on 30 September 2026 it held ₹14.2 crore of cash against a net burn of ₹1.85 crore a month — 7.7 months.

In the week of 19 July 2022, racing a festive window, the team scoped a server-driven content layer at six weeks and cut it; strings went hard-coded into the Android build and the web flow, and the release shipped eleven days early. Four years on, a word cannot change without an app release: changes are batched into a train, rollout takes six days, and roughly a quarter of the base is a release behind. Hindi and Marathi came in 2024 from a vendor working off a spreadsheet of string IDs, with no reviewer who had seen the screens.

In March 2025 Vayam signed Vasl Benefits FZ-LLC of Dubai, a Gulf employee-benefits platform. Schedule C of that contract freezes sixty-one disclosure and consent strings, thirty-five of which share string IDs with the consumer app, so a change in Bengaluru is a change in Vasl's product. Vasl pays ₹1.92 crore a year — ₹1.92 crore of the ₹4.3 crore enterprise line, or nearly 45 per cent of it.

3. The industry

Small-ticket digital credit in India is crowded and watched: Navi, Fibe, KreditBee and moneyview compete for the same tier-two borrower. Since the Reserve Bank's digital-lending directions the words are part of the regulated surface — the Key Fact Statement must carry a findable annual percentage rate, and the borrower must see who is lending. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act and its rules require an itemised consent notice in clear language, available in English or any language of the Eighth Schedule, of which the Vayam app supports three.

Repayment runs on UPI Autopay, so a failed mandate is an NPCI event with a response code that must become a sentence a borrower can act on. Vayam's own peak is the opposite shape to the Gulf's: in the Dhanteras-to-Diwali fortnight of 2025 Vayam disbursed ₹41.6 crore against ₹18.1 crore in the fortnight before, 2.3 times as much.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In June 2026 compliance opened a work item: the KFS and consent screens needed rewriting for the current reading of the rules. Gitesh Mondal, hired from a Berlin fintech in February 2025 as the only content designer, argued that thirty-eight rewritten disclosure strings inside an app whose errors still said Transaction declined: code E-114 would give a compliant screen inside an illegible product. He proposed 180 strings across five surfaces (Exhibit 1). Gitashree approved it; nobody designed a measurement.

Release v4.31 reached the Play Store on Monday 7 September 2026 and every device six days later. Analytics then compared the two version cohorts over the four weeks from Monday 14 September to Sunday 11 October: Exhibit 2, which is not a randomised test.

Three things have since come to light, and Figure A places them. On Wednesday 16 September, two days into the window, Vaarahi raised its bureau-score cutoff for new-to-credit applicants from 680 to 700. On Tuesday 22 September customer success escalated a Hindi error string: the sentence for an insufficient-balance mandate failure had come back from the vendor reading khata rok di gayi hai — your account has been stopped. With no server-side override, and the vendor's corrected file arriving after the next freeze, it stayed in the field, mitigated by an outbound SMS from 24 September. On Saturday 3 October a new log line revealed the empty state — No dues. You're all clear. — rendering when the dues fetch failed, not only when dues were nil: 1,143 times to 964 users in nine days to 11 October, of whom 71 missed the instalment presented on Monday 5 October. What it did before 3 October is unknown.

5. The people

Gitashree Mahanta, VP Product, Bengaluru, owns the recommendation, needs a bridge-round story, and holds the rewrite right and the measurement negligent. Unsaid: she never defined success.

Gunajit Medhi, co-founder and CEO, wants one number for the board, not a seminar on method. Unsaid: he has told an investor the rewrite "cut support volumes".

Gopa Mitra, VP Growth, Bengaluru, carries the quarter's disbursals and wants the non-mandated strings reverted in v4.33. Unsaid: her Diwali campaign was shot on the old screenshots.

Gourab Moitra, principal engineer, Pune, owns the release train and prices the content layer at nine weeks for three engineers. Unsaid: he thinks the layer is the only honest answer, and his estimate kills it.

Gitesh Mondal, content designer, Berlin, wrote the rewrite and holds the funnel contaminated and the complaint mix evidential. Unsaid: he has never seen a Marathi screen, and signed off the Hindi file from a spreadsheet.

Gyanendra Munshi, senior data scientist, Toronto, holds that nothing in Exhibit 2 can be attributed to copy; he warned about cohorting in July and was overruled. Unsaid: he recomputed the funnel a week ago and said nothing.

Gopesh Malakar, head of customer success, Singapore, wants the copy kept and the broken strings fixed. His contract runs on 112 seats, 84 on minimum commitment. Unsaid: eleven agents work from old scripts.

Guncha Mridha, head of enterprise sales, Jersey City, will not have Vasl's 30 November Arabic milestone jeopardised. Unsaid: she has shown the rewritten screens to two Gulf prospects.
