7. Voices

"Hold the cohorts against each other and the rewrite cost us 3.50 points of entered-to-disbursed: on 1,42,800 journeys, 4,998 loans, ₹7.10 crore of principal at our ₹14,200 ticket, ₹24.1 lakh of revenue at our 3.4 per cent fee. Against which: put the old cohort's 4.40 contacts per thousand (Exhibit 3) across all 25,70,000 sessions and you expect 11,308; we had 10,378, so 930 avoided. The support contract is ₹2.64 crore, so ₹2,544 a contact and ₹23.7 lakh saved. We are risking Diwali over a rounding error."

Gopa Mitra, #growth-war-room, Tuesday 13 October, 16:41 IST

"Two things. The ₹2.64 crore is annual. Four weeks of it is ₹2.64 crore × 28/365, or ₹20.25 lakh; over 10,378 contacts that is ₹195 a contact, not ₹2,544, and the saving is ₹1.81 lakh — thirteen times smaller. And 84 of our 112 seats are on minimum commitment, so most of even that is not cash. Second, both of your numbers apply one cohort's rate to the other cohort's base. Hold the approval rate at the older cohort's 65.94 per cent, 65.935 unrounded, and keep the newer cohort's own later-stage rates: 1,04,386 submissions give 68,827 approvals, 53,737 acceptances, 45,060 disbursals — 31.55 per cent of 1,42,800, against 32.21. The gap is 0.66 of a point, not 3.50: 942 loans, ₹4.5 lakh. Copy is not free. Nobody here has measured it."

Gyanendra Munshi, same thread, 09:12 in Toronto (18:42 IST)

"Indore transcript, 29 September, borrower in Jhansi. He had ₹340 in the account, the mandate bounced, and the screen told him his account had been stopped. He borrowed ₹2,000 from a neighbour to release it. We have 694 of these."

Gopesh Malakar, email to Gitashree Mahanta, 12 October

"Two strings out of 180 were wrong, and both were translation failures, not writing failures. Fees and charges run 14.7 per thousand disbursals on the new copy against 24.8 on the old — the largest improvement in the table, and the row nobody quotes."

Gitesh Mondal, copy review, 15:00 in Berlin (18:30 IST)

"Everyone is arguing about which words go in the box. There is no box. Every option here is a freeze, a store date and six days of rollout — thirteen days from Friday to the last phone. Until copy leaves the APK we are deciding what the app will have said a fortnight ago."

Gourab Moitra, copy review, 14 October

"Any Schedule C change needs our legal sign-off, ten business days from receipt, and our platform is frozen from 1 November: a request reaching us on 15 October clears on 29 October. Our counsel will also not accept disclosure text that can change from a server without a new build — we must reproduce the exact screen a worker saw, by build number, for eight years."

Gulrez Mustafi, product director, Vasl Benefits, Dubai, 13 October, 17:00 Gulf time (18:30 IST)

8. The options as Gitashree sees them

A. Revert everything but the thirty-eight mandated strings. Gopa's option, and the only one her Diwali assets survive: it restores copy that has run four years, removes both broken strings and costs ₹3.6 lakh (Exhibit 6). It also reverts the fees-and-charges wording with the largest improvement in Exhibit 5, and touches fourteen Schedule C strings: Vasl's sign-off arrives on 29 October, six days after the build reaches the store and the same day rollout completes, so those fourteen cannot be in v4.33 as costed.

B. Keep the rewrite; fix the two broken strings. Cheapest, fastest, touches nothing in Schedule C. It also means telling the board the funnel number stands unexplained until a test the app cannot yet support.

C. New copy for new users, old copy for returning users. Two string tables behind a flag. It doubles the QA matrix, ships into Vasl's build too, and cannot reach devices before 12 November, inside the festive freeze. A borrower who reinstalls sees a different product from the one she repaid on.

D. Build the content layer and freeze copy until it exists. ₹37.0 lakh, above the delegation limit, and it displaces Vasl's Arabic milestone of 30 November: ₹46 lakh of milestone revenue, and a service credit of 8 per cent of ₹1.92 crore, or ₹15.36 lakh, if it slips past 15 December.

Each option is a decision about words. Around the third blank document Gitashree had noticed that the thirty-eight strings she could not revert were the thirty-eight the rules required, and that under all four the 32,500 journeys of Exhibit 4 on an unsupported language still read English.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Code freeze for v4.33 is Friday 16 October at 18:00 IST; the build reaches the Play Store on 23 October and every device by 29 October. The next train, v4.35, is 6 November, inside both Vayam's festive freeze and Vaarahi's change freeze of 1 to 12 November. Dussehra takes out most of the Bengaluru and Pune teams next week. The board meets on Monday 19 October behind the 30 September close: ₹14.2 crore of cash and 7.7 months of runway. Vaarahi will not relax the cutoff before January. And there is one content designer, in Berlin, at a fully-loaded ₹1.07 crore a year against ₹38 lakh for the same seniority in Bengaluru — 2.8 times — which Gopa has twice asked about.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the surfaces in Exhibit 1 could plausibly move a funnel at all?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 5 come from the same 10,378 records and point opposite ways. Which denominator belongs to which decision?
  3. Gyanendra's recomputation leaves a gap of 0.66 of a point. Is that a measurement of copy, of underwriting, or neither?
  4. Exhibit 4 offers no before-and-after by language and no rewritten strings for the 22.8 per cent of v4.31+ journeys on an unsupported language. What does that do to the claims in section 7?
  5. The 2022 decision to hard-code strings was defensible then. What would have had to be true for it to be reopened before June 2026?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October. What does Gitashree put in v4.33 before Friday's freeze, what does she ask the board for, and what does she say when Gunajit asks, in front of the board, whether the words helped or hurt?

At 21:18 IST she opened the repayment screen's string file and typed a sentence she thought a borrower in Jhansi could act on. Then she read it again and could not say whether it was better or newer.
exp20v2-ux.content:
Content Design and Microcopy

Are the words in the interface doing their job?

1. Six rupees of silence

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Indrajyoti Phukan, group product manager at Anubha Pay, opened a spreadsheet that his support lead had sent the night before. Anubha Pay is a Bengaluru UPI payments app; UPI, the Unified Payments Interface, is the real-time bank transfer system run by the National Payments Corporation of India. The spreadsheet covered September. Users had attempted payments that failed 1,80,000 times in the month. Every one of those users had seen the same screen: a red banner reading "Payment failed. Error 5003." and a single button, "Retry". Code 5003 was the system's catch-all for any failed payment.

Support had logged 10,800 contacts from those failed attempts, 6 per cent of 1,80,000. At an average handling cost of ₹62 a contact, that came to ₹6,69,600 for the month. What bothered Phukan was a line from one call transcript. A user in Guwahati, whose money had left her bank account but whose payment had not reached the merchant, had asked the agent: "Is Error 5003 the one where my money is gone?" The code said nothing of the kind. It covered every failure alike, and in the commonest case, a bank that had not answered in time, the money would return on its own.

Diwali fell on 8 November, and festival weeks brought a surge in payments. Before then Phukan had to decide whether to have his content designer, Ishanvi Purkayastha, spend three weeks rewriting the failure states, or to spend the time on a faster retry path. Iravan Pramanik, the engineering manager, preferred the second: wording could not repair a slow bank. Phukan suspected the words were already part of the failure, and wanted to test that with arithmetic rather than taste.

2. The idea

Content design is the practice of deciding what an interface should say, to whom, and in what order, so that a person can finish a task. Microcopy is its smallest unit: the button labels, field hints, error messages, confirmations and empty-state prompts that sit inside the screen. An empty state is what a screen shows when it has nothing to display yet, such as a transaction list for a new user. Together they make the claim in the module's learning objective: words are interface. For a user who cannot see the code, the label is the product.

The discipline has two roots. Jakob Nielsen's usability heuristics of 1994 already asked that error messages be expressed in plain language, state the problem precisely and suggest a solution. The modern practice then grew out of the United Kingdom's Government Digital Service in the early 2010s, where Sarah Richards and colleagues argued that government pages should be built from what users need to do, not from what departments wish to announce. Her 2017 book named the approach content design. Kinneret Yifrah later popularised the term microcopy, and Torrey Podmajersky's work on strategic writing for interfaces tied word choice to business goals.

The problem it addresses: engineers name things as the system sees them, and a code such as 5003 is faithful to the system. A user sees only a stuck task and a worry. Content design translates. The sentence Phukan could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: every message on a screen answers three questions the user is silently asking, namely what happened, what it means for me, and what do I do now.

3. How it actually works

Purkayastha, a former journalist from Kolkata, begins with a step practitioners often leave implicit: she writes nothing first. She lists the states a screen can be in. For a failed payment there are not one but four underlying causes, and the old banner collapsed all four into a single sentence. Writing better copy for one generic failure is impossible, because no single sentence is true of all four.

The second step is to ask, for each state, which of the three questions the user cannot answer alone. A user who typed a wrong UPI PIN already knows what happened and only needs reassurance that the attempt is safe to repeat. A user whose bank timed out knows nothing, and fears the worst. The third is to write in the order of the user's anxiety: "your money is safe" before "try again". The fourth is to match the action to the cause. "Retry" suits a wrong PIN and is wrong for a timeout, where retrying risks a second debit.

The rewrite is not cosmetic. The left screen holds one fact, that something failed. The right holds three, and it replaces the "Retry" button, a product decision as much as a writing one. You cannot write the right sentence until the product has decided what the right action is.

4. A worked example

Phukan asked Purkayastha to size the prize by cause. September's 1,80,000 failures split as follows, from the payments log: 54,000 bank timeouts, 63,000 wrong PINs, 36,000 insufficient balances and 27,000 daily-limit hits. The measure was completion within 24 hours: the share of failed attempts after which the same user paid the same merchant by any route. September gave the "Before" column. The "After" column is not data but Purkayastha's assumption, which Phukan marked as such on every slide.

CauseFailuresBefore: completionBefore: completedAfter (assumed): completionAfter: completed
Bank timeout54,00040%21,60055%29,700
Wrong PIN63,00070%44,10078%49,140
Insufficient balance36,00045%16,20060%21,600
Daily limit27,00025%6,75050%13,500
Total / average1,80,00049.25%88,65063.3%1,13,940

Completed = failures x completion rate. The blended rates in the last row are pooled: 88,650 / 1,80,000 = 49.25 per cent and 1,13,940 / 1,80,000 = 63.3 per cent, not the mean of the four rates. Failures are attempts, not unique users.

The gain is 1,13,940 minus 88,650, or 25,290 additional completed payments a month. Anubha Pay earns about ₹3.50 of net revenue per completed payment, so the revenue effect is 25,290 x 3.50 = ₹88,515, close to ₹0.89 lakh. The larger effect sits in support. If the contact rate falls from 6 to an assumed 4 per cent, contacts fall from 10,800 to 7,200, saving 3,600 x ₹62 = ₹2,23,200, about ₹2.23 lakh. Together that is ₹3,11,715 a month, about ₹3.12 lakh.

Now change one input. Suppose the timeout recovery does not rise to 55 per cent but only to 40 per cent, because a user told to wait simply gives up. The timeout row then completes 54,000 x 0.40 = 21,600, exactly where it was, and the completed total falls by 8,100 to 1,05,840. The gain shrinks from 25,290 to 17,190, a fall of 32 per cent, and revenue to 17,190 x 3.50 = ₹60,165. The conclusion survives, but the fall shows how much of the case rests on one unmeasured assumption. Phukan took this as a reason to test the timeout message first and, as his own judgement, not an arithmetic result, to pair it with Pramanik's faster retry path.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Clarity is not brevity

Short copy is not automatically clear copy. "Error 5003" is brief and tells the user nothing. The target is the fewest words that still answer the three questions.

Voice is not the same as clarity

Brand voice, the personality of the language, is what teams argue about first and need least. A playful "Oops!" suits a quiz, not a user who may have lost money. Tone must move with the user's state; vocabulary stays constant.

Consistency of terms carries more weight than variety

If three screens say "beneficiary", "payee" and "recipient", users will reasonably conclude they are three different things. A glossary of approved terms is among the cheapest assets a team can own.

Words cannot repair a broken flow

Better copy lifts completion where the user is able to act, and does little where the product offers no useful action; which rows qualify must be measured. If a message needs three sentences to apologise for a step, the step is the defect.

Translation is not localisation

Anubha Pay's users write in Assamese, Bengali, Hindi and English. A sentence translated word for word keeps its structure and loses its assurance, and string length can change enough to break a button. UX across languages and cultures takes this up.

What it cannot tell you

Craft cannot tell you whether a message works; only behaviour does. Before relying on a rewrite, ask what the user did next, what share of users saw this state, and how you would know if the new words made things worse.

6. Consumer, business and marketplace products

In a consumer app such as Anubha Pay, the reader is anxious, in motion and rarely trained; copy must work in a glance. In a business product, the reader is paid to be there, tolerates length, and expects vocabulary that matches their accounting terms. In a marketplace there are two audiences for one event. A payment failure is a buyer's worry and a seller's lost order, and the two messages must not contradict each other or leak information the other party should not see.

Scale changes the economics. In an early-stage company one person writes everything, and the winning habit is a single page of rules. In a large company strings multiply across teams, the risk shifts from poor writing to inconsistency, and the investment goes into a style guide, a glossary and a review step. Anubha Pay sits between the two: it has one content designer for roughly forty engineers, so her three weeks were not free.

7. Common mistakes

Writing after the design is frozen. The symptom is cramped buttons and a message bent around the layout. The misunderstanding is treating words as paint. The diagnostic is to ask in each design review whether the real strings are on the screen.

Mistaking the system's name for the user's. The symptom is support tickets that quote the code. The misunderstanding is that accuracy to the system equals clarity. Count how many of twenty recent tickets repeat the on-screen words.

One message for many causes. The symptom is a rate that does not move after a rewrite. The misunderstanding is that one cleverly worded sentence can fit four situations. The diagnostic is the table in section 4: split the failure by cause before you write a word.

Declaring victory on opinions. The symptom is a team celebrating that the new copy "reads better". The misunderstanding is that taste is evidence. The diagnostic is a holdout group that still sees the old text.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Phukan's decision would look like this. Purkayastha drafts the four messages in one week rather than three, beginning with the two largest causes, which together account for 1,17,000 of the 1,80,000 failures, or 65 per cent. Pramanik ships the new strings behind a switch so that a random half of users see the old banner. Phukan states beforehand which number decides the matter, completion within 24 hours, and what result would make him stop.

9. Closing

Phukan decided on 9 October to fund the rewrite in two stages, timeout and wrong-PIN messages first, and to ask Pramanik for the faster retry path in the same sprint, since the two efforts address different rows of the table. The A/B test, with half the traffic held on the old banner, was scheduled to begin on Monday 19 October. He would judge it on completion within 24 hours and contact rate together, not one alone, because a message that cut calls by hiding bad news would look like a win on the second measure and a failure on the first.

The natural next topic is designing for errors and recovery, which asks what the product should do, not only say, when things go wrong. UX across languages and cultures follows, because every claim made here about words is tested again once the words change language.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of the last message that confused you in a product you use daily: which of the three questions did it fail to answer? Second, if a copy change raised completion but also raised complaints a month later, which of the two would you trust, and what would you want to know before deciding?
case20v1-ux.content:
Tantu: The Words on the Failure Screen

A decision case on content design and microcopy

1. Opening

At 4:30 pm on Thursday 15 October 2026, Eeshita Laskar closed the door of a small meeting room on the third floor of Tantu's Bengaluru office and dialled two colleagues in. In Berlin it was one in the afternoon; in Singapore, seven in the evening. Laskar, Tantu's head of product, had one question for them: which version of a single error message should reach customers before Diwali?

The message appears when a customer's UPI AutoPay request is not approved. Tantu's next app release was due to ship on Thursday 22 October and the engineering freeze fell the next day. Diwali was on Sunday 8 November. Laskar had to tell engineering by Monday 19 October which strings to put in the build, in which languages, because whatever missed this train would wait until after the festival.

2. Company background

Tantu, founded in Bengaluru in 2021, lets households set up automatic payments for school fees, insurance premiums, society maintenance and electricity bills. It earned ₹41 crore in the year to March 2026 from small fees on each mandate and from partner commissions, and it competes for the same customers as PhonePe, Google Pay, Paytm and CRED, all of which now offer their own recurring-payment features.

The set-up runs on UPI AutoPay, the NPCI mechanism under which a customer approves a standing instruction inside their own bank or UPI app. Tantu controls the screens before and after that approval, but not the approval itself. Its users read the app in five languages: English, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and Marathi. Each mandate that completes is worth, on Tantu's finance team's estimate, ₹480 in net revenue in its first year.

3. The situation

For two weeks, 14 to 27 September, Tantu's analysts followed every mandate set-up. Exhibit 1 shows what happened. Of 80,000 customers who began, 70,000 reached the bank's approval step and 60,000 were approved first time. The other 10,000 saw the failure screen, which read: "Mandate registration failed (ERR_U16). Please try again later." Only 24 per cent retried at once. Thirty per cent contacted support, and 46 per cent left.

Eshani Lekharu, who runs customer success from Singapore, had read a sample of the tickets. Her summary was blunt: customers did not know whether money had left their accounts, did not know whose fault it was, and did not know what to do next.

Evangeline Lodh, the senior content designer in Berlin, had drafted a replacement in August. It said what had happened, that no money had moved, and the one action the customer should take. From 28 September to 11 October it ran as a 50/50 test, but only among English-interface users. Exhibit 2 gives the result: more customers retried, fewer phoned, and abandonment barely moved. In effect the new words moved people from the helpline to the screen. Exhibit 3 shows the old and new text side by side.

The 4,000 test screens were every English-interface failure in the fortnight, 40 per cent of Exhibit 1's 10,000. The test left a hole. English is 40 per cent of Tantu's failure screens. Hindi is 30 per cent. No Hindi, Bengali, Tamil or Marathi version of the new copy had been tested, or yet written.

4. The people

  • Eeshita Laskar, head of product, Bengaluru. Owns the decision and the festival-season number. She wants the largest recovery she can defend.
  • Evangeline Lodh, senior content designer, Berlin. Wants every language written by a native content designer, not translated. She argues that a message that sounds foreign loses trust faster than a code does. Her day ends at 6 pm, which is 9:30 pm in Bengaluru until Berlin changes its clocks on 25 October.
  • Ekanth Lahon, engineering manager, Pune. Wants fewer strings in the build. Each language needs its own layout check and the freeze is fixed.
  • Eshani Lekharu, customer success lead, Singapore. Wants support contacts down before the festival peak, when her team's hold times lengthen.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets out the baseline; the 10,000 who never reached the bank are a separate problem.

Exhibit 2: English-interface test (last row modelled), 28 September to 11 October 2026 (2,000 failure screens per arm)

The 60 and 40 per cent completion rates are the Exhibit 1 rates, assumed unchanged by the new text. Value per failure screen: 44 extra completions × ₹480, plus 160 fewer contacts × ₹60, is ₹30,720 across 2,000 screens, or ₹15.36 a screen.

Exhibit 3: Old and new text on the failure screen (English)

The Diwali fortnight raises the stakes. Last year's equivalent fortnight ran well above normal, and Tantu's planners expect 1,68,000 set-up starts from 26 October to 8 November, which is 2.1 times a normal fortnight's 80,000. At 12.5 per cent, that is 21,000 failure screens. Exhibit 4 prices each option on those screens.

Exhibit 4: Languages and what each option earns in the festival fortnight, 26 October to 8 November 2026

Assumes the English effect holds in every language and that the failure rate is the same in each. Each cell is rounded to two decimals of a lakh. At full coverage the copy is worth ₹1.54 lakh in a normal fortnight (10,000 screens × ₹15.36).

Figure 1: Timeline at 20 pixels a day, each marker at the start of its day. The shaded band covers 26 October to 8 November inclusive.

6. The options

Option 1: ship the tested English copy alone on 22 October. It is proven, cheap at ₹0.6 lakh, and adds only English strings to Pune's build. It earns ₹1.29 lakh in the fortnight, a net of ₹0.69 lakh. But 60 per cent of failure screens would still show ERR_U16.

Option 2: hold everything and write all five languages natively, shipping Monday 16 November. This is Lodh's preference. It costs ₹4.5 lakh and earns nothing in the festival fortnight, but it gives every language the same quality. Its cost is the peak itself: the fortnight's ₹3.23 lakh is forgone.

Option 3: ship English and Hindi on 22 October, and queue the rest. Together they cover 70 per cent of screens and ₹2.26 lakh of value. Hindi would be written by Lodh with two Hindi-speaking agents from Lekharu's team reviewing, at a combined cost of ₹1.0 lakh for both languages (₹0.6 lakh English, ₹0.4 lakh Hindi). Hindi is untested, so a rollback trigger would be set before launch. Bengali, Tamil and Marathi follow after Diwali.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, what job were the old words failing to do, and what job did the new words do? Did they reduce abandonment?
  2. Which of Exhibit 4's figures rest on a tested result, and which on an assumption? How would you check the assumption for Hindi?
  3. Lodh argues that translation cannot carry trust. What evidence on this page supports or weakens her view?
  4. Which option would you take to Lodh, Lahon and Lekharu on Monday 19 October, and what would make you reverse it?

8. A note for the learner

Content design treats words as part of the interface, to be tested like any other control. The test question is whether the words do their job: say what happened, say what it means for the customer, say what to do next. Exhibit 2 shows words doing that job in English, and also shows their limit. Better text turned a phone call into a retry, but abandonment only moved from 920 to 900. Words repair confusion; they do not repair a bank approval that never arrives.

One defensible path is Option 3, with a condition. Option 1 forgoes ₹0.97 lakh of Hindi value for an extra ₹0.4 lakh of cost, and Option 2 gives up the whole fortnight. Option 3 nets ₹1.26 lakh (₹2.26 lakh less ₹1.0 lakh), the highest of the three in the window, before the later three languages, whose cost is not yet estimated. The risk is that Hindi is untested, so Laskar should state a rollback rule in advance: if the first 1,000 Hindi failure screens show fewer than 24 per cent retrying or more than 46 per cent abandoning (the old text's all-language rates), revert to the old text. She should then commission Lodh's native versions of the remaining three languages for November.

A strong answer names what the case cannot prove: that English results carry over to Hindi, and that festival-season customers behave as September's did.

Content design and microcopy

Words are interface: labels, errors, empty states — and the question that runs under all of them is whether a sentence is doing work the rest of the product failed to do.

1. Two decisions, four days apart

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, in a sixth-floor room off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru, Jonaki Roy had two proposals on the table and room for one. Roy is senior product manager for recurring investments at Bikalp Invest, a direct mutual-fund platform with 31.4 lakh registered accounts and 8.7 lakh of them carrying a live NACH auto-debit mandate. In an average week over the thirteen weeks to Sunday 4 October, 18,400 distinct account holders — about 2.1 per cent of the mandate base — saw a screen saying their monthly instalment had not gone through. Of those, 31.0 per cent had a successful mandate within 72 hours.

The growth lead wanted a two-week test of eleven wordings of that screen before the November systematic-investment push. Jharna Raychaudhuri, who leads content design, wanted something less glamorous: rewrite twenty-three error strings as a quality change, and before that, get engineering to split one failure code into four, because at present the screen cannot truthfully say why the debit failed. “We are being asked to write eleven sentences,” Raychaudhuri said, “about a state we cannot see.”

In Pune, on Thursday 8 October, Jyotirmoy Rajkhowa faced the same topic wearing enterprise clothes. Rajkhowa is director of product at Barnadi Systems, whose claims console is used by eleven general and health insurers across 640 named adjuster seats. In the quarter to 30 September 2026 the console took 1,21,000 claim submissions, of which 5,929 — 4.9 per cent — were returned to the submitter for correction. A Chennai insurer's claims head wanted one field renamed platform-wide; another tenant had already configured that same label to mean something else, for reasons its compliance officer traced to IRDAI intimation timelines. Rajkhowa's decision was not about wording. It was whether a string belongs to the platform or to the tenant.

2. The idea, and the six houses that disagree about it

Content design is the discipline of deciding what a user needs to be told, in what order, in what words, and — the part that distinguishes it from writing — whether telling them is the right fix at all. Microcopy is its smallest unit: the labels, button text, hint text, error messages, empty states, confirmations and system-status lines that sit inside the interface rather than around it. The working definition is functional, not literary: a string is correct when a competent reader, mid-task, can predict what happens next if they act on it.

The intellectual history has four tributaries. Readability measurement arrives first — Rudolf Flesch's reading-ease yardstick in 1948, Ernest Gowers writing Plain Words for British civil servants the same year and The Complete Plain Words in 1954 — bringing the idea that prose difficulty is measurable. Linguistic pragmatics arrives next: H. P. Grice's maxims of conversation, published in 1975, give us the vocabulary for why a message that is true but uninformative still fails. Usability engineering absorbs both — “speak the user's language” and “help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors” are two of Jakob Nielsen's ten heuristics from 1994. Finally, content strategy becomes an owned function: Kristina Halvorson's Content Strategy for the Web in 2009, then the work Sarah Richards and colleagues did at GOV.UK from the early 2010s, which contributed the field's sharpest claim — that the output of content design is often less content, or a different flow, not better sentences.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Plain language (Flesch, Gowers, plain-writing statutes)Ambiguity is a defect; reading cost is measurable.That warmth justifies an extra clause.
Content design (GOV.UK lineage)If a label needs a tooltip, the label is wrong; the unit of work is the task.That copy is a layer applied after the design is settled.
Voice and brand (voice-and-tone guides, 2010s)Interface words are where a product earns affection and is remembered.That a house style should flatten register across all states.
Pragmatics and conversation design (Grice; media-equation research)A message is a speech act; errors are a repair sequence.That shorter is automatically better.
Experimentalist growthNothing counts until it moves a metric at detectable scale.That craft judgement substitutes for measurement.
Regulatory and legalSome words are a contract and are mandated verbatim.That the disclosure should be simplified to fit the layout.

The six positions a practitioner will meet. The first four argue about what good words are; the last two argue about what authorises the choice.

The problem the discipline was invented to solve is not bad writing. It is that a product's internal model of the world — its states, its objects, its names for them — leaks into the interface through words, and users must act on that model without access to it. Microcopy is the translation layer. Which is why the most useful thing it does is diagnostic: a sentence that is hard to write usually means the thing behind it is badly designed.

3. Mechanics: how this is actually done

Expert practice starts not from screens but from an inventory. Raychaudhuri's team keeps Bikalp's 2,180 user-visible strings in one file, each tagged by function — label, hint, error, empty state, confirmation, system status, legal — and by concept rather than screen. The tagging is the work: it surfaces duplicates, the same string used in two meanings, and the ratio of explanatory to control strings over time.

For errors, the template experts converge on has three slots: what happened, in the user's terms; why, only if the cause changes what to do; and the next action, as one verb matching a control visible on the screen. The second slot is where competence shows: explaining a cause the user cannot act on differently is noise dressed as transparency.

That backwards arrow is the second-order effect practitioners underrate. Bikalp's twenty-three error strings are written against one code. Splitting it into four — insufficient balance, mandate expired, mandate revoked at the bank, bank unreachable — is an engineering change costed at eleven days, and the precondition for three of the four sentences anyone wants to write. Content design at this level generates observability tickets.

The quantitative treatment is thinner than the field pretends, with one exception: the power arithmetic for copy experiments. For a two-arm test of a binary outcome at 5 per cent two-sided significance and 80 per cent power, the sample needed per arm is approximately 16 × p(1 − p) / δ², where the 16 stands in for twice the squared sum of the two critical values and δ is the absolute lift you want to detect. Bikalp's baseline recovery rate is 31.0 per cent, so p(1 − p) = 0.31 × 0.69 = 0.2139, and 16 × 0.2139 = 3.4224. To detect one percentage point, δ² = 0.0001 and 3.4224 / 0.0001 = 34,224 users per arm.

Absolute lift to detectUsers per armBoth armsWeeks at 18,400/week

Each row is 3.4224 / δ² per arm, doubled, then divided by the 18,400 account holders who see the error in an average week. Denominator note: 18,400 is distinct users in a week, measured over the thirteen weeks to 4 October 2026, and the outcome is one successful mandate within 72 hours of the first failure in that week.

4. The conditions, stated so they can fail

Four claims decide whether microcopy is high-leverage here, and each can be tested. First: the next action is ambiguous from the controls alone. True for Bikalp's failed-debit screen, where four causes imply three different next steps; largely false for its one-tap SIP pause, where the control is self-describing. Second: the system's states are distinguishable. False at Bikalp today, which is why the honest first move is instrumentation; true at Barnadi, whose validation engine returns 31 distinct rejection reasons. Third: misreading costs money, time or a right — true in both cases. Fourth: the words are not already fixed. Bikalp's scheme-risk line is SEBI-mandated wording and not a design surface; its surrounding explanation is.

The idea becomes actively misleading when copy is used as spackle. A sentence that successfully explains a confusing flow has removed the pressure to fix it, in a way that looks like craft. The expert reflex is counterfactual: what would this screen have to look like for the sentence to be unnecessary? If the answer is cheap, write the ticket instead.

5. Hard edges, and what mature companies really do

Multi-tenant enterprise software is where these seams bite hardest, and Rajkhowa stands in it. When a label is tenant-configurable, the platform loses the ability to reason about its own vocabulary: documentation, support macros, training material and the validation messages all drift per tenant. When it is not, the platform overrides a term of art that legitimately differs between a health insurer and a motor insurer. What mature firms actually do is neither pole. They keep a small set of concepts owned centrally, one named owner each, and permit tenant aliases only where a glossary records the mapping — which is why such firms build a glossary before they write a style guide.

Two-sided products create a different seam: the same string is read by parties with opposed interests. “Order cancelled” is consolation to one side and lost income to the other, and a single string cannot carry both registers. Hardware adds physical limits and slow updates. Roy's previous employer, Beltola Freight, shipped driver handhelds with a two-line, twenty-character display — a forty-character budget, into which “Delivery not saved.” fits on the first line at nineteen characters and “Scan again.” on the second at eleven. Firmware shipped quarterly, so a wrong word lived in the field for months.

AI-native features move the problem again, because the output is non-deterministic. The copy that matters is no longer the label on the answer but the frame around it: what the feature was given, how confident it is permitted to sound, and the repair path when it is wrong. Raychaudhuri's position on Bikalp's fund-explainer assistant is that hedging without a repair control is worse than no hedge: it transfers risk to the user and offers nothing to do about it.

6. Nine distinctions that separate the expert

The tooltip as confession. A tooltip explaining a label is an admission the label failed. The tell is tooltip density rising release over release while support contacts stay flat: nobody complains, because users learn to ignore them.

Causes only earn words when they change actions. The obvious reading is that transparency is a virtue. The tell is an error whose middle clause names an internal system. If two causes imply the same next step, merging them is more honest.

Message specificity is capped by code cardinality. Experts ask in design review how many distinct failures the system can report. Three sentences on one code means two are guesses that will eventually be shown to the wrong person.

Empty states are the modal first experience. They look rare because they are transient, but nearly every new account passes through them, so their audience has the least context. The tell is empty-state copy in the bare imperative with no sample content and no statement of what will appear here.

Choice pairs must expose cost asymmetry. Two buttons are not two options but a framing. The tell is a dismissal label cheaper to read than the action it declines, in a decision where declining is the costlier path.

Register beats voice. Consistency of personality matters less than appropriateness at the moment of reading; research on how people respond to machines as social actors predicts that cheerfulness on a money-lost screen reads as indifference. The tell is a brand voice that survives intact into the failure states.

Reading level is a constraint, not the objective. A readability score on an eleven-word button is numerically meaningless. Experts test comprehension of the decision: show the screen, hide it, ask what happens next and what it costs.

Translation is an unusually cheap specification review. A translator's question list is a defect list. Jayatri Routh, who reviews Bikalp's strings from Berlin — three and a half hours behind Indian time until the European clocks change on 25 October, so her 7:00 pm call is 3:30 pm for her — routinely returns strings whose meaning depends on their position on screen. Those strings were always ambiguous; English merely hid it.

Legal review is routing, not negotiation. The amateur argues adjectives with counsel. The expert asks which words are mandated verbatim, which are mandated in substance, and which are the product's own — three different problems. The tell is a disclosure block that grows every release and that nobody can attribute.

7. Across product types and stages

The error template does not change across consumer, B2B and enterprise, and that should be said plainly. What changes is accountability. An enterprise user acts on behalf of a third party and will later be audited, so the words must name the record and the field, and warmth is at best irrelevant. Platforms and marketplaces add the two-sided register problem. Hardware adds character budgets and quarterly firmware. AI products shift the weight from labelling to framing and repair.

Stage changes the economics rather than the craft. At seed stage a string is nearly free to change: write fast and revise on contact. At Bikalp's stage, 2,180 strings shipped in eight languages are 17,440 translated strings, and a single label change carries eight translations plus one legal review. That multiplier, not taste, is why mature organisations push vocabulary decisions into a design system with named owners.

8. Three worked examples

The relabelling that worked, and the claim it cannot support

Barnadi's return-reason breakdown for the quarter to 30 September 2026 is the quarter's outcome rather than the intervention's basis — the relabel had already shipped on 1 September, so for the two pilot tenants the quarter carries one post-relabel month. Rajkhowa used it to size the rollout, not to justify the pilot.

Base: the 5,929 submissions returned for correction out of 1,21,000 received in the quarter, which is 4.9 per cent. Shares are of returns, not of submissions, and are rounded to one decimal.

At a mean handling time of 26 minutes per return, measured across 40 sampled returns, the 2,604 date-field returns consumed 67,704 minutes, or 1,128.4 hours. At an assumed loaded cost of ₹480 an hour that is ₹5,41,632 — about ₹5.42 lakh — in one quarter, or ₹21.7 lakh if the same quarterly rate held for four quarters. Barnadi shipped a relabel to two tenants on Tuesday 1 September 2026: two fields renamed, with an inline hint naming the event rather than the date. In the four weeks to Sunday 30 August those tenants submitted 5,840 claims with 128 date-field returns, a rate of 2.19 per cent; in the four weeks to Sunday 4 October they submitted 6,120 claims with 71 such returns, 1.16 per cent. That is a fall of 1.03 percentage points, a relative reduction of 47 per cent. It is not a randomised comparison: the windows sit either side of the monsoon claims peak and the two tenants volunteered. Rajkhowa's own summary called the result directional.

The experiment that should not be run

Roy's second example sits on her own table. Eleven variants against one control, at 18,400 users a week, with a plausible true effect on 72-hour recovery of about one percentage point, is not an experiment; it is a lottery with twelve tickets. The power table says two arms need 3.7 weeks for a one-point effect, and eleven comparisons against a shared control inflate the false-positive risk unless the threshold is tightened, which raises the sample again. The expert move is to shrink the question: one variant, one error, one pre-registered outcome, a holdout long enough to matter.

The rewrite that moved the metric and broke the product

In March 2026 Bikalp softened its nominee prompt. In the six weeks to Sunday 8 March, 31,270 of the 48,700 accounts reaching that step added a nominee: 64.2 per cent. In the six weeks to Sunday 26 April, after the change, 21,900 of 52,400 did: 41.8 per cent. The change nevertheless passed its own test, because the metric chosen was activation — a first instalment within fourteen days, measured fourteen days after each cohort closed, on 22 March and 10 May, so both figures are mature — which rose from 18,214 of 48,700, or 37.4 per cent, to 20,488 of 52,400, or 39.1 per cent. The 5 May revision reached only accounts arriving after both cohorts had passed the step. A faster, friendlier flow produced more investors and fewer protected ones. The recovery, on 5 May, restored a consequence sentence and returned the decline to a text link that asked for a reason; in the six weeks to Sunday 21 June, 32,450 of 55,100 accounts added a nominee, 58.9 per cent — better than the trough and still 5.3 points below the original. The lesson Roy draws is not that friendly copy is bad, but that the surrogate was chosen for convenience and no reviewer had asked which metric would get worse if the copy worked.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

  • Copy as spackle. Early sign: explanatory strings growing faster than control strings. Diagnostic: what would make this sentence unnecessary? Caught late, the rewrite arrives bundled with unbudgeted navigation surgery.
  • Undifferentiated errors. Early sign: one failure code, several messages. Diagnostic: can our logs distinguish the causes we claim to explain? Caught late, support cannot triage.
  • Register collapse. Early sign: the welcome screen's tone surviving onto the money-lost screen. Diagnostic: read it aloud to someone who has just lost ₹4,000.
  • Convenient surrogates. Early sign: a copy test whose metric is the one most easily moved. Diagnostic: which of our measures would get worse if this worked?
  • String-identifier drift. Early sign: one identifier used in two meanings. Diagnostic: is this string owned by a screen or by a concept? Caught late, the fix is a retranslation across every locale.
  • Translation last. Early sign: translator questions arriving after code freeze. Diagnostic: could this string be translated without a screenshot?

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The experimentalist position. Copy claims should be held to the same evidential standard as anything else, and large-sample tests in search and commerce have shown wording changes moving real revenue. For this to be wrong, the value of microcopy would have to concentrate in states that are rare per user but costly per event — disputes, failures, cancellations — where the population is too small to power the test being proposed and absence of evidence is a sampling artefact. Bikalp's error screen is that case for an eleven-arm design, though not for a two-arm one.

The standards position. Vocabulary and patterns should be centralised, because the dominant cost is inconsistency and rework, and because plain, uniform language is what makes a service usable by people under stress or with assistive technology. For this to be wrong, register differentiation would have to carry real, durable value in discretionary consumer products — in which case a house style is a tax levied on the teams closest to the user.

The voice position. Words are where a product becomes a character users choose; the effects are slow, show up in preference and word of mouth, and are invisible to any two-week test. For this to be wrong, measured register mismatch would have to damage trust precisely at the high-stakes moments, which would make voice a liability rather than an asset where it matters most. Nobody has settled this: the two bodies of evidence sit on different time horizons and have never been compared like for like.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this reads the string file before the mockups and keeps a list of states rather than screens. They write the error path before the happy path, because the error path is where the product's model is tested. They ask in design review how many failure codes exist, and will say when a test cannot be powered. They distinguish the three kinds of words in a disclosure — mandated verbatim, mandated in substance, and theirs — without calling counsel.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Tuesday 13 October 2026 Roy declined the eleven-variant test. She approved the eleven-day code-splitting work, the rewrite of all twenty-three strings as a quality change measured on 72-hour recovery with no causal claim attached, and — salvaged from the growth lead's proposal — one pre-registered two-arm test on the highest-volume error alone, which being a fraction of the 18,400 must run well beyond 3.7 weeks to detect one percentage point. Her stated reason: she could not buy evidence at the resolution the growth plan assumed, and preferred to say so before the push.

On Friday 9 October Rajkhowa refused the platform-wide rename. He moved both date fields into a central glossary with one named owner, Jahnabi Rajbongshi, permitted tenant aliases only where the mapping is recorded, and extended the relabel to the remaining nine insurers on a staggered schedule so that each tenant is its own pre-and-post comparison. He also recorded in the rollout note that the pilot's 47 per cent relative reduction is not a causal estimate.

  1. Roy spends eleven engineering days to make three sentences writable. Defend that to a growth lead holding a competing feature with a measurable two-week return.
  2. Barnadi's pilot is confounded and Rajkhowa rolled it out anyway. Was that right, and what would have changed your mind?
  3. The nominee rewrite improved activation and reduced nominee coverage. Which metric should have held veto power, and who should have held it?

13. Going deeper

  • UX fundamentals for PMs — the grammar words obey too; without it, critique collapses into taste.
  • Designing for errors and recovery — the direct sequel: this page's backwards arrow is that topic's subject.
  • UX across languages and cultures — where translation-as-specification becomes a programme.
  • Usability heuristics — the 1994 list that made “speak the user's language” auditable.
  • Information architecture and navigation — names are architecture; label fights are often IA fights.
  • User flows and task analysis — supplies the boundaries that fix what a string must say.
  • Usability testing — the comprehension test readability scores cannot replace.
  • Design systems and components — where a label becomes platform vocabulary, for good or ill.
  • Accessible and inclusive design — screen-reader order and link text make microcopy an access question.
